question: In recommendation systems, how are new methods that optimize diversity typically evaluated?

sections.title: Report
sections.text:
# Evaluating Diversity in Recommender Systems: Methods and Metrics


## Introduction



Recommender systems have traditionally been evaluated on accuracy (e.g. rating prediction error or click-through rates), but accuracy alone is not sufficient to ensure a satisfying user experience [files.grouplens.org][2]. Increasingly, researchers recognize the importance of *beyond-accuracy* objectives such as diversity, novelty, serendipity, and coverage, which can significantly impact user satisfaction and engagement [3][4]. Diverse recommendations help prevent over-specialization (the “filter bubble” effect) and encourage user discovery of new content [5][3]. For example, a recommendation list composed of very similar items (e.g. all from the same genre or by the same author) may appear monotonic and limit the user’s ability to explore the item catalog [5]. New recommendation approaches have been proposed to explicitly promote diversity, and rigorous evaluation methods are needed to assess their effectiveness. This report surveys how diversity-enhancing recommenders are typically evaluated, covering offline metrics, online experiments, common benchmark datasets, comparisons to traditional algorithms, and the challenges in measuring diversity. The language and structure are formal and precise, suitable for a graduate-level technical audience.


## Offline Evaluation Methods and Metrics



Offline evaluation involves measuring diversity-related metrics on historical datasets (with known user-item interactions) to quantify the *diversity* of recommendations without live user feedback [6]. Common metrics include **intra-list diversity**, **novelty**, **serendipity**, and **coverage**, among others [[7]([[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)the%20paper%20reflect%20the%20main)][[8]([[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)14%2C31%2C55%5D.)]. These metrics are computed over the recommendation lists generated for users in a test set. Crucially, they complement traditional accuracy metrics (like precision or NDCG) to capture qualities beyond accuracy. Below we summarize the key diversity metrics and how they are evaluated offline:


* **Intra-list Diversity (ILD):** This metric assesses the diversity *within* a single recommendation list (for an individual user). ILD is typically defined as the average dissimilarity among all pairs of items in the list [9][10]. A common formulation uses an item similarity function (based on item features or metadata) and computes 1 minus the average pairwise similarity of items in the recommendation set [11][10]. Lower intra-list *similarity* (or higher dissimilarity) means a more varied list. For example, if a user’s top-5 movie recommendations span different genres or themes, the ILD will be high, whereas five very similar romance movies would yield a low ILD (indicating poor diversity). The concept of ILD was popularized by Ziegler et al. (2005) in their topic diversification approach [11], and it has since become a standard way to quantify how diverse a single recommendation slate is. ILD does not depend on the order of items and can be tailored with different similarity measures depending on the domain [12].
* **Novelty:** Novelty measures how “new” or unexpected the recommended items are to the user. In practice, novelty is often quantified by the popularity of items: recommending less popular, long-tail items is presumed to increase novelty [13]. One simple metric is the average or proportion of recommended items that a user has likely never seen before. For instance, a recommender can be evaluated by the fraction of its recommendations that are *not* among the globally most popular items (since popular items are assumed to be known by many users) [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. Vargas and Castells (2011) introduced popularity-based novelty metrics, where an item’s novelty is inversely related to its popularity (e.g., using the inverse frequency of an item in the user community) [13]. A high novelty score means the system is retrieving items from the long tail of the catalog, thus giving users fresh content beyond their usual mainstream choices. However, assessing novelty requires some assumption about a user’s prior knowledge; offline, this is usually approximated by excluding any item the user interacted with in training data or by using popularity as a proxy for familiarity [15].
* **Serendipity:** Serendipity goes one step further than novelty by requiring recommendations to be both *unexpected* to the user and *useful or interesting* [16]. A serendipitous recommendation is a pleasant surprise – an item that the user is not likely to have found by themselves, yet ends up appreciating. Capturing serendipity in metrics is challenging because it involves modeling user surprise. Offline serendipity metrics typically combine an unexpectedness component (the recommendation is dissimilar to the user’s past preferences or profile) with a relevance component (the item is actually liked by the user) [16][[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=)utility%2C%20novelty%2C%20or%20serendipity%20of,]. For example, one formula defines serendipity for a user’s recommendation list as the proportion of recommended items that are *unexpected* (not similar to anything the user has already consumed) and also *relevant* to the user (the user would rate them positively) [16]. Unexpectedness can be operationalized by distance from the user’s profile or from the user’s typical item genre, while relevance is often proxied by whether the item is actually in the test hold-out set of things the user liked [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. Because of the difficulty of mathematically describing “surprise,” serendipity metrics are considered rough approximations [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. They often require domain knowledge or additional data (to determine what a user would find obvious vs. unexpected), making offline evaluation of serendipity complex.
* **Coverage (Aggregate Diversity):** *Coverage* measures how well the recommender spreads its suggestions across the whole item catalog [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. Whereas intra-list diversity is about variety within a single list, coverage is about variety *across all users*. One definition of item coverage is the fraction of distinct items in the catalog that are ever recommended to any user [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. A higher coverage means the algorithm is utilizing more of the item space instead of recommending the same popular items over and over. Researchers also use related measures like the **Gini index** or **Shannon entropy** of the distribution of recommended items to quantify aggregate diversity [[7]([[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)the%20paper%20reflect%20the%20main)][[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)of%20recommended%20items%20across%20all]. These metrics capture how evenly recommendations are spread over items: a low Gini (or high entropy) indicates that recommendations are not dominated by a small set of popular items [[7]([[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)the%20paper%20reflect%20the%20main)]. Another metric, **catalog coverage at K**, looks at the percentage of the catalog included in the top-K recommendations for all users. Furthermore, Kaminskas and Bridge (2016) discuss metrics like **Maximal Recall (MaxFreq@k)** – the proportion of recommendations taken up by the single most-recommended item – which should be low for a diverse system [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)of%20recommended%20items%20across%20all]. In summary, coverage-based evaluation checks if a diversity-enhancing method succeeds in recommending a broad array of items (including niche items) to the user base [[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=)match%20at%20L551%20,].



Offline evaluations of diversity-aware recommenders typically report a mix of accuracy metrics *and* the above diversity metrics [23]. This allows researchers to assess the trade-off between accuracy and diversity. For example, a study might report that a diversification algorithm slightly decreases precision@10 but significantly improves ILD and catalog coverage relative to a standard top-N recommender [files.grouplens.org][23]. Such offline metrics are computed using test datasets with known user preferences (often using a train/test split or cross-validation on historical data). While offline results cannot prove that users will prefer the recommendations, they are an essential first step for comparing algorithms under controlled conditions. A large number of research papers rely on these objective metrics to quantify diversity improvements before moving to user-facing tests [6].


## Online Evaluation Methods



Offline metrics, while convenient, are proxies that may not capture the true utility of diversity to users. Therefore, new diversity-optimizing methods are also evaluated through *online* methods that involve user interaction or simulation of real usage. The primary online evaluation techniques include **user studies** (controlled experiments with human subjects) and **A/B tests or field trials** (deployments in live systems with different algorithm variants) https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=systems%2C%20and%20judge%20the%20value,rate%20the%20recommendations%2C%20and%20the)] https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=offline%20evaluations%20sometimes%20contradict%20results,are%20probably%20not%20suitable%20to)]. These methods focus on user-centered outcomes such as satisfaction, engagement, and behavioral signals:


* **User Studies (Controlled Experiments):** In a user study, researchers present real users with recommendations (often comparing a diversity-optimized system against a baseline) and collect feedback. This can be done in a lab setting or as a "live" study in an online platform. Participants may be asked to rate the recommendation lists on various aspects – for example, their overall satisfaction, the perceived diversity of the list, the novelty of items, or how well the list matches their interests https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=receive%20recom%02mendations%20generated%20by%20different,experts%20%5B3%5D.%20A)]. By explicitly asking users, one can gauge subjective qualities like *perceived diversity*: do users notice a broader range of content, and do they find that valuable? Prior work has indeed incorporated such questions; for instance, one study had users rate how novel or “unexpected” the recommendations were https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=receive%20recom%02mendations%20generated%20by%20different,experts%20%5B3%5D.%20A)]. Qualitative feedback can also be gathered (e.g. open-ended questions about what users liked or disliked about the recommendations), although quantitative ratings are more common in recommender evaluations https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=receive%20recom%02mendations%20generated%20by%20different,experts%20%5B3%5D.%20A)]. Notably, several user studies have found that increasing diversity can improve user satisfaction up to a point, but if diversity comes at too high a cost to relevance, users may become frustrated [files.grouplens.org][28]. User studies help evaluate the *perceived* effectiveness of diversity enhancements, capturing factors like serendipity that are hard to measure offline. For example, Ekstrand et al. (2014) and Willemsen et al. (2016) conducted user experiments to see how diversifying recommendations affects users’ perceived accuracy and satisfaction [29]. These studies revealed nuanced interactions – users do appreciate diversity, but only when the recommendations remain relevant and not too “out of left field.” Because diversity is somewhat subjective, such studies are invaluable for validating that an algorithm’s improvements on novelty or serendipity metrics actually translate into a better user experience [29].
* **A/B Testing and Behavioral Metrics:** In industry settings and large-scale research prototypes, the ultimate test of a new recommender method is often an online A/B test (also called a controlled experiment). In an A/B test, a portion of live users is randomly assigned to a new algorithm (treatment group) while others remain on the existing algorithm (control group). The experiment runs for a period of time, and user behavior is tracked to compare the two groups [30]. The key metrics could include **click-through rate (CTR)** – the fraction of recommended items that users click on – as well as downstream metrics like conversion rate (purchases or other target actions), time spent on site, number of distinct items consumed, etc. For example, acceptance of recommendations in a live system might be measured by CTR: if out of 10,000 recommended items, 120 are clicked, that yields a CTR of 1.2% https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=rates%20of%20recom%02mendations%20in%20real,10%2C000%20recommendations%20and%20120%20are)]. A diversity-enhanced system can be evaluated by how these engagement metrics change: Does the diverse recommender lead to more clicks overall? Do users consume a wider variety of content over time (perhaps measured by the diversity of items or categories clicked)? Behavioral signals can also include **dwell time** (how long a user spends on recommended content), **repeat usage** (do users come back more often when recommendations are more varied?), or **bounce rate** (do users leave after seeing recommendations?). An important online measure related to diversity is whether the system successfully increases exposure to long-tail items *without* harming user engagement. For instance, an A/B test at a music streaming service might check if a diversity-focused algorithm causes users to listen to more varied artists, and whether this affects total listening time.



Crucially, online evaluations can reveal trade-offs that offline metrics might miss. It has been observed that offline accuracy metrics do not always correlate with real user satisfaction https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=offline%20evaluations%20sometimes%20contradict%20results,are%20probably%20not%20suitable%20to)]. A classic example is the work by Ziegler et al. (2005), who found that a recommender with a *diversified* list was preferred by users in a study, even though that list had lower predicted accuracy [files.grouplens.org]. Similarly, live experiments sometimes show that a small drop in accuracy (e.g. fewer immediate clicks) may be acceptable if users find the recommendations more novel and engaging in the long run [files.grouplens.org][32]. Online evaluations thus provide the ground truth on whether optimizing diversity truly improves user experience. They often require significant resources – running A/B tests or user surveys is time-consuming and context-dependent – so researchers typically use them to validate the most promising methods after offline analysis. When successful, online tests can demonstrate improvements such as higher user retention or satisfaction due to increased diversity [32]. For example, Abdollahpouri et al. (2019) showed that promoting diverse and serendipitous recommendations can increase user engagement on a platform [32]. Overall, a combination of user studies and live A/B evaluations is used to complement offline metrics, ensuring that diversity optimization methods are not just theoretically sound but also effective in practice.


## Common Datasets and Experimental Protocols



To benchmark diversity-aware recommenders, researchers rely on a variety of publicly available datasets and standardized experimental protocols. Using common datasets enables fair comparisons between algorithms in the literature. Typical benchmark datasets span different domains – for example, **MovieLens** (movies), **Last.fm** (music), **Netflix Prize** data (movies), **GoodBooks** or BookCrossing (books), **Amazon** product review datasets (various e-commerce categories), and more recently **MIND** (news) for diversification in news recommendations [33]. Each dataset provides a user-item interaction matrix (e.g. ratings or implicit feedback) which can be split into training and test sets for offline evaluation. Diversity-focused studies often choose datasets that have a rich item space (so that there is room for diverse recommendations) and that represent different *long-tail* characteristics. For instance, MovieLens (particularly the 1M or 20M version) is a common choice – it contains thousands of movies with genre information, which is useful for computing diversity and novelty metrics [34]. The Netflix Prize dataset (100M movie ratings) has also been widely used; although it is large and somewhat dominated by popular movies, it allows testing algorithms that try to recommend less popular films [34]. In the music domain, Last.fm data (user artist listening counts) is popular for evaluating diversity because music recommenders often aim to broaden users’ listening beyond their top artists [35]. Researchers have also used book recommendation data and even anime recommendation datasets to test how algorithms perform in domains with different content structures [33] (e.g., anime has very strong genre niches, which can test an algorithm’s ability to recommend across niche categories).



Experimental protocol usually follows the standard recommender systems evaluation process with modifications to incorporate diversity metrics. Typically, the data is split so that a portion of each user’s interactions is used for training the recommender model, and the remaining interactions are held out for testing. After training a baseline recommender (e.g., a matrix factorization or neighborhood-based CF) and the proposed diversity-aware recommender, each model produces a top-N recommendation list for each user in the test set. Accuracy is evaluated by whether the held-out items (what the user actually interacted with) appear in the recommended list (using metrics like Precision@N, Recall@N, or NDCG). Alongside, diversity metrics are computed on those same recommendation lists (as described in the offline evaluation section) [23]. Many studies adopt a **re-ranking protocol**: they first generate a candidate list of top-N items by a high-accuracy model, and then apply a diversification algorithm to reorder or filter that list for higher diversity [files.grouplens.org]. This reflects a practical approach where one doesn’t sacrifice all accuracy for diversity, but tries to achieve a balance by post-processing recommendations.



It is common to compare algorithms under multiple settings, such as varying the length of the recommendation list (e.g. N=5 vs N=20) or varying a parameter that controls the diversity/accuracy trade-off. For example, an algorithm might have a parameter λ that tunes how much emphasis is put on diversity over accuracy; experiments will report results for different λ values to illustrate the trade-off curve [23]. The evaluation often involves **baseline methods** which include: a standard collaborative filtering recommender (to represent high-accuracy but lower-diversity behavior), content-based recommenders (which may have different diversity characteristics), and sometimes simple popularity-based recommenders (which often have very poor diversity but serve as a control) [23]. By using identical train/test splits and evaluation metrics across methods, researchers ensure a fair comparison of how each method improves diversity metrics and at what cost to accuracy. For instance, one study might report that on MovieLens 1M data, their diversification approach improved catalog coverage by 30% relative to a basic matrix-factorization recommender, while reducing precision@10 by only 5% [34][23]. Statistical significance tests (such as t-tests or Wilcoxon tests) are frequently used to verify that differences in metrics (especially accuracy) are not due to chance [36][37].



The choice of dataset also influences what kind of diversity is evaluated. Some works specifically choose datasets with item metadata (like genre, tags, or knowledge graphs) to evaluate *semantic diversity* – e.g., how many distinct genres are present in a recommendation list [[38]([[39](https://papers-gamma.link/static/memory/pdfs/153-Kunaver_Diversity_in_Recommender_Systems_2017.pdf#:~:text=coverage%20,not%20repeat%20on%20the%20list))]. For example, the Netflix dataset includes movie genres, enabling metrics like genre coverage or an entropy over genre distribution per list [[38]([[39](https://papers-gamma.link/static/memory/pdfs/153-Kunaver_Diversity_in_Recommender_Systems_2017.pdf#:~:text=coverage%20,not%20repeat%20on%20the%20list))]. In news recommendation (e.g., with the MIND dataset), diversity might be measured by the variety of news topics or sources presented to the user. Researchers sometimes create additional *synthetic tasks* to stress-test diversity. An example protocol is the **topic diversification task** introduced by Ziegler et al. (2005), where they started with a user’s top-N list sorted by predicted rating and then algorithmically re-ranked it to maximize topic coverage using a taxonomy of items [files.grouplens.org]. Such protocols explicitly test an algorithm’s ability to inject diversity while maintaining relevance. In summary, diversity-aware recommenders are benchmarked on standard datasets (movies, music, books, etc.) using the usual train/test splits, but evaluated with extended metrics and often compared to baseline recommenders not optimized for diversity [34]. This experimental setup has become a de facto standard in the research community for demonstrating the effectiveness of new methods.


## Comparison with Traditional Recommenders (Collaborative, Content-based, Hybrid)



When new diversity optimization methods are proposed, they are typically compared against traditional recommender algorithms to highlight differences in both accuracy and diversity. The traditional methods include **collaborative filtering (CF)** approaches (user-based or item-based nearest neighbor models, matrix factorization, etc.), **content-based filtering** (which recommends items similar to those a user liked in the past, based on item attributes), and **hybrid systems** (which combine multiple techniques). Each of these has distinct characteristics in terms of the diversity of their outputs, and evaluations often examine these characteristics:


* **Collaborative Filtering vs Content-Based:** Pure collaborative filtering can sometimes introduce more diversity than content-based methods, because CF leverages other users’ preferences which might lead to unexpected items. However, CF is also prone to popularity bias (recommending what is popular in the community) and can produce homogenous lists if a user’s nearest neighbors have very similar taste [files.grouplens.org]. Content-based recommenders, on the other hand, often suffer from **over-specialization**: by design, they recommend items very similar to what the user already knows, which can narrow the recommendation scope [42]. For example, a content-based music recommender might keep suggesting songs of the same genre or by the same artist because it matches the user’s profile, failing to introduce novel genres. In contrast, a user-based CF might recommend a song from a different genre that “people like you” enjoyed, thereby adding some diversity – but it might also recommend a lot of generally popular items (reducing novelty). Recent research confirms these intuitions: one comparative study found that content-based approaches tend to produce *under-diversified* recommendation lists on average, while standard collaborative filtering produces *more diverse* lists that sometimes even overshoot the diversity of a user’s own profile [42]. In that study, the average intra-list diversity from a basic CF was higher than the diversity of the user’s past preferences, indicating CF could recommend a grab-bag of items beyond the user’s usual niche [42]. Neither approach is ideal on its own: content-based can miss serendipitous discoveries, and collaborative filtering can sometimes recommend irrelevant out-of-profile items in the name of diversity [43][28].
* **Hybrid Approaches:** Hybrid recommenders (e.g., combining CF and content, or using knowledge graphs, etc.) are often introduced to get the “best of both worlds,” improving accuracy while mitigating the diversity limitations of pure methods [44]. For instance, a content+CF hybrid might ensure that recommendations are similar enough to user interests to be relevant (addressing CF’s occasional wild recommendations) while also injecting some novel content (addressing content-based overspecialization). When comparing new diversity-aware algorithms, researchers include hybrids to see if the new method outperforms even those. Interestingly, some hybrid or graph-based algorithms naturally yield moderate diversity. The aforementioned study noted that knowledge-graph based recommenders and deep learning models produced recommendation lists with diversity levels closer to what the users’ profiles would suggest – neither too narrow nor too broad on average [44]. This suggests that newer algorithms, by using rich item relationships or latent factors, might inherently balance relevance and diversity better than older techniques. Evaluations often pit the proposed method against a set of baselines: a CF baseline (e.g. matrix factorization), a content-based baseline, and possibly a hybrid or graph-based model, to demonstrate where the new method stands on the accuracy-diversity spectrum [45][46].
* **Performance Comparison:** In terms of evaluation, a new diversity optimization method will be compared to these baselines on the same test data, reporting both accuracy metrics and diversity metrics for each. A successful approach might show, for example: “Method X achieved significantly higher diversity (higher ILD and coverage) than standard MF (Matrix Factorization) and content-based filtering, with only a small drop in precision” [23]. In many papers, results are presented as tables or plots that include the baseline algorithms. For instance, Adomavicius and Kwon (2012) compared their re-ranking strategy to a basic top-N recommender and showed it could greatly increase aggregate diversity (coverage and Gini) while maintaining nearly the same recall [47][48]. Similarly, Ziegler et al. (2005) compared a topic-diversified recommender to a pure CF recommender: the diversified version had lower accuracy scores, yet users in a study preferred it, indicating the value of diversity in practice [files.grouplens.org]. Modern evaluations continue this pattern: they often show trade-off curves where the proposed algorithm dominates a baseline by offering a better accuracy-diversity trade-off (e.g., for the same diversity level it achieves higher precision, or vice versa) [23]. It’s also common to see that content-based methods have high accuracy for niche users but low diversity, whereas collaborative methods have higher diversity but might include more “uninteresting” items – the new method aims to improve diversity *and* keep relevance high. By reporting metrics like Precision@10 alongside ILD, novelty, and coverage for each algorithm, researchers make the comparison concrete. In summary, new diversity-aware recommenders are validated by benchmarking against conventional CF, content-based, and hybrid systems, showing quantitatively how they increase diversity metrics and qualitatively (sometimes via user studies) that they produce more satisfying recommendations than those traditional approaches [45][files.grouplens.org].


## Challenges and Limitations in Evaluating Diversity



Evaluating diversity in recommendations poses several challenges and limitations, which have been discussed in the research literature:


* **Quantifying Subjective Concepts:** Many diversity-related concepts are inherently subjective and hard to reduce to a formula. *Serendipity* is a prime example – it involves the element of surprise, which is difficult to capture mathematically [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)]. An item that is unexpected for one user might be known to another, and the degree of “pleasant surprise” is not directly observable from data. Offline serendipity metrics use proxies (unexpectedness relative to a user profile, as discussed) [16], but they cannot fully guarantee that a user would feel delighted by the recommendation. Similarly, *novelty* depends on a user’s prior knowledge. Offline, we assume an item is novel if the user hasn’t interacted with it before, or if it’s unpopular overall [13]. In reality, a user might have heard of an item elsewhere. Thus, offline novelty metrics may misjudge what is truly new to the user. These limitations mean that offline metrics are at best rough indicators: two algorithms might score equally on a novelty metric, yet users could perceive one as more novel if it recommends items in unfamiliar *genres* rather than just less popular items. To mitigate this, some researchers incorporate user survey questions specifically about novelty/surprise, but such evaluations are labor-intensive https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=receive%20recom%02mendations%20generated%20by%20different,experts%20%5B3%5D.%20A)].
* **Trade-off with Accuracy and Utility:** There is an inherent tension between accuracy and diversity, making evaluation a multi-objective problem. Pushing diversity often means recommending items that are less likely to be relevant, so a naive optimization of diversity can degrade recommendation quality. A key challenge is evaluating whether an algorithm achieves a good *balance*. If Algorithm A has higher diversity but much lower accuracy than Algorithm B, which is better? The answer may depend on context and user preferences. Some evaluation approaches use combined or **multi-objective metrics** – for example, measuring *user utility* that accounts for the value of diversity. But there is no single agreed-upon metric that blends accuracy and diversity in a user-centric way [49][50]. Researchers often resort to plotting accuracy vs. diversity and discussing the trade-off qualitatively. This makes it hard to declare one method universally superior. Moreover, optimizing for diversity can lead to **diminishing returns** – the first boost in diversity greatly improves user experience, but beyond a point, extra diversity yields little benefit and could even harm satisfaction (the recommendations may become too eclectic) [28][51]. Determining that “sweet spot” requires careful evaluation. Some studies have noted that adding a small amount of diversity yields positive results, but aggressive diversification (especially via post-processing) can overshoot, producing recommendations that feel random or mismatched [28]. This is a limitation in current evaluation practice: metrics like ILD will keep rising as you inject more dissimilar items, but user happiness will not increase indefinitely and may decline if relevance suffers.
* **Lack of Personalization in Diversity Evaluation:** Different users have different tolerance and desire for diversity [52]. One user might love very diverse recommendations (finding them exploratory and fun), while another prefers a narrow focus on a genre they like. Most offline evaluations use one-size-fits-all diversity metrics, not accounting for individual “optimal” diversity levels. Recent research has pointed out that the *ideal* diversity of a recommendation list might be related to the diversity of the user’s own profile or tastes [53][54]. If a user listens to a very wide range of music, they may expect and enjoy a wide variety in recommendations; conversely, a specialist may be annoyed if recommendations stray too far. A limitation of many current approaches is not evaluating whether the system can *adapt* diversity to the user. When we only use aggregate metrics (like average ILD across users), we might miss that an algorithm over-diversifies for some and under-diversifies for others. Some advanced evaluations have started to compare the diversity of recommendations to the diversity in the user’s profile (e.g., using R² to measure correlation) [45][46]. They find that none of the common algorithms perfectly calibrate diversity to individual needs (often R² < 0.2, essentially low correlation) [45][46]. This is an area of ongoing research, and it means current evaluation metrics might be too coarse.
* **Metric Interdependence and Validity:** There is also the issue that many diversity metrics can be gamed or can give misleading signals if taken in isolation. For example, a trivial way to increase catalog coverage is to recommend at least one random long-tail item to every user. This would boost coverage and entropy metrics, but could reduce user satisfaction if those random items are irrelevant. Existing diversity measures typically do not distinguish *why* diversity increased [55]. An algorithm that smartly finds relevant-but-novel items and an algorithm that simply injects randomness might score similarly on ILD or novelty metrics. Thus, diversity metrics must be interpreted alongside accuracy metrics to ensure the diversity is *useful*. This limitation is often overcome by evaluating *combined outcomes* (e.g., precision at various levels of catalog coverage) or by performing user studies to verify that high diversity is coming from meaningful recommendations, not just noise [files.grouplens.org]. Another problem is that the choice of similarity metric (for ILD) or popularity threshold (for novelty) can affect results. An item similarity used for ILD might not align with users’ perception of diversity – for instance, two movies might be considered similar by genre metadata but a user might find them quite different in other aspects (or vice versa) [12]. So if the evaluator’s similarity measure is imperfect, the ILD metric might not reflect true diversity as seen by users. This is a known issue: *“the details matter”* in how we compute these metrics [12]. Researchers have to carefully choose or learn a good similarity function for evaluating intra-list diversity, sometimes even learning it from user feedback about diversity preferences.
* **Offline vs. Online Discrepancies:** Finally, a major limitation is that improvements in offline diversity metrics do not always translate to better online performance. As noted, offline evaluations are necessary for rapid prototyping, but studies have found they can be poor predictors of real-world success https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=offline%20evaluations%20sometimes%20contradict%20results,are%20probably%20not%20suitable%20to)]. An algorithm might look superior on paper (e.g., much higher novelty and only slightly worse precision), but an A/B test could show users actually interact less with it – perhaps because the slight precision drop affected some key recommendations. Or users might not even notice the diversity as much as expected. For example, a system might diversify by recommending one out-of-domain item which the user simply ignores, while the rest of the list remains conventional – the metrics would record an increase in diversity, but the user’s behavior might barely change. Such nuances mean that truly validating a diversity-optimization method requires deploying it or at least conducting user trials. The expense and complexity of online testing is a bottleneck, and not all research prototypes get this far. This creates a gap in evaluation: many papers demonstrate diversity gains offline, but relatively fewer confirm improvements through online studies. The community is aware of this and encourages multi-method evaluation https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=systems%2C%20and%20judge%20the%20value,rate%20the%20recommendations%2C%20and%20the)] https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=offline%20evaluations%20sometimes%20contradict%20results,are%20probably%20not%20suitable%20to)], but practical constraints often limit evaluations to offline metrics.



In summary, while there are established metrics and methodologies to evaluate diversity in recommender systems, one must be cautious in interpreting them. Diversity is multi-faceted and user-dependent, and current evaluation techniques have to balance quantitative rigor with capturing subjective user experiences. Ongoing work in the field aims to develop better metrics (e.g., personalized diversity measures, or unified metrics combining relevance and diversity [50]) and better evaluation frameworks (such as simulation of user interaction or improved user study designs) to address these limitations. The challenges underscore that evaluating “how good” a diversity-optimized recommender is cannot be reduced to a single number – it requires a holistic analysis of trade-offs, user satisfaction, and context.


## Conclusion



Diversity-aware recommendation methods are assessed through a combination of offline and online evaluations, each providing different insights. Offline metrics like intra-list diversity, novelty, serendipity, and coverage allow researchers to quantify how varied and unexpected the recommendations are [9][13]. Online evaluations – including user studies and A/B tests – are critical for determining whether those diversity gains actually enhance user satisfaction and engagement in practice [files.grouplens.org] https://docear.org/papers/A%20Comparison%20of%20Offline%20Evaluations,%20Online%20Evaluations,%20and%20User%20Studies%20...%20(preprint.pdf#:~:text=receive%20recom%02mendations%20generated%20by%20different,experts%20%5B3%5D.%20A)]. Common public datasets (MovieLens, Netflix, Last.fm, etc.) and standardized protocols are used to ensure consistency and reproducibility in experiments [34][33]. New diversity-focused algorithms are typically benchmarked against traditional collaborative filtering, content-based, and hybrid recommenders, showing how they improve on or differ from these baselines [23][42]. The evaluation of diversity, however, comes with challenges: metrics are imperfect proxies for subjective qualities, and there is a continual need to balance diversity with accuracy and to tailor recommendations to individual user preferences [[14]([[16](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311784289_Diversity_Serendipity_Novelty_and_Coverage_A_Survey_and_Empirical_Analysis_of_Beyond-Accuracy_Objectives_in_Recommender_Systems#:~:text=),)][28]. As research progresses, more sophisticated evaluation approaches (such as personalized diversity metrics and long-term longitudinal studies of user behavior) are being developed to address these limitations. By combining rigorous offline measurements with careful online validation, the field aims to ensure that optimizing for diversity truly leads to better recommender systems that broaden users’ horizons without compromising relevance [files.grouplens.org][32].

question: In robotics, what are the leading methods for learning terrain traversibility costs automatically from robot experience?

sections.title: Report
sections.text:
# Learning Terrain Traversability from Robot Experience


## Introduction



Terrain traversability refers to a robot’s ability to safely move across a region, which depends on both the terrain properties and the robot’s own capabilities [1]. Estimating a *traversability cost* (or risk) for terrain is crucial for autonomous navigation in complex environments, from urban streets to off-road wilderness. A high cost typically signifies areas where the robot may get stuck, tip over, or suffer damage, whereas low-cost areas are easier to traverse [1][2]. The challenge is to learn these costs automatically from robot experience, rather than relying purely on manual engineering. Recent research (especially in top robotics venues like ICRA, IROS, RSS, RA-L, TRO) has made significant strides in learning traversability models that adapt to real-world conditions. Below, we survey the leading methods, organized by approach, and highlight how they apply to different robot types (e.g. legged vs. wheeled) and environments (off-road vs. urban).


## Classical Approaches: Probabilistic and Rule-Based Models



Early traversability analysis relied on hand-crafted rules and geometric reasoning. Terrain was characterized by features such as slope steepness, surface roughness, or obstacle height, and simple models would decide traversability based on thresholds or formulas [3][4]. For example, a classical heuristic might label any grid cell with slope > 30° as non-traversable and assign a high cost, while flat areas get low cost. Such **analytical models** are intuitive but often brittle, since a single threshold can’t capture all situations [3].



One representative rule-based method introduced a *Fuzzy Traversability Index* to combine multiple terrain attributes. Howard and Seraji (2001) designed a fuzzy logic system that takes inputs like terrain roughness, hardness, and discontinuities, and outputs linguistic categories (e.g. *SAFE*, *RISKY*, *UNSAFE*) corresponding to different traversability levels [5][6]. The fuzzy rules effectively encode expert knowledge (e.g. “if terrain is very rough *and* very soft, then it’s *Unsafe*”) and produce a quantitative index of ease-of-traversal. This approach improved robustness to sensor noise over rigid mathematical formulas, but it still required experts to define membership functions and rules upfront [7][8].



Another line of classical methods used probabilistic maps. Instead of a binary traversable/not-traversable assessment, these methods estimate a probability or cost of traversal for each location. Sock *et al.* (2016) presented a system that fuses 3D LIDAR and camera data to build a probabilistic traversability map [9]. Each cell in the map stores a traversability probability derived from sensor readings (for instance, combining point cloud roughness with color cues of terrain). Similarly, Ahtiainen *et al.* (2017) developed a **Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) map** using 3D LIDAR, which models the surface shape within each grid cell as a Gaussian distribution and assesses how “flat” or “traversable” that cell is [10]. These probabilistic models explicitly represent uncertainty (useful for risk assessment) and can be tailored to a specific vehicle. For instance, later work by Kim *et al.* (2017) focused on *lateral slope* as a key feature for Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs), identifying side-slopes that a particular UGV could safely handle [11]. Overall, classical approaches provided the first mapping of terrain to traversal cost, but their fixed criteria struggled with the diversity of real terrain (e.g. a 31° slope might be impassable for one robot but manageable for another).


## Machine Learning Techniques: Supervised and Reinforcement Learning



To overcome the limitations of manual tuning, researchers turned to machine learning on robot data. In supervised learning approaches, one trains a model (e.g. a classifier or regressor) on examples of terrain labeled with traversability outcomes. Early work by Kim *et al.* (2006) even demonstrated *unsupervised* online learning: the robot’s vision system would cluster and learn traversable vs. non-traversable image patches on the fly, without explicit labels [12]. This was an initial step toward robots *learning from experience* by adjusting to new terrain in real-time. More commonly, supervised methods require human-provided labels or simulations for training. For example, some studies treated traversability as a **binary classification** problem (traversable or not) [13], while others used **multi-class terrain classification** (e.g. labeling each patch as *mud*, *gravel*, *grass*, etc., and mapping these to different cost values) [13]. Gonzalez and Iagnemma (2018) showed that identifying the specific terrain type can inform the expected difficulty, and Chavez-Garcia *et al.* (2018) demonstrated reliable traverse vs. no-go classification using 3D sensor data [13]. The drawback, however, is that supervised learning demands a large number of labeled examples – typically requiring humans to drive the robot and annotate the traversable regions in each frame [14]. This is labor-intensive and often environment-specific.



**Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL)** offers a way to learn a cost function from expert demonstrations, rather than manual labels for every patch. In IRL, one assumes an expert (human or a well-tuned planner) is choosing paths that optimize some hidden cost map; the algorithm then back-infers a cost function that would make the demonstrated paths optimal. Pflueger *et al.* (2019) applied IRL to planetary rover data, using a neural network (Soft Value Iteration Network) to learn a traversal cost map that explains the human-driven paths on Mars-like terrain [15]. Zhu *et al.* (2020) similarly used deep IRL for off-road ground vehicles, learning a cost function that balances progress vs. difficulty by imitating expert drivers [16]. These IRL-derived costmaps can then be used by standard planners to navigate new routes [17].



In contrast to learning from demonstrations, **Reinforcement Learning (RL)** lets the robot learn traversability through trial and error. The robot is given a reward for successful navigation (or penalties for getting stuck/unstable) and the RL algorithm adjusts the robot’s policy or cost predictions to maximize long-term reward. For example, Weerakoon *et al.* (2022) trained a deep RL policy to reliably plan paths in uneven outdoor environments, by implicitly learning which terrains to avoid – their system TERP used a deep network to estimate future path reward (in effect, a traversability cost-to-go) and steer the robot accordingly [18]. Other works incorporate RL into costmap learning by simulating many navigation trials: the robot roams in simulation, experiencing successes and failures, and uses that feedback to label terrain in a self-supervised way. This approach was taken by Fan *et al.* (2021), who learned a *risk-aware* traversability costmap with a neural network that predicts not just the expected cost but also the uncertainty (variance) of that cost [19][2]. By training on a wide range of simulated trials (with randomized terrains), the network learned to assign higher costs to areas with a higher probability of failure, enabling more cautious path planning [19]. A common theme in these learning-based methods is tailoring the traversability prediction to the *robot’s actual performance*. Unlike classical methods with fixed thresholds, ML approaches can discover, for instance, that a grassy slope is traversable when dry but not after rain, if such experiences are in the training data.


## Deep Learning-Based Methods: CNNs, GNNs, and Self-Supervised Learning



Modern deep learning techniques have greatly advanced terrain assessment, thanks to their ability to process high-dimensional sensor inputs (images, point clouds) and capture complex terrain features. A popular strategy is to use **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)** for semantic segmentation of the environment. The CNN takes an image (or a 3D voxel map) and classifies each region into terrain categories or directly into traversable vs. non-traversable areas [4]. For example, Shaban *et al.* (2022) trained a CNN to perform *semantic terrain classification* for off-road driving, labeling pixels as dirt road, vegetation, sky, etc., to inform the vehicle which regions are navigable [20]. Similarly, Gao *et al.* (2021) developed a contrastive-learning-based segmentation model to produce fine-grained off-road maps (distinguishing, say, solid ground vs. shrub) [21]. These vision-based models are especially useful in **urban settings**, where traversability often correlates with recognizable classes (road, sidewalk, wall, curb). A deep network can be trained on city datasets to detect drivable road or ramps with high accuracy. However, a limitation noted in recent works is that segmentation by itself doesn’t yield a numeric *cost* – one still has to assign a cost to each class (e.g. treat “mud” as high cost). If those assignments are wrong or too crude, the planner may make suboptimal decisions [22]. For instance, a semantic segmentation might label both tall grass and a brick wall as “obstacle”, but the cost of trying to drive through grass is clearly much lower than driving into a wall. This has motivated research into directly learning **continuous traversability costs** with deep regressors.



Instead of outputting discrete labels, some deep models output a continuous score (or cost) for each terrain cell. Recent approaches train CNNs or other deep networks to map sensor inputs to a *traversability costmap*, often incorporating additional sensor modalities like inertial measurement units (IMU) to gauge how bumpy or unstable a ride would be [23]. For example, Yao *et al.* (2022) introduced a “ride comfort-aware” network that uses camera images together with IMU readings to predict how comfortable (low cost) or uncomfortable (high cost) a path would be for a wheeled robot [24]. By learning from data – in this case, by driving over many terrains and recording the vibration levels – the network automatically infers that, say, a terrain full of large rocks leads to high vibration (high cost) [25]. Other teams have used **deep inverse reinforcement learning** to directly learn a cost function: Zhu *et al.* (2020) in the context of off-road driving learned a deep cost model that, when optimized, reproduces expert trajectories [26]. In parallel, deep RL-based systems (discussed earlier) also fall under “deep learning” since they utilize deep neural networks as function approximators for cost or policy [23].



**Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)** have also emerged as a tool in this domain, especially for modeling relational or spatial aspects of traversability. Unlike CNNs (which excel on grid-structured data like images), GNNs can operate on arbitrary graph-structured representations. One innovative example is using GNNs to incorporate a **robot’s kinematic structure** into the learning model. Butterfield *et al.* (2025) propose a morphology-informed GNN for legged robots, where each node in the graph corresponds to a robot joint (or foot) and edges correspond to physical links [27]. The GNN processes proprioceptive sensor data (joint forces, angles) across this graph to predict whether each foot is in stable contact with the ground [27]. This effectively tells the robot if a given foothold is traversable or if it’s slipping – a crucial piece of traversability for legged locomotion. By structuring the neural network as a graph matching the robot’s morphology, they imbue the model with built-in knowledge of the robot’s form, leading to efficient learning of contact outcomes. While this GNN is focused on contact *perception*, it can feed into higher-level traversability assessment (if a foothold is predicted unsafe, the terrain there gets a high cost). More generally, GNNs and graph-based methods are useful when terrain can be represented as connected regions or when multi-robot systems share information via graphs [28][29]. However, CNNs remain more common for mapping tasks, and GNN-based traversability learning is a newer, experimental avenue.



*Figure 1:* A legged robot (ANYmal quadruped) learns a visual traversability model through self-supervised experience. In this example, a human operator first drives the robot through *traversable* areas (teleoperated demo). The robot’s deep model uses this experience to learn to distinguish safe vs. unsafe terrain from camera images. Within minutes, the robot can autonomously navigate and avoid obstacles in complex outdoor environments [30][[31]([[39](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss19/p054.pdf#:~:text=It%20is%20difficult%20to%20infer,build%20upon%20deep%20neural%20models))].



One of the most exciting developments in recent years is **self-supervised learning for traversability**. In a self-supervised approach, the robot creates its own training labels from its interactions with the environment, rather than needing human-labeled data. The image above illustrates this concept: the robot starts with no prior training (the traversability network is initially random), and as it is driven around, it collects sensor feedback (e.g. “I drove here successfully” vs “I stumbled or stopped here”) to label areas as traversable or not. Frey *et al.* (2023) demonstrated an online self-supervised system called *Wild Visual Navigation* where a quadruped uses a short teleoperated drive in a field to automatically generate training data, and quickly learns to segment the camera view into traversable vs. non-traversable terrain [30][32]. The key idea in self-supervision is to use **internal sensors or proprioception** as the ground truth: for instance, Zürn *et al.* (2020) leveraged *audio and vibration cues* – when the robot drives over gravel vs. grass, the sounds and IMU vibrations differ, providing a signal of terrain type, which was used to train a visual terrain classifier without manual labels [33]. Likewise, Wellhausen *et al.* (2019) employed a legged robot’s *force/torque feedback* to learn terrain properties; essentially, the robot learns from *feeling* the ground. They deployed the robot to walk on various surfaces and used unexpected slips or foot sinkage as indicators of low traversability, which in turn supervise a CNN that looks at images of the terrain and predicts how stable it would be [34]. Several recent studies follow this paradigm: Seo *et al.* (2023) introduced a framework (SCATE) for purely self-supervised traversability learning in unstructured environments [35], and Guaman Castro *et al.* (2023) in *How Does it Feel?* used vehicle suspension accelerometers to learn a costmap that correlates with how rough the ride is [36]. Self-supervised methods are powerful because they inherently tailor the cost estimation to the *robot’s experience* – e.g., if the robot starts slipping on wet leaves, it will assign higher cost to that terrain in the future. A downside is that the robot must experience a variety of conditions (including some failures) to learn effectively; this can be addressed by first training in simulation or using cautious exploration strategies.


## Adapting to Robot Type and Environment



Traversability is highly context-dependent: a path that is easy for a tracked rover might be impossible for a wheeled robot, and terrain navigable by a legged robot might pose no-go areas for a drone (and vice versa). Therefore, learning methods often consider the specific robot type. For **wheeled or tracked vehicles**, terrain costs tend to depend on geometry and traction – e.g. wheel robots are sensitive to steep grades, step obstacles taller than the wheel radius, and low-friction surfaces. Many classical and learning approaches for wheeled UGVs emphasize geometric features like slope and roughness captured by LIDAR or stereo cameras [10]. In contrast, **legged robots** can traverse discontinuous terrain (stepping over gaps or rubble) and thus benefit from learning foothold-based metrics. Legged systems often incorporate proprioceptive measures: for instance, Hutter’s group showed that using leg force sensors to detect slip or sinkage can improve a learned traversability model for quadrupeds [34]. In practice, modern traversability learning frameworks try to encode robot kinematics and dynamics into the model. The MI-HGNN GNN model mentioned earlier is one example focusing on legged morphology [27]. Another example is the meta-learning approach by Visca *et al.* (2022), which trained a global model to predict energy consumption on various terrains and rapidly adapt it per robot – effectively customizing the cost of traversing *the same terrain* for different platforms [37][38].



Environmental differences also play a role. **Off-road environments** (e.g. forests, deserts) are unstructured and have high variability, which makes learning indispensable. Robots in off-road settings often encounter deformable terrain (mud, sand), vegetation (tall grass, shrubs), and uneven surfaces that can confuse traditional sensors (for example, LIDAR might report thick grass as a solid obstacle) [[31]([[39](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss19/p054.pdf#:~:text=It%20is%20difficult%20to%20infer,build%20upon%20deep%20neural%20models))]. Learning-based methods, especially those using vision and self-supervision, have been successful here: by learning visual cues of what *is* traversable in a forest (e.g. the robot learns that it can push through grass but not through a tree trunk), they outperform hand-crafted rules [[31]([[39](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss19/p054.pdf#:~:text=It%20is%20difficult%20to%20infer,build%20upon%20deep%20neural%20models))][[31]([[39](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss19/p054.pdf#:~:text=It%20is%20difficult%20to%20infer,build%20upon%20deep%20neural%20models))]. Some methods explicitly handle perceptual ambiguities common in off-road scenes – for instance, classifying *vegetation vs. solid obstacle* using deep semantic segmentation [[31]([[39](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss19/p054.pdf#:~:text=It%20is%20difficult%20to%20infer,build%20upon%20deep%20neural%20models))] or anomaly detection. In contrast, **urban environments** present more structured challenges: curbs, stairs, and man-made obstacles that are often well modeled by simple geometry. A lot of urban autonomous navigation uses *prior maps* or high-level road semantics, but when learning traversability, the focus might be on specific features like curb negotiation or stair climbing for a given robot. Supervised learning has been used to classify stair traversability or to detect driveable gaps in urban settings. Overall, the more structured the environment, the more a model can rely on known semantics (e.g. “red = stop sign, avoid”; “sidewalk = safe for a pedestrian robot”), whereas in natural terrain, the model must generalize from raw experience. Encouragingly, recent studies show that combining data from **multiple environments** can yield robust traversability predictors: meta-learning frameworks train on diverse terrain types (sand, rocks, grass, mud) and learn a global model that can quickly adapt to any new terrain by just a few real-world trials [40][23]. This ability to transfer knowledge across environments is vital for field robots that may be deployed in entirely new sites.


## Conclusion



Learning traversability costs from robot experience has evolved from early heuristic approaches into a rich field combining computer vision, machine learning, and robotics insights. Classical methods established the foundation by quantifying terrain difficulty with human-designed metrics [3], but they fell short in unknown or complex conditions. Machine learning approaches introduced adaptability, allowing robots to *learn* what is traversable based on data rather than fixed rules. With deep learning, robots can leverage high-capacity models (CNNs, GNNs, etc.) to predict traversability from raw sensor inputs and even improve online through self-supervision. The most advanced systems today integrate multiple modalities (vision, LIDAR, IMU, proprioception) and learning paradigms (e.g. combining supervised pre-training with self-supervised online adaptation [41]) to achieve reliable navigation. Notably, there is a trend toward **platform-aware** and **context-aware** traversability estimation – recognizing that “traversable” is not an absolute label but depends on *which* robot and *where*. The literature from top conferences (ICRA, IROS, RSS) in recent years reflects this, with influential studies demonstrating terrain learning on legged robots in the wild [30], autonomous off-road vehicles tackling new trails via learned costmaps [23], and even planetary rovers leveraging IRL to explore Mars-like landscapes [15]. Going forward, we can expect even more generalizable traversability models, possibly combining physics simulations, meta-learning, and large-scale self-supervised data, enabling robots to confidently chart their path through the most challenging terrains.

question: what are the most important open challenges in using neural networks in combination with PDE solvers for fluid simulation?
