# Open-Source Publishing Platforms and the Global Distribution of Academic Publishing


## Overview of Open-Source Publishing Platforms



Open-source publishing platforms – including open-access journals, repositories, and preprint servers – have dramatically reshaped academic publishing in the past two decades. These platforms make research literature freely accessible online, allowing anyone in the world to read and use scholarly work without subscription barriers. The open access movement gained momentum in the early 2000s (e.g. the 2002 Budapest Open Access Initiative) with the principle that scientific knowledge is a public good that should be available to all [1]. Today, the growth of open-access publishing is evident: between 2013 and 2023, the share of research papers published as immediate open access (“gold OA”) worldwide increased from just 11% to about 38%, while subscription-only articles fell from 70% to 52% of output [2]. This shift illustrates how open platforms are becoming a dominant mode of dissemination [3].



Open-source journal platforms like *Open Journal Systems* (OJS) have been pivotal in enabling this global dissemination. OJS (developed by the Public Knowledge Project) is free, open-source software that any institution can use to manage and publish an academic journal online.  *Figure: Global distribution of active scholarly journals using the Open Journal Systems (OJS) platform (2020). Darker shading indicates more OJS-based journals in a country. OJS has enabled a truly worldwide ecosystem of journals, with significant adoption in Latin America, Asia, Africa, and other regions outside traditional publishing centers.* As of 2021, over 34,000 active journals were using OJS to publish about 1.46 million articles per year [4] – a volume that even exceeds the annual output of the largest commercial publisher (Elsevier published ~600,000 articles that year) [4]. OJS journals publish in over 60 languages across 146 countries, roughly 80% of which are in the Global South [5]. This demonstrates how open-source platforms have lowered barriers for communities around the world to host their own journals, fostering *bibliodiversity*, i.e. a diversity of languages and local publications [6][5]. Beyond journals, open repositories and preprint servers further expand global access: for example, the arXiv preprint server hosts millions of free research papers and by late 2024 was receiving ~24,000 new submissions each month [7], making cutting-edge findings immediately available internationally. The Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) now indexes over 21,500 open-access journals from 138 countries in 89 languages, collectively offering more than 11 million articles to readers worldwide [8]. In short, open-source and open-access publishing platforms have enabled unprecedented global participation in scholarly communication – both in who can **publish** research and who can **access** it.


## Increases in Accessibility and Readership Across Global Regions



By removing paywalls, open-access platforms have vastly increased the accessibility of academic research across all global regions. Researchers, students, and the public no longer need expensive journal subscriptions to access literature, which is especially transformative for those in developing countries and under-resourced institutions. A growing body of evidence shows that open-access articles reach **more readers in more places** than paywalled articles. For instance, a 2024 study reported that open-access papers “have a greater reach than paywalled ones in two key ways: they attract more total citations, and those citations come from scholars in a wider range of locations, institutions, and fields” [9]. In other words, making an article free to read not only boosts its citation count but also diversifies *who* is citing it (geographically and institutionally), indicating a broader global readership. This phenomenon has been dubbed the “open-access citation advantage” and “citation diversity advantage” [9].



Open access is clearly linked to higher usage. A comparative study by Springer Nature on books found that open-access books have **far greater readership and usage** than non-OA books: on average, an OA book saw significantly more downloads and was cited 2.4 times more often than its closed-access counterparts [10]. Likewise, a large-scale analysis of 281 open-access books versus 3,653 closed books showed that the OA titles had higher *geographic diversity* of usage (being downloaded and read in a wider range of countries), higher download counts, and more citations across all subject areas [11]. Notably, the open-access books reached traditionally underserved regions much more effectively [11]. In summary, open-source publishing platforms have *democratized* access to knowledge: a researcher in Kenya or Bangladesh can now obtain the same literature as one in Western Europe with a click, leading to increased visibility of research in the Global South and enabling scholars everywhere to build upon the latest findings. The proportion of literature that is freely accessible continues to rise each year, further closing the global accessibility gap. Major publishers report surging readership for their open content (for example, Springer Nature saw double-digit growth in downloads of OA articles and books [12]), reflecting the unmet demand that open access is fulfilling. Across diverse disciplines and regions, the net effect is that academic knowledge is no longer circulating only within wealthy universities – it is reaching clinicians, educators, policymakers, and citizens around the world who can put it to use.


## Impacts on Traditional Academic Publishers and Journals



The rise of open-source and open-access publishing platforms has significantly impacted traditional academic publishers and journal business models. **Subscription-based publishers**, which long dominated academic publishing by selling journal access to libraries, have been pressured to adapt in response to the open access movement. As noted, the share of papers available via subscription-only access has dropped from 70% to nearly half of global output in the last decade [2]. This trend threatens the traditional subscription revenue model and has forced many publishers to explore new approaches. Almost all major publishers now offer some form of open access option: thousands of established journals have become “hybrid” (allowing authors to pay a fee to make their article open access in an otherwise paywalled journal) or have completely “flipped” to open access. Every year, numerous journals convert from closed to open access, and studies indicate this generally brings positive outcomes for the journals. For example, a bibliometric analysis of journals that *flipped* to OA found that, on average, these journals **increased their publication output and impact** after the transition, compared to similar journals that remained subscription-based [13]. Post-flip, the open journals attracted more submissions and saw their citation metrics (e.g. impact factor and average citations per article) rise faster than their closed-access peers [13]. This suggests that moving to an open model can enhance a journal’s visibility and influence, as broader accessibility draws in more authors and readers.



At the same time, **traditional publishers** have sought to maintain their profit margins in the open-access era by shifting costs to the publishing side. Many big commercial publishers now levy article processing charges (APCs) on authors (or their funders) to publish open access. Paradoxically, the publishing oligopoly (five large corporations) still controls more than half of scholarly output and has continued to post record profits even as open access expands [14]. They have achieved this in part by embracing open access on their own terms – for instance, Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, and others each publish hundreds of fully open-access journals alongside their traditional titles, often charging APCs that range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per article. The overall volume of open-access content is also being driven by new players outside the traditional giants, such as born-OA publishers (e.g. PLOS, BioMed Central, MDPI, Frontiers) that have rapidly grown by using scalable online platforms and APC-funded models. This has increased competition and diversified the publishing landscape. Libraries and research consortia, on the other hand, have negotiated “transformative agreements” with publishers – essentially bulk contracts that convert subscription fees into payments for open access publishing – as a strategy to unlock paywalled journals. While these deals aim to accelerate the shift to open access, they also signal how publishers are adapting: the focus is moving from selling content to providing publishing services. In sum, open-source publishing platforms have disrupted the traditional journal business, forcing journals and publishers to innovate. Many legacy journals have successfully transitioned to open access (or launched open siblings), leveraging the greater visibility to their advantage [15]. Yet the commercial publishing industry remains deeply involved in open access, meaning that the **financial and power structures** of academic publishing are evolving rather than disappearing – a point further examined under challenges.


## Equity and Inclusivity in Global Academic Knowledge Production



A core promise of open-access publishing is to advance equity and inclusivity in the production and consumption of knowledge globally. By eliminating paywalls, open platforms help level the playing field for researchers and readers in less-privileged contexts. There is evidence that **lower-income countries have embraced open access enthusiastically** as both consumers and producers of research. A recent analysis of millions of publications found that researchers in low- and lower-middle-income countries tend to publish a higher proportion of their work open access and also cite open-access literature more heavily than the world average [16][17]. For example, during 2015–2019, Sub-Saharan African countries published and cited open-access research at **higher rates than the rest of the world** [18]. This suggests that scholars in these regions rely on open access to overcome paywall barriers and to increase the visibility of their own work. In contrast, some upper-middle-income regions (such as parts of Asia and the Middle East) had lower-than-average open access uptake [18], potentially because they receive fewer APC waivers or policy mandates – highlighting that global adoption is uneven and policy support matters. Nonetheless, open platforms have clearly reduced the information divide: a scientist in a developing country can now access tens of millions of papers in open repositories or journals that were once behind paywalls, enabling more inclusive participation in science and scholarship [14].



Open-source publishing platforms have also empowered more **geographically and linguistically diverse** knowledge production. The widespread use of platforms like OJS by universities and independent publishers in the Global South means that thousands of local journals are now disseminating research globally. As noted earlier, roughly 80% of the over 34,000 OJS-powered journals are based in the Global South, and many publish in local languages or bilingually [5]. This decentralization challenges the traditional dominance of North American and European publishers and English-language outlets. Initiatives such as *SciELO* (a network of open-access journals from Latin America, Africa, and Spain) and *African Journals Online* have further ensured that research from historically underrepresented regions is openly available and indexed internationally. Moreover, open access facilitates **community and practitioner access** to research (for example, physicians in remote areas accessing medical studies, or teachers downloading educational research), thereby integrating global knowledge into local practice.



Despite these gains, there are ongoing concerns about equity in open-access publishing. One major issue is that high publishing fees (APCs) can exclude authors from resource-poor institutions. Ironically, studies have found that open-access journals have **fewer authors from low-income countries** as lead authors compared to paywalled journals [19], even when fee waivers are offered. The implication is that APCs pose a significant barrier for many researchers in the Global South, who may opt for traditional journals (with no author fees) or face rejection if they cannot secure funding for open-access fees. To address this, many publishers waive fees for the poorest countries and new funding models are emerging. Notably, a substantial subset of open-access journals do *not* charge authors at all – the so-called **diamond open access** model. According to DOAJ, over 13,700 journals (about 63% of those indexed) have no author fees [8], relying on institutional support or volunteers. Supporting and scaling such inclusive models is seen as key to ensuring that open access truly benefits researchers globally, not just those with grant funding. Organizations like UNESCO have advocated for Open Science policies that include equitable access to publication opportunities for researchers from low and middle-income countries [20][21]. In summary, open-source publishing platforms have made knowledge more globally inclusive than before, but achieving equity in who can publish remains a work in progress. The next challenge is to prevent new barriers (like publishing fees or language bias) from replacing the old ones.


## Challenges and Criticisms of Open-Access Models



While open-access publishing platforms have undoubtedly advanced global access to knowledge, they also face **significant challenges and criticisms** regarding their implementation and impact. Some of the key issues include:


* **Author Fees and Inequity:** The business model for many open-access journals shifts the cost burden to authors via APCs. Critics argue that the *“noble intent”* of open access has been co-opted by commercial publishers turning it into a profit-driven model [[22]([[23](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/358670181_Open-access_publishing_fees_deter_researchers_in_the_global_south#:~:text=,))]. High APCs – often thousands of dollars for elite journals – create a new form of exclusion, whereby researchers without ample funding (disproportionately those from the Global South or smaller institutions) struggle to publish their work [[22]([[23](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/358670181_Open-access_publishing_fees_deter_researchers_in_the_global_south#:~:text=,))][19]. This *pay-to-publish* system risks reinforcing inequalities in who gets to disseminate research. Even well-intentioned mechanisms like transformative agreements (bulk library contracts that cover APCs) have been criticized for **perpetuating exclusion**: they primarily benefit authors at institutions that can afford these deals, while others are left out, thus merely shifting the barrier from readers to authors [[22]([[23](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/358670181_Open-access_publishing_fees_deter_researchers_in_the_global_south#:~:text=,))]. In short, the open-access model can introduce financial biases in knowledge production if not managed equitably.
* **Predatory Journals and Quality Control:** The rapid growth of open-access publishing has been accompanied by the rise of **predatory publishers** – entities that exploit the OA model by charging fees without providing proper peer review or editorial services. These sham journals often target academics (especially early-career or those under pressure to publish) with solicitations, accepting substandard papers for a fee and thereby undermining scientific quality. Predatory publishing has become a global concern, as it tarnishes the open-access movement’s reputation. It is defined as the practice of *“exploiting the OA publishing model by charging researchers high fees to publish their work”* without rigorous quality control [24]. Researchers who inadvertently publish in such journals may see their work hidden from the credible literature, and important research (e.g. in health sciences) may be lost or not taken seriously. Efforts are underway to educate authors about how to identify legitimate OA journals (via whitelists like DOAJ and blacklists of predatory outlets) [25], but the prevalence of predatory journals remains a challenge that critics point out as a downside of open publishing frameworks.
* **Financial Sustainability:** Another criticism of open-source publishing is the question of how to sustainably finance scholarly publishing in the absence of subscription income. High-impact open-access journals often depend on APC revenues or heavy subsidies. Smaller journals, university presses, and scholarly societies worry about covering operational costs (editorial work, platform maintenance, archiving) under open models. Many diamond-OA journals rely on volunteer labor and occasional grants, which may not be reliable long-term. Thus, skeptics question whether the open-access system can scale indefinitely without **compromising quality or collapsing smaller outlets**. Publishers also highlight that managing peer review, copyediting, and indexing has real costs; if those aren’t recovered, it could strain the scholarly communication ecosystem. That said, new funding models – from consortium funding to institutional publishing platforms – are being tested to support no-fee open journals, and studies show that the overall cost per article can be lower in open access than in subscription systems (due to the efficiencies of online distribution) [26]. Ensuring global *financial models* that keep open publishing inclusive and high-quality remains an ongoing concern.
* **Conservatism and Academic Recognition:** Open-access platforms also face sociocultural hurdles. Academic hiring and promotion committees often value journal prestige and impact factors, many of which are associated with long-established subscription journals. There can be a bias where open-access journals (especially newer ones) are perceived as less rigorous, even if that is not the case. This can discourage some authors from publishing in open venues or lead them to pay high fees for well-known hybrid journals rather than support newer fully-OA journals. Additionally, certain research communities or regions have been slower to embrace open access due to lack of awareness, tradition, or concerns about career implications. Overcoming these perceptions and ensuring that openly published research is fully recognized in research evaluations is part of the cultural challenge ahead.



In summary, open-source and open-access publishing models have **ushered in a new era** of global academic knowledge sharing – one marked by greater access, readership, and participation across borders than ever before. The benefits in terms of visibility, citation impact, and inclusivity are well-documented and significant. However, the transformation is still ongoing, and it comes with complex challenges that require careful management. The academic community and policymakers are actively debating solutions: from regulating APC prices and supporting fee-free journals, to cracking down on predatory publishers, to crafting policies that reward open science practices. The continued evolution of these open publishing platforms will determine how successfully we can create a scholarly communication system that is both **open to all** and **rigorous and sustainable**. question: How do large language models like ChatGPT impact the diversity of published scientific ideas?

sections.title: Report
sections.text:
# Impact of LLMs on the Diversity of Published Scientific Ideas


## Introduction



Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have swiftly entered the realm of scientific research and publishing. This report examines how LLMs influence the **diversity of published scientific ideas**. Key areas of impact include widening or narrowing access to scientific publishing, potential biases in knowledge production, changes in novelty and innovation in research, effects on peer review processes and publication norms, and differences in how LLMs are affecting various regions and disciplines. Below, each subtopic is explored in detail with evidence from recent peer-reviewed studies.


## Influence on Access and Participation in Scientific Publishing



LLMs offer the promise of democratizing scientific writing by helping more researchers articulate their ideas. These AI tools can assist authors—especially those for whom English is a second language or who lack extensive writing training—in producing clearer, more formal academic prose [[1]([[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13629v1#:~:text=In%20addition%20to%20disciplinary%20differences%2C,speaking%20counterparts))][2]. For example, early evidence suggests junior scholars and non-native English speakers adopt LLM-based writing aids at higher rates than their senior or native-speaking peers, indicating that LLMs may help lower language and experience barriers to publication [[1]([[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13629v1#:~:text=In%20addition%20to%20disciplinary%20differences%2C,speaking%20counterparts))]. By providing feedback on grammar and style, LLMs can "demystify" Western academic writing conventions and improve access to knowledge from the Global North [4]. In a Delphi study, experts predicted that generative AI could foster a greater diversity of voices in science and enable more collaboration across different communities [2]. However, true democratization requires equitable access to these tools. Currently, advanced LLM technology is **concentrated in a few languages and regions** – by one estimate, only about 3% of the world’s languages are well-supported by modern language AI [5]. This imbalance raises the concern that researchers in under-resourced linguistic communities might remain marginalized even as LLMs expand participation elsewhere. Overall, LLMs have a dual impact on access: they can empower more people to contribute to scientific literature, but without deliberate efforts to include diverse languages and contexts, they might extend the dominance of already privileged groups in scientific publishing [6][7].


## Reinforcement or Mitigation of Epistemic Bias



A critical question is whether LLMs reinforce existing epistemic biases in science or help mitigate them. Because LLMs are trained on large corpora of text, often dominated by Western and anglophone sources, they risk perpetuating **dominant knowledge paradigms**. Researchers have observed that current LLMs remain *“biased toward dominant norms and knowledge paradigms”*, reflecting the perspectives prevalent in their training data [4]. This can lead to subtle forms of **epistemic injustice**, wherein viewpoints outside the mainstream (e.g. non-Western or indigenous knowledge systems) are under-represented. In fact, AI ethicists point out that *language modeling bias* – a systematic favoring of certain languages, dialects and cultural expressions – can yield AI systems that are very fluent in the discourse of dominant groups but *“limited in the expression of socio-culturally relevant notions of other communities”* [8]. Without corrective measures, LLMs could thus amplify the visibility of already well-represented theories and suppress minority perspectives, reinforcing the status quo in published science [9][10]. On the other hand, if carefully designed and used, LLMs might help surface a broader range of ideas. For instance, they could assist with translating or summarizing research from underrepresented languages, potentially *decolonizing* knowledge by bridging disparate literatures. Some scholars are calling for *“epistemic alignment”* approaches that ensure AI systems support diverse ways of knowing rather than impose a single viewpoint [11]. In practice, realizing this will require conscious efforts in curating training data and setting guidelines for LLM use. At present, the evidence suggests that **LLMs more readily reinforce existing epistemic biases** unless intentionally steered otherwise, meaning the onus is on the scientific community to use these tools in a way that broadens rather than narrows our collective knowledge base [12][9].


## Effects on Novelty and Innovation



One concern is whether heavy reliance on LLMs will stifle scientific novelty or, conversely, generate more innovative ideas. LLMs are fundamentally predictive engines that remix existing information, so there is a risk they could produce *homogenized* research narratives. Linguists warn that because LLM outputs are based on “shallow statistical associations,” they tend to drive writing toward *homogeneity and uniformity*, lacking the genuine creativity that human scientists bring when crossing linguistic and stylistic boundaries [12]. In line with this, an expert Delphi panel cautioned that if generative AI overly amplifies mainstream voices, the result could be a *“loss of research diversity,”* with fewer truly novel perspectives making it into print [10]. Initial empirical studies paint a nuanced picture. On one hand, LLMs have demonstrated an ability to suggest **novel research ideas**. In a controlled comparison, ideas generated by an LLM were judged by blinded experts as *more novel* on average than ideas from human researchers (p < 0.05), although they were also deemed slightly less feasible [13]. This suggests that LLMs might be useful for brainstorming unconventional hypotheses or interdisciplinary connections that humans might overlook. On the other hand, there is evidence that widespread use of AI can reduce the **collective diversity** of ideas. A recent experiment in *Science Advances* found that while generative AI assistance boosted the creativity of individual writers (especially less experienced ones), it also made the group’s outputs more similar to each other, decreasing overall uniqueness [14]. The authors note a potential *“downward spiral”*: if everyone uses the same AI suggestions to optimize creativity, the outputs converge and true innovation may suffer [15]. In summary, LLMs can both contribute to scientific creativity and risk homogenizing it. They may spark novel combinations of existing knowledge, but without checks they could lead researchers to settle into AI-suggested patterns, thereby dampening the radical originality that drives paradigm shifts.


## Implications for Peer Review and Publication Norms



The rise of LLMs is already challenging traditional norms in peer review and authorship. A striking development is the quiet incorporation of AI into the peer-review process: at major computer science conferences, *up to 17% of peer reviews are now written with the help of AI*, including ChatGPT [16]. This trend has prompted calls for guidelines to ensure responsible use of AI in evaluating manuscripts [16]. Proponents argue that LLMs can expedite review by quickly summarizing papers or checking for clarity, but there are serious concerns about accuracy, accountability, and transparency in AI-generated reviews. Journals and publishers are scrambling to set policies. Many have clarified that AI tools **cannot be listed as authors** (since they lack accountability) and that any use of LLMs in manuscript preparation or review should be disclosed. Indeed, a recent survey of 226 global researchers found that while 18.7% had used LLMs in preparing publications (most commonly to fix grammar or formatting), a large fraction (over 40%) of those users did *not* acknowledge the AI’s role [17]. This has raised alarms about transparency and prompted some publishers to require authors to declare any AI assistance in writing [18]. The same survey showed researchers are divided on LLMs’ impact: about 50.8% predicted an overall positive effect on research, yet 78.3% agreed that regulations are needed to prevent misuse of AI in science [19]. Key ethical issues include **authorship integrity**, plagiarism and “hallucinated” references, and the possibility of paper mills leveraging LLMs to generate fraudulent studies [20]. Encouragingly, organizations like COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) have begun issuing guidelines for AI in scholarly writing, emphasizing that authors are responsible for all content – including anything produced by an AI assistant. In peer review, editors are weighing whether to allow AI-generated referee reports; some conferences now explicitly forbid undisclosed AI-written reviews as they could undermine the rigor and trust in the process. Overall, the advent of LLMs is forcing a re-examination of publication norms, with a push toward greater disclosure and new standards to ensure that the use of AI bolsters rather than erodes the quality and credibility of scientific literature [21][22].


## Regional and Disciplinary Disparities in Influence



The influence of LLMs on scientific idea diversity is not uniform across the globe or academic fields. **Regional disparities** are evident in who has access to these powerful models and in which languages the models perform well. As noted, the vast majority of training data for models like ChatGPT is in English and a handful of other major languages, which can marginalize research communicated in less common languages [5][9]. Scholars warn that a simplistic approach to “inclusivity” in AI – for example, merely adding more data from smaller languages without cultural context – may backfire, failing to capture the true diversity of scholarly thought and even misrepresenting marginalized communities [9]. There is also a risk that Global South researchers might feel pressure to use LLMs to write in English, potentially diluting their authentic voice or modes of expression to fit AI-driven norms [6]. At the same time, if leveraged wisely, LLMs could help bridge gaps by translating and disseminating findings across linguistic divides, somewhat leveling the playing field in international academia.



Beyond region, there are clear **disciplinary differences** in LLM uptake and impact. Fields that are computationally oriented or have a preprint culture have moved fastest to integrate LLMs. One large-scale analysis of arXiv papers found that by late 2023, about 20–22% of abstracts in fields like computer science and engineering had been revised with GPT assistance, whereas in mathematics the rate was only ~3.5% [23]. Likewise, researchers in domains such as biology or economics showed moderate adoption (~10–11% of abstracts edited by GPT), indicating heterogeneity in how comfortable or applicable AI writing is across disciplines [23]. These disparities suggest that LLMs might be accelerating idea generation and paper writing in certain fast-moving fields, potentially leading to an explosion of output (for better or worse) in those areas, while other disciplines remain comparatively unaffected. Moreover, differences in funding and infrastructure play a role: well-resourced institutions (often in North America, Europe, or East Asia) can afford the latest LLM tools and thus may benefit more, whereas scholars in resource-limited settings might lag behind, widening an existing gap in research output. On the positive side, early adopters demonstrate how LLMs can be used as equalizers within a field – for instance, the arXiv study also found that **junior scientists and non-native English writers were significantly more likely to use GPT for writing help** than senior or native English authors, hinting that LLMs are serving as a support tool for those who traditionally face disadvantages in academic publishing [[1]([[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.13629v1#:~:text=In%20addition%20to%20disciplinary%20differences%2C,speaking%20counterparts))]. In summary, the impact of LLMs on idea diversity will depend on how these regional and disciplinary disparities are managed: the technology could either exacerbate the concentration of scientific influence in certain hubs, or if access widens, it could empower a more geographically and disciplinarily diverse cohort of researchers to contribute novel ideas.


## Conclusion



In conclusion, LLMs like ChatGPT are poised to both reshape and reflect the diversity of scientific ideas being published. They lower some barriers to entry in academic publishing, potentially broadening participation and aiding underrepresented researchers. At the same time, without careful oversight, LLMs may entrench existing biases – privileging dominant languages, disciplines, and epistemologies – and lead to more uniform, less pluralistic scientific literature. The net effect on innovation is double-edged: LLMs can spark creativity and generate unconventional ideas, yet pervasive use of the same AI systems could homogenize thinking and writing styles across the research community. To ensure that these tools enrich rather than diminish the diversity of scientific ideas, the research community is developing new norms: requiring transparency in AI use, formulating ethical guidelines, and striving to make LLM technology inclusive across different languages and fields. Ultimately, LLMs are a powerful aid for scientific creativity and communication, but realizing their positive potential for diversity will require conscious human guidance and a continued commitment to valuing a wide range of perspectives in science [24][14].
