# LLMs for Tabular Data via In-Context Learning: A Comparative Evaluation


## Introduction: Tabular Data and Traditional ML Approaches



Tabular data (structured rows and columns) is ubiquitous in domains from finance to healthcare. However, it poses unique challenges compared to image or text data. **Heterogeneity** of feature types (mixing numerical, categorical, binary, etc.) is common, along with **sparsity** (missing values, imbalanced labels) and **dependency on careful preprocessing** (e.g. encoding categories, normalization) [1][2]. Over the years, specialized machine learning models have excelled on tabular tasks (classification and regression). In particular, **tree-based ensemble methods** like gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT, e.g. XGBoost, LightGBM) remain state-of-the-art for many tabular benchmarks [3]. These methods are valued for their high accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability on structured data. Indeed, despite numerous deep learning architectures proposed for tables (from differentiable neural trees to attention-based tabular networks), boosted trees *still outperform* most deep nets on typical tabular datasets [4]. Classic ensembles require relatively small training time and tuning effort, and often win data science competitions on tabular data. That said, traditional models have limitations: they can be sensitive to manual feature engineering (especially for high-cardinality categorical features), and they struggle to naturally incorporate sequential or textual information per feature [5]. This has prompted research into whether the powerful **large language models (LLMs)** that revolutionized NLP can also tackle tabular prediction tasks in new ways.


## In-Context Learning with LLMs for Tabular Tasks



**In-Context Learning (ICL)** refers to an LLM’s ability to learn a task *from examples provided in the prompt*, without any parameter update [6]. Instead of training a separate model, we simply give the LLM a description of the task and a few input-output examples, and then ask it to predict the output for a new input. This emergent capability became prominent with GPT-3 (175B) [7], which showed that even large models with fixed weights can perform new tasks given a well-crafted prompt. To apply ICL on **tabular data**, the key is to **serialize the table rows into text** that the LLM can understand. For example, Hegselmann *et al.* (2023) convert each data row into a natural-language sentence or template, listing feature names and values, followed by the target label [8]. A prompt to the LLM might include several such serialized rows as demonstrations, then a final row with features only, asking the model to predict its label. An illustrative prompt snippet could be:



```



yaml




Copy



Example 1: age=25, education=Bachelor's, income= >50K  
Example 2: age=40, education=High School, income= <=50K  
...  
Now predict for: age=30, education=Master's, income= ??



```


During inference, the LLM will produce a completion for the "??", ideally the predicted class. Designing effective serializations and prompts is an active area of research [9]. Some works use simple templates (e.g. *"Feature: Value"* pairs in a sentence), others try more complex natural language descriptions or even chain-of-thought reasoning prompts. Notably, one study found that a straightforward text template of feature–value pairs yielded strong results across many tasks [10]. Overall, in-context learning allows LLMs to tackle tabular problems *without* bespoke model architecture changes or gradient-based training on the tabular data. This “no-code” approach (sometimes called *language-interfaced learning*) repurposes the rich background knowledge in LLMs for structured data tasks.


## Benchmarks: LLMs vs. Traditional Models on Tabular Data



How well do LLMs (through prompting or minimal fine-tuning) compete with dedicated tabular ML models? Recent studies have benchmarked LLMs like GPT-3/4 and others on classic datasets (e.g. UCI and Kaggle competitions), often comparing against strong baselines like XGBoost. Table 1 summarizes key findings from several peer-reviewed studies:



**Table 1: Selected studies comparing LLM-based approaches to traditional tabular models.** (LLM = large language model; GBDT = gradient-boosted decision trees like XGBoost)






| Study (Year) & Method | Datasets (Examples) | Key Comparative Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dinh *et al*. (2022)** – LIFT, fine-tune GPT-3/GPT-J on tabular [11] | 10 small classification/regression tasks (OpenML/UCI) | LLM matched the *best* traditional model in many cases, especially on classification, when data dimensions were low [11]. (Performance was on par with or even equal to baselines like XGBoost in several tasks.) However, LLM accuracy degraded when the number of classes was very large (~hundreds), where tree and ensemble methods maintained an edge [12]. |
| **Hegselmann *et al*. (2023)** – TabLLM, prompt or fine-tune T0 (11B) [13][14] | 9 tabular datasets (UCI, Kaggle) for binary/multi-class (≤50k rows, ~5–20 features) | LLM-based few-shot classification *outperformed deep learning* models (TabNet, etc.) and was **competitive with GBDTs**. In the *very-low-data regime* (e.g. <32 examples), TabLLM often surpassed XGBoost by a large margin [15]. It achieved non-trivial **zero-shot** accuracy using just the model’s prior knowledge [16]. As data increased, performance between TabLLM and traditional models converged, with tree ensembles catching up once a few hundred examples were available [17][15]. |
| **Bordt *et al*. (2024)** – GPT-3.5 & GPT-4 via 20-shot ICL [18] | Well-known public datasets: Titanic (survival), Adult Income, FICO credit risk, etc. | With 20 prompt examples, GPT-4 achieved **near state-of-the-art accuracy** on some tasks. For instance, on the Kaggle Titanic set it reached ~98% test accuracy, exceeding what a fully-trained GBDT would typically achieve [18]. This was attributed to likely memorization or prior exposure (Titanic is a very popular dataset). GPT-3.5/4 also showed strong performance on the UCI Adult income classification, matching or beating the tree model’s accuracy [19]. Notably, on a genuinely novel dataset (a medical Pneumonia dataset that the LLM had not seen in pre-training), GPT’s accuracy dropped substantially below the trained model’s, indicating that without prior knowledge the LLM still struggled to generalize [20]. |









**Benchmarks in Context:** The above results illustrate a pattern. LLMs can **hold their own** against traditional ML on tabular data, particularly when the number of labeled examples is very small. In Hegselmann *et al.*’s experiments, the TabLLM approach outperformed or equaled XGBoost and other baselines up until roughly 256 training samples per class [15]. The advantage is most pronounced in the extreme few-shot or zero-shot scenarios – e.g. GPT-based models achieved meaningful accuracy with *zero* training data on tasks like bank marketing or blood donation prediction, whereas a tree model cannot function at all with zero examples. This highlights the power of LLMs to leverage prior knowledge: by “knowing” typical feature distributions or real-world facts (from pre-training on text), an LLM can make informed guesses on unfamiliar data [21]. For example, an LLM might know that **“Masters degree” is generally associated with higher income than “High school”** from its training corpus, giving it a head start on the Adult income classification without seeing many labeled samples.



On the other hand, with **larger training sets**, conventional models catch up and often surpass the LLM. In the TabLLM study, once a few hundred examples were available, a specialized TabPFN model or XGBoost could reach the LLM’s performance or exceed it [22][15]. This makes sense, as the LLM’s advantage of built-in knowledge becomes less crucial when ample data is present to directly learn from. Additionally, LLM prompts are constrained by context length, limiting how many examples or features can be provided. In practice, fine-tuned GBDTs trained on all data still set the bar for best performance on many tabular benchmarks (especially if the LLM hasn’t seen the domain before).



Another interesting finding is the role of **memorization vs. generalization**. Bordt *et al.* (2024) discovered that GPT-4’s impressive accuracy on certain public datasets could be due to it having effectively *memorized the dataset* during pre-training [19]. The Titanic and Adult datasets, being very popular, likely appeared in some form in the model’s training data. GPT-4 was able to recall or model these so well that with minimal prompting it rivaled a fully trained classifier. But when tested on truly novel data (e.g. a new Kaggle challenge or a proprietary dataset), the LLM’s accuracy fell off, sometimes significantly below a model trained from scratch on that data [20]. This suggests that while LLMs can **quickly solve known problems**, they might still lag on completely new tasks unless given enough examples or fine-tuning.



In summary, today’s large LLMs (GPT-3.5/4, PaLM, Claude, etc.) *can* be applied to tabular prediction tasks with surprisingly strong results. They especially shine in low-data settings or when the feature semantics resonate with real-world knowledge. However, traditional ML remains very competitive, particularly as data scales. The next section delves into the general strengths and limitations behind these outcomes.


## Strengths of LLMs on Tabular Data (ICL)


* **Requires Little Training Data:** LLMs come with extensive world knowledge stored in their parameters. This allows them to achieve reasonable accuracy with few or zero labeled examples [23]. In other words, an LLM can leverage what it “knows” about feature values (from reading about similar patterns in text) to make predictions without extensive new training. This is invaluable in scenarios where collecting labels is hard or expensive. Researchers have shown even *zero-shot* classification on tabular data is possible – yielding non-trivial performance without any dataset-specific training [16].
* **Incorporating Feature Semantics:** Each column and value in a table often has a meaning that an LLM might understand. Unlike a one-hot encoded feature in XGBoost, a textual feature like *“Occupation: doctor”* or *“Education: PhD”* will trigger an LLM’s understanding of those concepts. By using natural-language field names and values, in-context prompts let the model tap into semantic context [21]. This can improve generalization. For example, GPT-4 might infer that a “Hybrid” car engine type is between gas and electric if asked to predict emissions – something a standard model would only learn if shown enough examples.
* **Strong Few-Shot Learning Ability:** With a handful of examples provided, LLMs can adapt to the format and quirks of a new task. Studies found that a prompted LLM could beat deep neural network models and even approach tree ensemble performance with as few as 16–32 training samples [13][14]. In ultra-sparse data regimes (e.g. 10 labeled points), boosted trees often overfit or fail, whereas an LLM can leverage prior knowledge to make more sensible guesses [15].
* **Unified Model for Many Tasks:** A single large language model can, in principle, handle a wide variety of tasks – from image captions to SQL queries and also tabular classification – just by changing its prompt. This means one can use an off-the-shelf LLM (via an API like GPT-4 or an open source model) to solve a tabular problem *without developing a new model from scratch*. This “model reuse” is convenient: for instance, a data analyst could feed a small dataset description to ChatGPT and get predictions or insights, bypassing a full ML pipeline. The **ease-of-use** is high – many LLM-based tools (e.g. ChatGPT) offer natural language interfaces to query data, requiring no coding or model training to get started [24].
* **Prior Knowledge and Reasoning:** In some cases, LLMs can perform reasoning or incorporate external knowledge that traditional models lack. For example, an LLM might know about causal relationships or physical constraints that correlate with the data. There is evidence that LLMs can follow instructions and perform step-by-step reasoning on structured inputs [25]. This could be useful for tasks like deriving a conclusion from multiple table entries or handling missing values by making educated guesses (a form of imputation using common sense). Moreover, LLMs have been used for *data cleaning* and augmentation tasks on tables – e.g. using GPT-3 to fill in missing entries or correct inconsistencies – often with excellent results given only a handful of examples [26].


## Limitations of LLMs on Tabular Data (ICL)



Despite their promise, current LLM approaches face several limitations when applied to structured data:


* **Context Length and Scalability:** In-context learning requires fitting the relevant data into the prompt. Even advanced models like GPT-4 max out at a few thousand tokens, which means they cannot directly ingest large datasets. You might only be able to show a small subset of examples or features at once. This makes it hard to scale LLMs to tasks with many thousands of samples or very high-dimensional tables. Traditional models do not have this limitation – they train on the full dataset regardless of size. While techniques exist (e.g. clever sampling of in-context examples), the context window remains a bottleneck for using LLMs on “big data” tables.
* **Need for Careful Prompt Design:** LLMs are notoriously **sensitive to prompt formatting** and content [25]. Small changes in how you present the table or query can lead to different answers. Crafting an optimal prompt (selecting which examples to include, how to phrase feature names, etc.) often requires trial and error. Hegselmann *et al.* note that serialization method alone can affect accuracy significantly in few-shot settings [10]. This adds an extra burden, whereas algorithms like XGBoost just take numeric input as-is. Research is ongoing into prompt engineering strategies (e.g. example selection by similarity [27]), but the dependency on prompt quality is a fragility that pure ML models don’t have.
* **Lack of Tabular Pre-Training:** Out-of-the-box LLMs are trained on internet text, not on tabular data. They have no inherent understanding of tables, numbers, or structured relationships beyond what can be inferred from text. Converting tabular data to a prose format is an imperfect solution – it may introduce ambiguity or lose subtle structure. As one study pointed out, relying solely on text serialization without any table-specific pretraining limits the LLM’s potential on data science tasks [28]. The model might struggle with numerical precision, or with understanding that certain columns are related (e.g. *year* and *month* might be better treated as date). In contrast, purpose-built tabular models have inductive biases for these (e.g. trees can naturally handle mixed types and missing values).
* **Lower Performance with Sufficient Data:** When plenty of labeled data is available, LLMs generally do *not* beat dedicated models. After all, an LLM’s strength is using prior knowledge to compensate for meager training data. But if you have, say, 10,000 labeled examples, a well-tuned GBDT or a deep tabular network can fully learn the relationships, often achieving higher accuracy than an in-context LLM that’s trying to parse all that data from a prompt. Empirical results show LLM advantages evaporate in high-data regimes [17][15]. Moreover, fine-tuning an LLM on large tabular datasets (instead of just prompting) is possible but computationally expensive and not guaranteed to surpass tabular-specific algorithms.
* **Output Constraints and Reliability:** LLMs generate free-form text, which can be problematic for strict tabular outputs. A language model might **hallucinate** an answer that is not a valid category or produce extra commentary around the prediction [29]. Ensuring the LLM outputs exactly one of the allowed labels (and nothing more) can require careful prompt instructions or post-processing. This is easier to guarantee in a conventional classifier. Similarly, LLMs do not provide calibrated probabilities out-of-the-box, whereas tree models can give well-calibrated probability estimates for uncertainty.
* **Interpretability and Debugging:** In regulated industries, the explainability of a model’s decisions on tabular data is crucial. Tree-based models can offer straightforward explanations (e.g. feature importance or decision rules). LLM decisions, on the other hand, are hard to interpret – they involve the complex vector interactions of a massive neural network. While one can prompt an LLM to *explain its reasoning*, these explanations may not be reliable. The lack of transparent reasoning is a hurdle for trusting LLMs in sensitive tabular applications. As noted in a recent survey, interpretability and explanation methods for LLM-based tabular predictions are still largely unexplored [30]. Current LLMs can also reflect or even amplify biases present in their training data, raising **fairness concerns** if used for decisions like credit scoring or hiring [29].
* **Computational Cost:** Running a large LLM (especially via API) can be orders of magnitude slower and costlier than running a lightweight model like XGBoost. For example, classifying 1,000 rows with GPT-4 may require 1,000 separate prompt invocations, which is not trivial in time or money. In contrast, a single trained XGBoost model would predict 1,000 rows in milliseconds on a CPU. This gap means that for large-scale inference or deployment, the LLM-in-context approach may be impractical without significant optimization or model distillation.


## Recent Research and Advances (2022–2025)



The convergence of LLMs and tabular data is a very active research area. A number of recent peer-reviewed works are pushing the boundaries and addressing the above limitations:


* **Tabular-Specific Foundation Models:** Zhang *et al.* (2024) introduced the concept of **Tabular Foundation Models (TabFMs)**, which involve pre-training LLMs on a large collection of tabular datasets to endow them with a “universal” understanding of structured data [31]. Their TabFM model uses a pretrained language model as a base and fine-tunes it on table data with specialized objectives. The result is a model that *excels at instruction-following for table tasks (zero-shot and ICL)* and even *matches or surpasses GPT-4* on certain tabular benchmarks [32]. Moreover, TabFM showed improved efficiency when fine-tuned on small data, and competitive performance with lots of data – indicating that pretraining on tables can yield a more data-efficient learner. This line of work suggests future “GPT-for-tables” models could combine the best of both worlds: LLM flexibility with tabular savvy.
* **Prompt Engineering & Fairness:** How to optimally prompt an LLM for tabular tasks is under study. Aside from choosing good example rows (some methods select examples similar to the test query to improve accuracy [27]), researchers are also looking at prompts to mitigate bias. One approach (Yang *et al.*, 2023) found that **flipping the demographic group labels in a few-shot prompt** can partially mitigate fairness disparities in LLM predictions [33]. Essentially, by demonstrating in-context that certain sensitive attributes swap outcomes, the LLM can be nudged toward more fair predictions – though often at a slight cost in overall accuracy. This kind of prompt-based intervention is a novel way to impose constraints or values on an LLM without retraining it.
* **Hybrid Models (Model Grafting):** Another direction is combining LLMs with dedicated encoders for structured features. Belyaeva *et al.* (2023) propose a *model grafting* technique, mapping non-text features into an LLM’s token space via specialized encoding networks [34]. For example, a numeric time-series or a set of categorical variables can be transformed into pseudo-words (embedding vectors) that are fed into the language model alongside text tokens. This allows models like GPT-3/4 to ingest heterogeneous data in a format they can process, potentially improving performance on tasks that involve not only text but also raw signals or numbers. The HeLM model is one such example that integrated medical spirogram data with patient text notes, using an LLM to model both [34]. While promising, these approaches increase complexity and sacrifice some of the end-to-end simplicity of pure prompting – but they indicate how LLMs might be extended to better handle non-language fields.
* **Open Models and Numeric Reasoning:** Recognizing LLM limitations with numbers, some recent open-source LMs have been adapted to better handle numerical data. For instance, researchers found that tweaking the tokenizer to treat each digit as a separate token (instead of whole numbers) improved arithmetic problem solving for LMs [35]. Such tokenizer and architecture adjustments (e.g. for units, dates, or large categorical vocabularies) could translate to better performance on certain tabular features. There is also an increasing array of open LLMs (LLaMA-2, etc.) that can be fine-tuned on domain-specific data, including tables, at lower cost. As these models become more capable, practitioners may not need to rely on closed-source APIs for tabular ICL, especially if they can fine-tune an open model on similar tasks.
* **Surveys and Benchmarks:** A comprehensive survey by Fang *et al.* (2024) catalogued the fast-growing literature on LLMs for tabular data [36][37]. It provides a taxonomy of tasks (from prediction to data synthesis and table Q&A), common datasets, and evaluation metrics. The survey highlights current limitations (e.g. hallucination, preprocessing burdens, lack of interpretability) and calls out open problems [29]. Such overviews are valuable for guiding future research. Meanwhile, new benchmarks are being proposed – for example, to test LLMs on *truly novel* tabular tasks to ensure we measure generalization rather than memorization [38][20]. The community is increasingly aware that as LLMs are applied to tabular data science, careful evaluation (and sometimes new metrics) are needed to assess their real-world utility versus traditional methods.


## Conclusion: When (and Whether) to Use LLMs for Tabular Tasks



**LLMs with in-context learning** offer an exciting new tool in the tabular data toolkit, but they are not a silver bullet for all cases. Based on current evidence, a few guidelines emerge on when one might favor an LLM over traditional ML for tabular tasks:


* **Small Data or Few Labels:** If you have very limited labeled examples (e.g. a few dozen to a few hundred), an LLM can be remarkably effective. It can leverage prior knowledge to make reasonable predictions where a standard model might overfit or fail to train. For instance, in a medical dataset with only 50 samples for a rare disease, GPT-4 with a well-crafted prompt may glean insights from medical background knowledge that no classical model could. In such low-data scenarios, LLMs often outperform even tuned XGBoost models [15].
* **Need for Rapid Prototyping:** If you want to *quickly test* an idea or get a baseline result without a complex pipeline, using an LLM via ICL is very convenient. There’s no need to clean data into numeric format, select features, or tune hyperparameters – you can paste the data (in text form) into a prompt and ask the model to predict or explain. This agility is useful in early exploratory phases of a project. Tools like GPT-4 can also provide natural language justifications for each prediction if prompted, which can aid understanding (though these justifications should be taken with caution).
* **Rich Textual Features or External Knowledge:** When your tabular data includes text fields or categorical values that have meaning in the real world, LLMs have an edge. They can read a product description, job title, or medical code and incorporate vast contextual knowledge about it. Traditional models would require embedding those text features numerically and might not capture nuances. Similarly, if the task would benefit from common-sense reasoning or external facts (e.g. predicting house prices might benefit from knowing neighborhood crime rates or school quality, which an LLM might infer from the address), an LLM can implicitly use such information.
* **Ad-hoc Queries and Mixed Tasks:** LLMs are ideal for interactive, ad-hoc analysis on tables. If a user wants to ask a question in English about their data (combining a bit of computation, reasoning, and domain knowledge), an LLM-based assistant can handle it more flexibly than a fixed ML model. For example, “Which region had the largest increase in sales quarter-over-quarter, and is that increase statistically significant?” is a query that involves understanding the table and performing a comparison – something an LLM (especially fine-tuned for table QA) can do on the fly, whereas a traditional model would not even know how to approach the question without explicit programming.



On the other hand, **there are plenty of situations where traditional tabular ML remains preferable**:


* If you have **large amounts of data** and the goal is pure predictive accuracy, a dedicated model (GBDT or a specialized deep network) trained on that data is likely to outperform an in-context LLM. For example, in a Kaggle competition with tens of thousands of examples, fine-tuned models almost always beat zero/few-shot GPT-style approaches in the leaderboard. The LLM’s advantages diminish as the dataset grows [17], and it may be unable to even ingest all the data due to context limits.
* If **computational efficiency** and deployment cost are concerns, traditional models are vastly lighter. Deploying a 100 KB XGBoost model to make millions of predictions per hour at near-zero cost is routine. Querying an LLM of 100+ billion parameters for each prediction will be several orders more expensive. Thus, for low-latency or high-throughput production systems (fraud detection running continuously, for instance), LLMs are not yet practical as the primary predictor.
* When **interpretability, robustness, and compliance** matter, one might stick to simpler models. A bank might prefer a transparent logistic regression or decision tree for credit approval decisions rather than an opaque LLM, to satisfy regulatory requirements. Likewise, if the input distribution shifts, an LLM might hallucinate strange outputs, whereas a well-understood model’s behavior is easier to audit and trust. Current LLMs can also inadvertently incorporate biases present in their training data, so using them for high-stakes tabular decisions requires careful fairness and bias evaluation [29].
* **Privacy considerations** also come into play. Using an API-driven LLM on sensitive tabular data means sending that data to a third-party server, which may be unacceptable for personal, medical, or confidential information. In such cases, training a local model that stays on-premise can be safer. While there are on-premise LLMs, they often require significant resources to run, unlike a lightweight Random Forest.



In conclusion, large language models have demonstrated an intriguing capability to solve traditional tabular ML problems through in-context learning. They bridge the gap between human-like reasoning on data and automated pattern recognition, bringing in external knowledge to boost predictions on small data tasks. The **research frontier (2022–2025)** has shown proof-of-concept that LLMs can sometimes rival specialized models even on structured data [13][11]. Yet, this approach complements rather than replaces the conventional toolkit. For many real-world tabular applications, especially those with ample data or strict requirements, gradient boosting machines, linear models, or custom networks remain the go-to solution [4]. We should view LLMs as a powerful new option in our arsenal: one that shines in low-data, high-knowledge scenarios and for flexible AI-driven data analysis, but one that must be applied with awareness of its limits. Going forward, as research produces better hybrid models and tabular-aware LLMs [32], we may see the line continue to blur – bringing more of the strengths of both approaches together to tackle the age-old challenge of making sense of rows and columns.

# Insights into Developer Behavior on GitHub from Commits and Pull Requests


## Introduction



GitHub is the largest platform for collaborative software development, with tens of millions of repositories and an immense volume of commits and pull requests (PRs) forming its activity stream [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. Analyzing this rich data has become a cornerstone of research in software engineering and human-computer interaction. By mining commit histories and PR discussions, researchers can uncover patterns in how developers write code, collaborate, and respond to feedback. Such insights can inform better tooling and practices for development teams [2]. *At the same time, not all repositories or contributions are alike.* Many GitHub projects are personal or short-lived, and a significant portion of commits may be trivial changes that are quickly reverted [3]. Therefore, studies carefully filter and interpret data to avoid misleading conclusions [4]. In the sections below, we summarize key findings from peer-reviewed research on developer behavior as revealed by commit and PR analytics, covering coding patterns, collaboration styles, productivity indicators, responsiveness to code review, evolution of code quality, temporal activity trends, team dynamics, and open-source contribution characteristics.


## Coding Patterns in Commits



**Granularity and frequency of commits:** Empirical studies show that commit activity on GitHub is extremely skewed. In a large sample of over 5,000 repositories, *almost one-third had fewer than 50 total commits and the majority under 100*, indicating that many projects see only light development [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. Furthermore, about 20% of these projects were active in less than two distinct months overall (i.e. development occurred in one burst), underscoring how short-lived many efforts are [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. Conversely, a small fraction of projects sustain heavy, long-term commit activity. Such differences are sometimes correlated with technology: for example, repository primary language has been linked to commit patterns. Projects written in certain languages (e.g. Unix scripting or markup languages) often show lower commit counts and shorter active periods, whereas others (like popular application languages) tend to sustain more continuous commits [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. These patterns suggest that commit frequency alone must be contextualized by project type and language.



**Micro-commits and follow-up fixes:** Many developers adopt a style of making very small commits to address minor issues. Recent research on *“micro commits”* (tiny changes affecting only a few tokens of code) found that these are common and often serve to fix bugs or fine-tune behavior [8]. For instance, a micro-commit might simply adjust a constant or correct a variable name – a minimal change that nonetheless improves correctness or clarity. In a similar vein, developers frequently perform *“quick remedy” commits*: a commit that closely follows a previous commit by the same author to remedy something overlooked or introduced by that prior change [9]. For example, after committing a refactoring that renames a function, a developer might realize they missed updating a call site and commit a quick fix for the broken reference. These follow-up commits can also include minor improvements like renaming a newly added variable for better clarity [9]. Recognizing such commit patterns is important for mining software repositories: one study provided a taxonomy of omitted-change fixes and cautioned that certain categories, like *reverted commits* (where a change is entirely undone by a subsequent commit), can introduce noise if not accounted for in analyses [10]. In short, developers often use a rapid, iterative commit style – committing incomplete changes and then immediately adjusting them – which reflects an incremental approach to coding and debugging.


## Collaboration Styles on Pull Requests



**Discussion and decision processes:** Pull requests on GitHub facilitate not only code integration but also rich discussions among developers. Qualitative analysis of PR discussions reveals that reviewers and contributors discuss two main aspects of a contribution: (1) the appropriateness or desirability of the problem being addressed, and (2) the correctness and quality of the proposed solution [11]. It’s common for core project members and even third-party stakeholders (such as developers from dependent projects or interested users) to join these conversations [11]. They may suggest changes or even alternate solutions during the review. Interestingly, different stakeholders can influence the outcome by rallying support from various communities (for example, a company backing a PR or maintainers of projects that use the code voicing their needs) [12]. This social negotiation means PR outcomes are not purely a matter of code quality. In fact, the outcome of a PR review can be more complex than simple *accept* or *reject*. One study documented cases where a PR was formally rejected, yet the core team implemented a solution of their own that achieved the same goals the contributor had – essentially fulfilling the contributor’s idea through an alternative path [13]. Such scenarios show that even a closed PR can influence project direction.



**Influence of social factors:** Collaboration style on GitHub is also shaped by who the contributor is and their history with the project. Prior relationships and reputation can significantly sway the process. For example, a study of pull request evaluations found that contributions from developers who had previous interactions or a established rapport with the project were far more likely to be accepted – even when controlling for technical factors [14]. In contrast, drive-by contributors or newcomers often face more skepticism and stricter scrutiny, sometimes having their PRs summarily rejected for not aligning with project norms [15]. Additionally, the tone of discussion can differ: core members tended to communicate more patiently or politely with contributors who were familiar faces, whereas entirely new contributors might receive more direct or terse feedback [15]. These findings highlight that GitHub collaboration is not a purely meritocratic review of code; it is a social process where trust, communication style, and community norms play important roles alongside the technical content.


## Productivity Indicators from Commit Data



**Commit metrics as productivity signals:** The number of commits and frequency of updates are often used as rough indicators of a developer’s productivity or engagement on a project [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. For instance, consistent daily commits or a high total commit count may suggest a highly active contributor or team. Recruiters and managers have even begun examining candidates’ GitHub commit histories as evidence of productivity and skills [2]. Research leveraging GitHub data indeed aims to quantify such activity. In one large-scale study, projects with long-running, steady commit activity were contrasted against those with only short bursts of development [selab.netlab.uky.edu][selab.netlab.uky.edu]. The analysis confirmed that sustained high commit counts over time are relatively uncommon – many repositories are inactive after a few commits – so a consistently active project stands out as productive [selab.netlab.uky.edu]. Additionally, correlations between primary programming language and commit frequency were observed (e.g., repositories in certain scripting or markup languages tend to have slower update rates) [selab.netlab.uky.edu], suggesting that what “high productivity” looks like can depend on the technology context.



**Interpreting commit-based metrics carefully:** While commit counts, commit frequency, and PR throughput are useful quantitative measures, researchers urge caution in treating them as straightforward productivity scores [4]. GitHub’s vast ecosystem contains *noise* that can distort these metrics. A significant portion of repositories are one-person projects or experiments that never intended long-term development [3]. Moreover, many commits are very small (typo fixes, cosmetic changes) or are later reverted; counting these naively as equal to substantial feature development can be misleading [3]. As one empirical analysis noted, there is a *“long tail”* of developers who make very few commits: filtering out about 70% of the least active contributors only removed 10% of total commits, meaning a minority of developers account for the bulk of contributions [17]. This long-tail phenomenon implies that raw commit totals need context (such as thresholds to focus on active developers or weighting by significance of change). In summary, commit and PR metrics are valuable productivity indicators, but they must be interpreted in context, with attention to project size, commit significance, and the presence of trivial or churned changes.


## Responsiveness to Code Review Feedback



**Time to first response:** The speed with which maintainers or peers respond to a pull request is a critical factor in the PR’s outcome and the contributor’s experience. Studies have quantified the *“time to first response”* on GitHub PRs and found it to be strongly linked to overall PR latency. In particular, a prompt human review can dramatically shorten how long a pull request remains open [18]. One large-scale analysis showed that the time until a human reviewer first comments explains roughly **65%** of the variance in total PR turnaround time (i.e. time to merge or close); by contrast, an immediate automated response (from bots or CI checks) had virtually no effect on speeding up the process [18]. In other words, it’s the human engagement that matters most in moving a contribution forward. This has important implications for project maintainers: triaging new PRs quickly – even with a brief initial feedback or acknowledgment – can significantly accelerate integration.



**Impact on contributor behavior:** Responsiveness is not only about efficiency; it also influences whether developers, especially newcomers, remain engaged. Recent research found a clear correlation between fast reviewer feedback and future contributions by new developers [19]. Newcomers who received a first human response to their pull request within a day were substantially more likely to submit subsequent PRs, whereas those left waiting for extended periods often did not return [19]. This suggests that timely feedback makes contributors feel welcome and motivated to continue. Additionally, certain characteristics of the PR and project can affect response times. Simpler, smaller PRs tend to get a faster first review, as do PRs where the contributor has communicated well with the maintainers (e.g. following contribution guidelines or discussing changes in advance) [19]. Conversely, complex changes or lack of prior communication can lengthen the wait. In summary, being responsive to PRs is a key aspect of healthy project behavior: it improves merge times and encourages ongoing participation. Projects may use these findings to set goals (like responding to new contributions within 24 hours) in order to foster productivity and community growth.


## Evolution of Code Quality Over Time



**Developer experience and code quality:** As developers gain experience through continuous contributions, their personal code quality tends to improve. Evidence from mining Git repositories shows that *more experienced or active developers introduce fewer bugs* in their commits on average [20]. One study quantified this by analyzing the bug-fix history of projects: developers with a high volume of past commits (or longer tenure on the project) had a lower percentage of their commits flagged as buggy, compared to less experienced contributors [20]. Similarly, developers who regularly commit (daily or weekly) tend to produce more stable changes than those who commit infrequently [20]. These findings intuitively align with the idea that practice and familiarity with the codebase lead to higher-quality code. It’s also notable that no single “worst” time or day for code quality applies universally – for example, some projects found more bugs on weekends, others on weekdays – indicating that each team’s dynamics and schedules affect quality in nuanced ways [20]. Nonetheless, a particularly striking pattern was observed in one classic study: **late-night code commits (between midnight and 4 AM) were found to be significantly more prone to bugs, whereas commits made in the morning (roughly 7 AM to noon) were less likely to be buggy** [21]. This suggests that factors like developer fatigue or circadian rhythms can impact code quality, and developers (or teams) might consider avoiding critical deployments during the “wee hours” whenever possible [21].



**Improvement through feedback and refactoring:** At the team and project level, code quality can evolve positively over a project’s lifetime, especially when systematic practices like code review and refactoring are in place. A longitudinal study of a large industrial project (and replicated on an open-source project) found that over time the nature of code review feedback shifted towards more specific, technical issues – indicating that trivial problems were gradually eliminated and reviewers focused on deeper design or context-specific concerns [22]. This evolution of feedback suggests that the codebase was improving (fewer basic mistakes to catch) and that reviewers were honing their skills, thereby *increasing the return on investment of code reviews in later stages of the project* [23]. In open-source settings, continuous refactoring and architectural improvements can likewise yield measurable quality gains. For example, a case study on the long-running **TestNG** project tracked software quality metrics across five major versions and observed clear improvements: complexity and coupling metrics decreased and maintainability indices improved, reflecting that the framework became more stable and easier to modify over the years [24]. These improvements were attributed to conscious efforts by developers to pay off technical debt and enhance the design iteratively [24]. Such evidence reinforces that code quality is not static – it can trend upward as a project matures, developers become more experienced, and feedback loops (like code reviews and testing) catch issues early. Successful teams cultivate this by fostering a culture of continuous improvement.


## Temporal Activity Patterns



**Daily and weekly cycles:** Developer activity on GitHub often follows temporal cycles. Broadly, many open-source developers contribute during evenings or weekends (outside regular work hours), whereas those working on company time might commit during weekdays 9–5. These differences aside, studies have uncovered some general patterns. One noteworthy finding is that *the time of day* a commit is made correlates with its quality: commits stamped in the late night hours (midnight to early morning) tend to have a higher likelihood of bugs, whereas commits made during normal morning working hours see relatively fewer bugs [21]. This phenomenon, observed in a study of multiple projects, hints that fatigue or reduced alertness at night can lead to more mistakes. Additionally, researchers looked at the day-of-week effect on buggy commits. While no single day is universally worst across all projects, individual projects have found their own “hazardous” days – for example, one project saw more buggy commits on Sundays [25][20]. Such variations likely reflect each project’s work patterns (some may do heavy development on weekends, others during weekdays). The takeaway is that both human factors and project schedules create temporal peaks and valleys in productivity and quality. Projects may leverage this knowledge by scheduling critical reviews or releases at times when developers are likely to be fresh and attentive.



**Lifecycles of contributor involvement:** Temporal patterns also emerge over longer timescales in a developer’s or contributor group’s activity trajectory. Open-source communities, in particular, exhibit a **core–periphery dynamic** that changes over time. New contributors often start at the periphery (occasional or one-off contributions), but some will increase their involvement and move toward the core (becoming frequent, primary contributors) before possibly fading out. A temporal analysis of contributors in several long-lived GitHub projects identified *three main patterns* in how individuals transition from peripheral to core roles [26]. Some contributors followed a **steep ramp-up**, quickly becoming very active (often due to being hired or dedicating significant time), while others showed **slow-and-steady growth** in contributions. There were also **bursty contributors** who had an intense period of activity and then dropped off [27]. Understanding these patterns is important for project maintainers trying to nurture new talent: it can help predict which newcomers might become long-term core members and which might disengage. Additionally, research on collaboration networks over time found that the *overall structure of contribution evolves*: as a project grows, the core group’s internal collaboration patterns can become more tightly knit and central, while the peripheral contributor base expands in number [[28]([[29](https://livablesoftware.com/collaboration-patterns-of-the-active-developers-in-github/#:~:text=,between%20each%20programming%20language%20and))]. In essence, thriving projects manage to continually integrate new contributors (broadening the periphery) while still maintaining a coordinated core team over the project’s timeline.


## Team Dynamics in Development



**Core vs. peripheral contributors:** Developer teams on GitHub – whether open-source or within organizations – often have an uneven distribution of work. A relatively small *core team* typically contributes the majority of code, while a larger group of peripheral contributors make smaller, infrequent contributions. Empirical evidence supports this classic pattern: one study of top-starred GitHub repositories showed that by filtering out ~70% of the least active developers (those with very few commits), the remaining active developers were responsible for about 90% of the code commits [17]. This long-tail distribution means most casual contributors collectively account for only a small share of changes. The core developers not only contribute more but also collaborate differently. They tend to form a closely connected subgraph within the project’s social network. In fact, comparing the “active developer” network to the entire GitHub developer network, researchers found that the active core is **less densely connected overall but more centralized** – essentially a tight nucleus rather than a broad, flat community [[28]([[29](https://livablesoftware.com/collaboration-patterns-of-the-active-developers-in-github/#:~:text=,between%20each%20programming%20language%20and))]. In those projects, a giant cluster of core collaborators works on the majority of the code, while others are only loosely connected. These core teams also exhibited stronger *community structure* (sub-teams or modules) within themselves [[28]([[29](https://livablesoftware.com/collaboration-patterns-of-the-active-developers-in-github/#:~:text=,between%20each%20programming%20language%20and))]. Such team dynamics indicate clear role differentiation: core members coordinate closely and carry most of the development burden, whereas peripheral contributors provide drive-by fixes, minor features, or documentation, often with less direct interaction with others.



**Knowledge sharing and project resilience:** The core-periphery team structure has implications for knowledge flow and project resilience. A highly centralized collaboration pattern (where one or two developers dominate) might speed up decisions, but it also raises the **bus factor** concern – if those key individuals leave, the project could stall. Some teams mitigate this by encouraging pair programming, extensive code review, or documentation so that knowledge is shared beyond the core. Studies comparing collaboration metrics over time found that the core’s centralization can fluctuate: for instance, as projects mature, sometimes more contributors join the core (reducing centralization), or conversely the core becomes even more solidified around a few experts [[28]([[29](https://livablesoftware.com/collaboration-patterns-of-the-active-developers-in-github/#:~:text=,between%20each%20programming%20language%20and))]. Tracking these shifts is part of understanding team health. A positive sign of dynamic team growth is when peripheral contributors successfully transition to core roles, increasing the project’s resilience. Research has indeed observed cases of this progression (from “periphery to core”) and identified common pathways, such as a contributor starting with small bug fixes, then taking on larger features, and eventually being granted direct commit access as a maintainer [26]. On the other hand, projects with stagnant or closed-off cores may struggle to attract or retain new talent. Overall, team dynamics on GitHub highlight the importance of balancing a strong, expert core with an active, renewing outer layer of contributors.


## Contributions to Open-Source Projects



**Volunteer vs. paid contributions:** A notable trend in recent years is the significant involvement of paid developers (those funded by companies or organizations) in open-source projects. Research on projects like **Mozilla’s Rust** language has shed light on differences between volunteer hobbyists and corporate-supported contributors working side by side. In Rust, for example, it was found that *core paid developers tend to contribute far more frequently*, essentially acting as full-time maintainers, while volunteer core contributors might have more sporadic activity [30]. Interestingly, one-off contributions by paid developers (e.g. when a company engineer submits a single large patch) tended to be **larger in size** than one-off contributions from volunteers [30]. This suggests companies sometimes engage by landing big features or integrations through dedicated sprints. Paid peripheral contributors were observed to focus on feature implementation more than bugfixes, perhaps aligning with company feature roadmaps [30]. Moreover, being a paid contributor correlated with a higher likelihood of sticking around long-term in the project’s community (the companies effectively invest in sustained involvement) [30]. From the volunteers’ perspective, studies indicate there can be some tension or perception gaps – some unpaid contributors express concern or *“prejudices”* that paid developers might exert too much influence or have different motivations [31]. However, the reality is often that projects benefit greatly from corporate contributions, and many projects actively welcome companies’ help as long as it aligns with community goals.



**Scale and growth of OSS participation:** Open-source projects draw contributors from around the world, and their growth has accelerated. Recent analyses estimate that a substantial share of open-source work is done during normal work hours, implying employer support. By using commit timestamps as a proxy, one study estimated that roughly **50% of OSS contributions are made by developers during 9–5 weekday hours**, which strongly suggests those contributions are part of their paid job duties [32]. Major tech companies now encourage employees to contribute to or even lead open-source projects, blurring the line between volunteer and professional work. At the same time, the pool of volunteer contributors continues to expand. GitHub’s yearly Octoverse reports have noted record numbers of first-time OSS contributors each year, indicating that the barrier to entry is lowering. The challenge is retaining these newcomers. Many open-source projects see a large influx of one-time contributors (for example, people who submit a single fix or translation and then disappear). The earlier observation of a long tail of developers making very few commits underscores this pattern [17]. Successful projects put effort into onboarding and mentoring to convert drive-by contributions into repeat participation. Community practices like labeling easy issues for first-timers, conducting mentorship programs, and being responsive to PRs (as discussed above) all aim to improve newcomer retention. Indeed, when new contributors have a positive experience (timely feedback, their contribution accepted, and guidance offered), they are more likely to become regular contributors. In summary, open-source contribution behavior is shaped by a mix of motivations and support structures: some developers are intrinsically motivated volunteers, others are salaried to work on OSS, and together they form the vibrant ecosystem we see today. Understanding these dynamics helps communities ensure sustainable project growth and collaborative harmony.


## Conclusion



Analysis of GitHub commits and pull requests offers a window into the practices and patterns of modern software development. We have seen how developers’ coding patterns include frequent small commits and quick fix follow-ups, and how collaboration styles on PRs blend technical evaluation with social interaction and negotiation. Simple metrics like commit counts can serve as productivity indicators, but they must be applied thoughtfully, given the diversity of project types and contributor behaviors. The responsiveness of maintainers – particularly in providing prompt, constructive code review feedback – emerges as crucial for both project efficiency and community health, influencing code quality and contributor retention. Over time, both individuals and teams tend to improve: experienced developers introduce fewer bugs and projects that invest in code review and refactoring become more maintainable. Temporal analyses remind us that *when* and *how* developers work (from daily cycles to multi-year contribution trajectories) can affect outcomes, highlighting the human element in software engineering. Team dynamics often manifest as a core-periphery structure, underscoring the need to cultivate new core members and share knowledge broadly. Finally, the landscape of open-source contributions is evolving with increasing professional involvement, and successful projects learn to integrate paid and volunteer efforts while encouraging newcomers. All of these insights, backed by empirical research [9][11][19], contribute to a deeper understanding of developer behavior. Such understanding can inform better project management strategies, tooling (e.g. intelligent code review assistance), and community practices to improve productivity, code quality, and developer satisfaction in the software ecosystems of today.
