# Correlations Among Fairness Metrics Across Models and Datasets


## Introduction



Machine learning fairness is typically evaluated using **group fairness metrics** – statistical criteria that compare model performance or outputs across different demographic groups. Common metrics include *demographic parity*, *equalized odds*, *predictive parity*, and *calibration*. These metrics capture different notions of what it means for a model to be "fair." However, they are not always compatible with one another. This report provides an overview of major fairness metrics and their definitions, examines known theoretical relationships (and incompatibilities) between these metrics, and reviews empirical studies that compare multiple fairness metrics on various datasets (such as COMPAS and the UCI Adult dataset) and across model types (logistic regression, random forests, neural networks). We also discuss conditions under which these metrics tend to correlate or diverge, and summarize key findings in tables and figures where appropriate.


## Major Fairness Metrics and Definitions



Several key fairness metrics have been proposed in the literature, each formalizing a different fairness criterion. Below is an overview of the major metrics, along with their definitions:


* **Demographic Parity (Statistical Parity)** – Requires the model’s positive prediction rate to be the same for each protected group. In other words, the prediction $\hat{Y}$ should be independent of the sensitive attribute $A$ (e.g., race or gender) [[1]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Demographic%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,risk%20for)]. Formally, $\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=\text{group}_1) = \Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=\text{group}_2)$ for all groups. This criterion (an *independence* condition) ensures each group receives positive outcomes at equal rates, though it does not account for actual outcome rates in each group.
* **Equalized Odds** – Requires the model’s error rates to be equal across groups. In particular, the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR) should be the same for each protected group [[2]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Equalized%20odds%20asserts%20that%20the,if%20the%20ROC%20curves%20do)]. Equivalently, $\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=\text{group}_1) = \Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=\text{group}_2)$ and $\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=0, A=\text{group}_1) = \Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=0, A=\text{group}_2)$. This criterion (a form of *separation*) ensures no group has disproportionately higher misclassification rates [[2]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Equalized%20odds%20asserts%20that%20the,if%20the%20ROC%20curves%20do)]. A related, relaxed metric is **Equal Opportunity**, which demands only equal TPR across groups (focusing on the “advantaged” outcome) [[2]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Equalized%20odds%20asserts%20that%20the,if%20the%20ROC%20curves%20do)].
* **Predictive Parity** – Requires that **precision** (positive predictive value) is equal across groups [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. In other words, among those predicted positive, the proportion who truly are positive should be the same for each group: $\Pr(Y=1 \mid \hat{Y}=1, A=\text{group}_1) = \Pr(Y=1 \mid \hat{Y}=1, A=\text{group}_2)$. Some definitions of predictive parity also require equal negative predictive value across groups [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. Predictive parity is an example of the *sufficiency* criterion, meaning the model’s output (score or label) has equal meaning for all groups. In practice, predictive parity means a positive prediction is equally reliable regardless of group membership.
* **Calibration (Calibration Within Groups)** – A model is calibrated if its risk scores correspond to true outcome probabilities in each group. Formally, for a well-calibrated classifier, individuals given a predicted risk score $p$ should have approximately $p$ probability of the outcome, regardless of group [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. Equivalently, $Y \perp!!\perp A \mid \text{score}$ (outcome is independent of group when conditioning on the score) [4]. Calibration *within each group* is essentially the condition that each group’s predictions are probabilistically sound. Notably, **predictive parity at a single threshold** (equal PPV) is a special case of calibration by group for binary decisions [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. Calibration is often desirable in domains like healthcare, to ensure risk scores have the same interpretation across populations.



**Table 1: Common Fairness Metrics and Their Notions of Fairness**






| Fairness Metric | Notion of Fairness | Formal Criterion (Group 1 vs Group 2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Demographic Parity** (DP) | **Outcomes independent of group** (equal selection rates) [[1]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Demographic%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,risk%20for)] | $\Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1) = \Pr(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=2)$ |
| **Equalized Odds** | **Errors independent of group** (equal misclassification rates) [[2]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Equalized%20odds%20asserts%20that%20the,if%20the%20ROC%20curves%20do)] | TPR$*{1}$ = TPR$*{2}$, FPR$*{1}$ = FPR$*{2}$ |
| **Predictive Parity** | **Accuracy of positive predictions equal** (equal precision) [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)] | PPV$*{1}$ = PPV$*{2}$ (and often NPV$*{1}$ = NPV$*{2}$) |
| **Calibration by Group** | **Scores have same meaning across groups** [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)] | $\Pr(Y=1 \mid \text{score}=s, A=1) = \Pr(Y=1 \mid \text{score}=s, A=2)$ |









*(TPR = True Positive Rate, FPR = False Positive Rate, PPV = Positive Predictive Value, NPV = Negative Predictive Value.)*



Each metric above captures a different facet of fairness. **Demographic parity** focuses on equal acceptance rates, ignoring true outcomes. **Equalized odds** demands parity in errors, focusing on the model’s performance balance. **Predictive parity** and **calibration** focus on the *meaning* of a prediction or score, ensuring that a given score or decision has equivalent outcome likelihoods across groups. These criteria are often in tension with each other, as discussed next.


## Theoretical Relationships and Incompatibilities



Research in algorithmic fairness has established that many fairness metrics are **mutually incompatible** – a single predictor cannot generally satisfy all metrics at once unless under special conditions. Key theoretical relationships and trade-offs include:


* **General Impossibility of Satisfying All Metrics:** A well-known result by Kleinberg et al. (2016) proved that no non-trivial classifier can simultaneously satisfy **demographic parity, equalized odds, and predictive parity** (calibration) at the same time, except in degenerate cases [5]. In other words, at most one of these fairness criteria can hold in a classifier that also has any reasonable degree of accuracy, when group distributions differ [5]. This “impossibility theorem” underlines that one often must choose which fairness definition to prioritize.
* **Predictive Parity vs. Error Rate Parity:** When base rates (prevalence of the positive outcome $Y=1$) differ across groups, it is **impossible to achieve both predictive parity and equalized error rates** at the same time [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)][[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))]. If a model is calibrated and has equal PPV for each group, it will necessarily produce different false positive or false negative rates if one group has a higher underlying incidence of the outcome [[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))]. This was formally shown by Chouldechova (2017) and others: *any instrument that satisfies predictive parity (equal PPV) must have imbalanced false positive or false negative rates when prevalences differ* [8]. In short, requiring equal precision across groups forces a trade-off in error rates (and vice versa) whenever one group is a priori more likely to have the positive outcome [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)].
* **Calibration vs. Equalized Odds:** Calibration (sufficiency) and equalized odds (separation) are fundamentally at odds under realistic conditions. Kleinberg et al. showed that a classifier that is **well-calibrated within each group cannot also have equal false positive and false negative rates** unless the groups have identical outcome distributions [9]. Achieving equal error rates often requires setting different decision thresholds per group (especially if one group has a higher base rate), which typically destroys overall calibration [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Thus, one cannot generally have a model that is simultaneously calibrated *and* satisfies equalized odds, except in special cases such as when the groups have equal prevalences or when the model is perfect (or trivial) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)].
* **Demographic Parity vs. Accuracy/Other Metrics:** Demographic parity often conflicts with metrics that consider the true label, like equalized odds or predictive parity, especially when the protected attribute is correlated with the outcome. If one group actually has a higher prevalence of the positive outcome, enforcing demographic parity means artificially increasing positive predictions for the other group, potentially causing higher error rates. As one source notes, demographic parity “does not consider if the prevalence of the outcome is different” across groups, and equalizing positive rates can lead to **“equal treatment rates but disparate outcomes”** for the groups [[10]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)via%20the%20constraint%20,disparate%20outcomes%20between%20Black%20and)]. In practice, maximizing accuracy will generally violate demographic parity (since the model will assign more positives to the high-prevalence group), and enforcing parity usually entails an accuracy cost or uneven error rates.



In summary, these theoretical results highlight that fairness metrics embody different, sometimes competing, principles. A classifier can be tuned to satisfy one definition (e.g. achieving equalized odds by adjusting thresholds per group), but this typically causes deviation from another definition (losing calibration or predictive parity, for example) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)][8]. The only situations where all group fairness metrics coincide are **trivial cases** – for instance, if the groups have identical distributions and risk, or if the model makes no informative predictions at all (e.g., randomly predicting or predicting everyone as the same label). In most real-world scenarios with differing base rates and imperfect model accuracy, a fundamental trade-off exists and one cannot optimize all fairness criteria simultaneously [5].


## Empirical Comparisons Across Datasets and Models



Empirical studies have compared how different fairness metrics manifest on various benchmark datasets and for different model architectures. We review findings from several well-known contexts: the COMPAS criminal recidivism dataset, the UCI Adult income dataset, and examples from healthcare risk prediction. We also note differences observed across model types like logistic regression, random forests, and neural networks.


### COMPAS Recidivism Dataset (Criminal Justice)



The COMPAS dataset, which contains criminal defendant data used to predict recidivism risk, became a case study in how different fairness definitions give divergent conclusions. ProPublica’s analysis of COMPAS found racial disparities in error rates: notably, the algorithm had a much higher false positive rate for Black defendants than for white defendants [11]. This means COMPAS violated **equalized odds** (Blacks who did not re-offend were more often incorrectly labeled high-risk). Northpointe (the COMPAS vendor), however, argued the tool was **fair by predictive parity**, noting that the percentage of high-risk defendants who re-offended was roughly equal for Black and white groups [12]. Subsequent research clarified this tension:


* **Predictive Parity vs. Equalized Odds in COMPAS:** COMPAS was found to be *approximately well-calibrated* and to satisfy predictive parity (similar precision for Black vs. white defendants) at the chosen risk threshold [13]. However, it **failed to achieve error rate balance**: both the FPR and FNR were significantly worse for Black defendants [13]. An empirical assessment showed that at various score cutoffs, COMPAS could not attain both equal PPV and equal FPR/TPR simultaneously [14][[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))]. For example, with a threshold yielding roughly 60% classification accuracy, the COMPAS risk score had a false positive rate for Black defendants nearly twice that of whites, even though the fraction of those labeled high-risk who re-offended (PPV) was almost the same [11][12]. This aligns with the theory: because recidivism base rates differed by race (in the data, ~51% of Black defendants re-offended vs ~39% of whites [16]), **one cannot have equal FPR/FNR and equal PPV at the same time** [[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))]. Chouldechova (2017) demonstrated this empirically and theoretically for COMPAS [[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))].
* **Effect of Model Adjustments:** Researchers explored adjusting COMPAS or training alternative models to satisfy other fairness metrics. Hardt et al. (2016) showed that by applying a post-processing threshold adjustment per group, one can achieve **equalized odds** on COMPAS (equalizing error rates) [[17]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)differently%20from%20demographic%20parity%2C%20equalized,can%20be%20seen%20in%20the)]. However, the result is a model that is no longer calibrated and fails predictive parity – for instance, after enforcing equal error rates, the precision for Black vs. white can diverge substantially [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Corbett-Davies et al. (2017) argued that strictly enforcing equalized odds in this setting can lead to distortions (e.g., letting high-risk individuals from one group go free to equalize stats) and suggested considering the **cost context** (e.g., the higher cost of false negatives in public safety) [18][8]. In summary, on COMPAS *an unconstrained model* was fair by predictive parity but very *unfair by error rates*, whereas a model adjusted for equalized odds would flip the situation – illustrating the trade-off concretely [[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))].
* **Correlation of Metrics:** A recent comprehensive study analyzed multiple fairness metrics on COMPAS across many model variants [19]. It found that **several group fairness metrics tend to correlate on COMPAS**: for example, **Statistical Parity Difference (SPD)**, **Equalized Odds Difference (EOD)**, and **Average Odds** difference were all positively correlated with each other on this dataset [20]. Intuitively, a model that reduced bias in one of these measures (say, reducing the gap in positive prediction rates) also tended to reduce gaps in TPR/FPR. This is likely because in COMPAS, much of the disparity comes from the overall decision boundary being different for the groups, so many bias measures move together. However, metrics like the **False Omission Rate Difference (FORD)** showed a *negative correlation* with others in COMPAS [21]. In particular, as the SPD/EOD improved (decreased) for a model, the gap in false omission rates (which relates to NPV disparity) sometimes increased [21]. This again reflects the tension between focusing on positive outcomes vs. negative outcomes: improving parity in who is labeled high-risk can worsen parity in who is labeled low-risk.


### UCI Adult Income Dataset (Employment)



The UCI Adult dataset (predicting whether an individual earns >$50K) is another widely used benchmark for fairness in ML. The **sensitive attribute** is often gender or race (e.g., comparing male vs female income predictions). In this data, there is a real historical disparity: a much smaller fraction of women have high incomes than men. This leads to differing base rates, which pose challenges for simultaneous fairness criteria.



Studies on Adult have reported: an unconstrained model (e.g., logistic regression) will typically **violate demographic parity**, predicting “high income” for males at a higher rate than for females, simply because the model learns the true statistical fact that more men in the training data have high incomes. For example, if ~30% of men but ~11% of women have income >$50K, a high-accuracy model might predict positive for a substantially higher percentage of men, yielding a large **statistical parity gap**. Mitigating this gap (to satisfy DP) would require raising predictions for women or lowering them for men, which can hurt accuracy or introduce more errors for one group.



Empirical work with fairness algorithms on Adult shows the trade-offs in action. When researchers apply interventions to improve one fairness metric, others can suffer:


* **Demographic Parity vs Performance:** Enforcing demographic parity on Adult (e.g., via a constraint or reweighting) significantly reduces the disparity in positive prediction rates, but can increase classification error. One study noted that methods which equalize selection rates across gender led to a drop in overall accuracy and could increase false negatives for the previously disadvantaged group [[10]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)via%20the%20constraint%20,disparate%20outcomes%20between%20Black%20and)]. Essentially, to equalize outcomes, the model might have to predict “high income” for more women who are actually below $50K (raising FPR for women), or deny some predictions for men who are actually above $50K (raising FNR for men). Thus equalized odds or equal opportunity may worsen when pure output parity is enforced.
* **Error Rate Parity and Calibration:** If instead one focuses on **equalized odds or equal opportunity** in the Adult dataset, the interventions typically involve adjusting decision thresholds for men vs women. For example, to equalize TPR (true positive rate) across gender (equal opportunity), one might use a lower threshold for the group with fewer positives (women) to improve their recall. This can succeed in equalizing TPR [[17]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)differently%20from%20demographic%20parity%2C%20equalized,can%20be%20seen%20in%20the)]. However, it often leads to **different precision** by group – i.e. violates predictive parity and calibration. After such adjustment, the confidence in a “>$50K” prediction may differ by gender (e.g., the PPV for women might drop because more women are being predicted positive to boost TPR) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. This mirrors the COMPAS situation: whenever base income levels differ, one cannot equalize both error rates and predictive value.
* **Metric Correlations on Adult:** The same multi-metric study mentioned earlier found that on the Adult dataset, the correlations between fairness metrics were **weaker and more varied** than in COMPAS [19]. Statistical parity difference, equalized odds difference, etc., did *not* all move in unison to the same extent. Notably, **false omission rate difference (FORD)** had a strong *negative* correlation with statistical parity on Adult [22]. This implies that models which improved parity in positive decisions (lower SPD) tended to *worsen* parity in false omission (who gets incorrectly labeled low-risk) on this dataset. The divergence is likely because the Adult dataset’s imbalance and the nature of errors means focusing on one side of the classification (positive outcomes) directly harms the other side’s fairness. Overall, different fairness metrics painted different pictures: a model could look fair by equal opportunity (similar TPR for men and women) yet still have unequal PPV or selection rates, and vice versa. This underscores the importance of **which metric is chosen** to evaluate fairness [23][24].
* **Models and Fairness on Adult:** Comparisons of classifiers (logistic regression vs random forests, etc.) on the Adult data have shown no clear winner in terms of inherent fairness. Simpler models like logistic regression sometimes exhibit slightly smaller disparities in certain metrics, while more complex models (random forests) might find subtle patterns that unfortunately align with group differences (potentially increasing disparity). However, a recent study found **no model type consistently outperforms others on fairness metrics across datasets** [25]. For instance, on Adult, applying a bias mitigation technique (like a fairness constraint) to logistic regression improved fairness considerably (reducing group disparities) [26]. The same intervention on a random forest or gradient boosted model might also help but perhaps to a different degree. In general, there is variation: in some runs logistic regression had lower disparity, in others a decision tree did – the *dataset-specific* factors and tuning mattered more than the algorithm family. This suggests that **fairness is not simply a property of model architecture**, but of how the model interacts with data distribution and what objectives are used during training [25].


### Healthcare Risk Prediction (Health Datasets)



Fairness in health-related machine learning has gained attention recently, with examples like risk scores for disease or health management algorithms. In these settings, **calibration** is often emphasized – a risk score is typically expected to be well-calibrated for all patients. At the same time, we want to avoid situations where one demographic group consistently experiences higher error rates (e.g., higher false negatives in diagnosis). This leads to the familiar tension between calibration (predictive parity) and equalized odds.


* **Calibration vs Equality of Opportunity:** In clinical prediction tasks, different racial or demographic groups often have different prevalence of conditions (due to underlying health disparities). For example, suppose an algorithm predicts risk of kidney failure for transplant allocation. If Black patients have a higher incidence of kidney failure than white patients, a calibrated model will reflect that – yielding higher risk scores on average for Black patients. Such a model can be **calibrated within each group** (so that, say, a 20% predicted risk means about 20% incidence in that group) [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. It may also satisfy **predictive parity** by having similar positive predictive value for Black and white patients (since calibration implies sufficiency) [[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. However, this scenario will generally **not satisfy equalized odds**: if no adjustments are made, the group with higher prevalence will likely also have a higher false positive rate at any given threshold (because more of them are positive overall) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. As discussed earlier, to equalize FPR/TPR, one would have to use different thresholds or alter the score distribution by group, breaking calibration. Indeed, it is formally shown that *when prevalence differs between groups, you cannot simultaneously have equalized odds and predictive parity* in the model [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. This is highly relevant in healthcare, where prevalence of diseases often differs by demographics.
* **Case Study – Kidney Transplant Risk Score:** A recent *Nature Medicine* perspective gave an example of a kidney transplant waitlist model [27][[3]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)Predictive%20parity%20asserts%20that%20the,This%20threshold)]. Enforcing **demographic parity** in that scenario (equal selection rates for transplant across racial groups) could be harmful: since Black patients have higher need on average, requiring equal selection could leave many at-risk Black patients not receiving transplants, resulting in worse outcomes [[10]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)via%20the%20constraint%20,disparate%20outcomes%20between%20Black%20and)]. On the other hand, a purely predictive model that is calibrated might allocate more transplants to Black patients (reflecting higher need), achieving sufficiency but leading to differences in the rate of selection (violating DP) and potentially in error rates if thresholds differ. This illustrates the trade-offs: **which fairness metric is appropriate depends on the context** [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)fairness%20criteria%20can%20have%20different,served%20by%20different%20fairness%20criteria][[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)not%20intersect,can%20be%20seen%20in%20the]. In life-critical decisions, many argue that *equalizing error rates* (e.g., equal false negative rates so no group is undertreated) or ensuring calibration (so that risk predictions are trustworthy for all groups) is more important than equalizing the raw selection percentages – but these choices must be made explicitly, as they cannot all be met simultaneously [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)].
* **Empirical Fairness in Health Models:** Empirical studies in healthcare ML have started to measure multiple fairness metrics. One study on clinical risk prediction models found that applying fairness constraints (like equal opportunity regularization) yields heterogeneous effects on other metrics [30]. For example, a method that equalized TPR across groups might increase calibration error between groups, or vice versa [31][[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. It was observed that optimizing for one fairness criterion (say, lowering the difference in FPR) often led to statistically significant differences in how other metrics changed – some disparities improved, others worsened [24]. This aligns with the theoretical expectations. The study emphasizes that fairness metrics should be chosen in light of domain context: *“Different applications may be better served by different fairness criteria.”* [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)match%20at%20L501%20fairness%20criteria,served%20by%20different%20fairness%20criteria] In domains like medicine, there is also a push to consider the **absolute harm**: for instance, a small increase in false positives may be acceptable to reduce false negatives for a vulnerable group, depending on the clinical trade-offs (this goes beyond metrics into cost-sensitive analysis).
* **Model Architecture:** Similar to other domains, in healthcare no single model type is inherently the fairest. Simpler models might be easier to constrain for fairness or interpret, while complex models might inadvertently exploit subtle correlations that increase disparity. There is evidence that **fairness interventions (pre-processing or regularization)** can have different efficacy depending on the model – e.g., one experiment showed that adding a fairness regularizer improved group calibration in a linear model but had less effect in a deep neural network [25]. Nonetheless, the overall finding is that fairness outcomes are dataset-specific. For a given health dataset, one may need to experiment with multiple models and mitigation strategies; a random forest could exhibit less bias than a neural net on one problem, but on a different dataset the result could flip. This reinforces that fairness has to be evaluated case by case, using the appropriate metrics for the context.


## When Fairness Metrics Correlate vs. Diverge



From both theory and empirical evidence, it is clear that different metrics sometimes align – improving one can improve another – and other times conflict. Understanding **when metrics correlate or diverge** is important for navigating fairness assessments:


* **Similar Concepts Yield Correlated Metrics:** Metrics that capture related notions of fairness often move in tandem. For instance, *statistical parity, equalized odds, and average odds difference* all measure some form of overall group disparity, and these were observed to have **strong positive correlations** with each other in studies across multiple datasets [20]. In practice, if a model’s predictions are less skewed by group (improving DP), it often also has more balanced error rates (improving EO), especially if the disparity primarily came from a decision threshold favoring one group. We saw this in COMPAS and other cases: reducing the gap in positive prediction rates tended to also reduce the gap in FPR/TPR for those models [19]. Thus, when the **source of bias is a general skew** in how a group is treated, many group fairness metrics will collectively indicate improvement or deterioration together.
* **Competing Definitions Lead to Divergence:** Metrics that emphasize different aspects (e.g. output distribution vs. error calibration) will diverge when those aspects trade off. A clear example is **predictive parity vs. equalized odds**: if one group has a higher base rate, any attempt to equalize error rates will force the precision or calibration to differ, and vice versa [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Empirically, this appears as *negative correlations* between certain metrics. In the Adult dataset, improving statistical parity (aiding output equality) was associated with **worsening false omission rate parity** [33] – essentially, efforts to equalize positive outcomes made the negative outcomes less equal. Likewise, models optimized to be well-calibrated often exhibited larger disparities in error rates, because they sacrifice some error parity to preserve calibration [34][[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. These divergences are pronounced under **differing prevalence or skewed label distributions**. When one group is a minority or has lower incidence of the positive class, metrics will inherently conflict more: a classifier that does well by overall accuracy will favor the majority, boosting predictive parity but hurting equal opportunity for the minority; a classifier adjusted to help the minority’s TPR will often overshoot and reduce precision for that group.
* **Conditions for Alignment:** Fairness metrics tend to align under certain conditions. If **base rates are equal across groups**, many conflicts disappear: a classifier can potentially be both well-calibrated and have equal error rates, since the groups behave similarly. Similarly, if a model is **perfectly accurate** (no errors), it trivially satisfies equalized odds (zero FPR and 100% TPR for all groups) and also achieves calibration and predictive parity (since it never makes mistakes) – though it may fail demographic parity if one group truly has more positives. On the other extreme, a **totally random or uninformative model** that outputs positive at a fixed rate for all groups can satisfy demographic parity by design (and even equalized odds if tuned to output positives proportional to prevalence), but will not be calibrated or useful. These are edge cases. In realistic moderate scenarios, partial alignment can occur: e.g., if two metrics are mathematically related (equalized odds implies equal opportunity as a subset), or if a mitigation strategy addresses a root cause that influences multiple metrics (like removing a strongly biased feature might improve both DP and EO). Moreover, when a protected attribute has **no correlation with the outcome** in the data (truly no structural bias), then most fairness metrics will naturally be satisfied together – but this situation is rare in the domains of concern.
* **Dataset and Model Factors:** The extent of metric correlation can be dataset-specific. Researchers found that the **Adult dataset’s metrics diverged more** than COMPAS’s [19], likely because Adult has a more uneven class distribution and a greater imbalance in outcomes by group, forcing harsher trade-offs. In contrast, the German Credit dataset (another fairness benchmark) showed high correlation between SPD, EOD, AOD metrics similar to COMPAS [20] – possibly because the bias patterns were simpler or base rates not as skewed. **Model complexity** can also affect this: a highly complex model might fit the data in a way that unintentionally maximizes one type of fairness at the cost of another (or vice versa). For example, a neural network might find a way to be well-calibrated overall, whereas a logistic model might have had more unequal residual errors – or the opposite, depending on regularization. No matter the case, one consistent observation is that **improving fairness is not one-dimensional**: one must decide which metric(s) align with the ethical or legal goals for the application, and accept trade-offs with other criteria [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)fairness%20criteria%20can%20have%20different,served%20by%20different%20fairness%20criteria][[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)].


## Conclusion



Fairness in machine learning is a multi-faceted concept, and different formal metrics capture different definitions of “fair” outcomes. We have defined the major group fairness metrics – demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity, and calibration – and reviewed known theoretical results that show these metrics are often incompatible with each other in practice. The impossibility of satisfying all fairness criteria simultaneously (except in trivial cases) means that practitioners must make principled choices about which definition to prioritize for a given application.



Empirical studies across datasets reinforce these trade-offs. On the COMPAS dataset, we saw an algorithm that satisfies predictive parity inevitably produce disparate error rates [13][[7]([[15](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.0056#:~:text=prevalence%E2%80%93i,to%20think%20of%20how%20these))], whereas enforcing equalized odds would undermine calibration [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. On the UCI Adult data, mitigating one kind of bias (e.g., selection rate disparity) can exacerbate another (e.g., error rate or predictive value disparity) [22]. In each dataset, the correlations between fairness metrics can differ – some biases are “universal” and show up in many metrics, while others surface as a conflict between metrics. Table 2 summarizes typical relationships observed:



**Table 2: Examples of Fairness Metric Relationships in Different Datasets**






| Dataset | Observations on Fairness Metrics |
| --- | --- |
| **COMPAS (Recidivism)** | High base rate disparity by race. Unconstrained model had **equal PPV (predictive parity)** but **unequal FPR/FNR** (violating equalized odds) [13]. Enforcing equalized odds requires different thresholds and breaks calibration (PPV disparity arises) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Metrics like statistical parity, TPR/FPR parity, and average odds were **strongly correlated** in experiments (all improved or worsened together), while parity of false omission rate diverged (trade-off with others) [19]. |
| **Adult Income (Gender)** | Large underlying outcome imbalance (men higher income rate). **Demographic parity** is violated by default; equalizing it hurts accuracy. **Equal opportunity** (equal TPR) can be achieved by lowering threshold for women, but then **precision** differs by gender (predictive parity fails) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Studies show **weaker correlation** among metrics: improving output parity can worsen error rate parity (e.g., higher FNR for one group) [22]. Careful selection of metric is needed based on whether one prioritizes selection rates, error rates, or calibrated outputs. |
| **Healthcare Risk** | Often focuses on **calibration** (so risk scores have same meaning across groups). If outcome prevalence differs (common in health disparities), a calibrated model will have unequal error rates by group [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. Ensuring equal TPR/FPR (equalized odds) may require sacrificing calibration (risk thresholds differ by group, making scores not directly comparable) [[6]([[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)impossibility%20to%20satisfy%20all%20criterion,seen%20in%20the%20following%20expression)]. The appropriate fairness metric may depend on clinical context (e.g., one might prioritize equal false negative rates to ensure no group is under-diagnosed). Different fairness criteria are evaluated, but as theory predicts, cannot all be met simultaneously [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)not%20intersect,can%20be%20seen%20in%20the]. |









Ultimately, the interplay of fairness metrics is complex. Certain fairness measures will correlate and reinforce each other under some conditions, while others inherently conflict. Recognizing these relationships allows researchers and practitioners to better interpret fairness evaluations and to communicate the **trade-offs** involved. The literature strongly suggests there is no one-size-fits-all metric: **the choice of fairness metric should be guided by the context and values at stake**, and one should be transparent about which metric is optimized and what the implications are for other dimensions of fairness [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10632090/#:~:text=)fairness%20criteria%20can%20have%20different,served%20by%20different%20fairness%20criteria]. By examining multiple metrics together, as we did in this report, one can gain a more complete picture of model behavior across demographic groups and make informed decisions about model deployment or further bias mitigation.
