# Tree Compression Algorithms and Their Computational Complexity


## Overview of Tree Compression



Tree compression refers to techniques for reducing the space required to store tree-structured data (e.g. XML documents, syntax trees, tries) while often preserving the ability to traverse or query the tree. Trees can be large (XML DOMs can be many times larger in memory than on disk), so compressing them can save memory and improve cache utilization [1][2]. Compression exploits redundancies in tree structure or labels – for example, repeated subtrees, repetitive patterns along paths, or skewed frequency of labels. By removing these redundancies, a compressed tree representation can be **much smaller** than the explicit pointer-based representation. In some cases, operations (like navigation or search) can be performed directly on the compressed structure without full decompression [3][4]. Tree compression is useful in domains like XML data management, where large trees with repetitive structures appear, and in indexing structures like suffix trees or tries, where an uncompressed structure might be prohibitively large.


## Grammar-Based Tree Compression



**Grammar-based compression** represents the input tree by a context-free grammar (usually a *straight-line tree grammar* that generates exactly one tree). The idea is to replace repeated patterns (subtrees or partial structures) with nonterminal symbols and production rules, so that the grammar generates the original tree. This approach generalizes grammar compression from strings to trees [5]. A well-chosen grammar can be **exponentially more succinct** than explicitly storing all nodes. In fact, a tree grammar can be exponentially smaller than the tree’s minimal DAG in the worst case [6]. For example, a long chain of identical-labeled nodes (which contains no identical subtrees and thus defeats DAG compression) can be compressed by a grammar to size O(log *n*) by recursive production rules, versus O(*n*) for a DAG representation.



Finding the *smallest* grammar for a given tree is NP-hard [7] (mirroring the NP-hardness of the smallest grammar problem for strings [8]). Therefore, practical grammar compressors rely on heuristics. Notable grammar-based tree compression algorithms include:


* **BPLEX** (Busatto *et al.* 2005): An early grammar-based compressor for XML trees [9][10]. It achieves good compression ratios but is significantly slower than newer methods [11].
* **RePair on trees**: A simple and fast heuristic adopted from the RePair string compressor by Larsson and Moffat (2000). It repeatedly replaces common adjacent patterns (in a bracketed tree string) with a new nonterminal. Applied to a parenthesis-encoded tree, RePair runs in linear time and produces a straight-line grammar [12][13]. The resulting grammar can support basic navigational queries (with additional index structures) in *O*(log *n*) time [14].
* **TreeRePair** (Lohrey, Maneth, Mennicke 2010): A generalization of RePair directly on ranked trees, producing a linear straight-line context-free tree grammar [13]. The algorithm runs in **linear time** on the tree size [13] and typically achieves the best compression ratios among grammar methods [15]. A succinct encoding of the resulting grammar can further reduce space without losing the ability to navigate the tree [16]. One drawback is that the grammar depth can be linear in worst case, so fast navigation (sublinear in output size) is not yet fully solved for TreeRePair-compressed trees [17]. In practice, traversing TreeRePair’s compressed trees is about 5× slower than using succinct (uncompressed) trees for small documents [18].
* **TtoG (Tree-to-Grammar)** (Jez and Lohrey 2013): A theoretical algorithm providing a guaranteed approximation of the minimal grammar size [19]. It has a good worst-case ratio but has not been evaluated in practice [19].



**Complexity:** Many grammar-based methods are efficient. RePair and TreeRePair run in O(*n*) time for a tree of *n* nodes [13], making them scalable. Decompression (expanding the grammar) is essentially a tree traversal using the production rules and takes O(*N*) time to reconstruct *N* output nodes (linear in the original tree size). In terms of the compressed size *g* (number of grammar symbols), decompression is O(*N*) which is generally O(poly(*g*)) since *g* ≪ *N* when compression is effective. The **trade-off** is that grammar compression can achieve very high compression (even for cases where no two subtrees are identical) at the cost of a more complex representation. Some queries (like random access to a node or subtree) can be supported on grammar-compressed trees in O(log *n*) time with additional indexing [14], but this adds overhead. Grammar compressors are especially well-suited for **highly repetitive tree data**, such as XML datasets with many repeated structures or computational trees with recurring patterns. For example, XML tree compressors based on grammar methods have shown strong compression ratios and memory savings [9][10]. If a tree has little repetition (e.g. very heterogeneous data), grammar compression will offer minimal reduction (producing a grammar almost as large as the tree itself), in which case its extra complexity yields little benefit.


## DAG-Based Tree Compression



A simple and widely-used approach to compressing a tree is **DAG compression**, which identifies *identical subtrees* and merges them. In the compressed structure, any subtree that appears multiple times in the original tree is stored only once, and multiple parent nodes point to this shared subtree. The result is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that “unfolds” to the original tree. The smallest such representation (the **minimal DAG**) is essentially obtained by maximal subtree merging and is unique for a given labeled tree [20][21]. The minimal DAG can be constructed in **linear time** O(*n*) by hashing or canonical form comparisons of subtrees [21] (a classic algorithm by Downey *et al.*, 1980). For example, if an XML document has many identical record subtrees, DAG compression will store one copy of the record subtree and link all occurrences to it, potentially saving a lot of space.



DAG compression is **lossless** and preserves exact tree structure. It can yield exponential compression in favorable cases (for instance, a perfectly balanced full binary tree with all leaves identical compresses dramatically because many subtrees are identical) [3]. However, it only exploits *exact* equality of subtrees. In the worst case – e.g. a long chain of nodes with the same label but all different in size – no two subtrees are identical, so the minimal DAG is no smaller than the original tree [22]. This highlights a limitation: DAG compression misses internal repeated **patterns** that are not whole subtrees [23]. It cannot compress a repetitive structure unless a full rooted subtree repeats with identical labels throughout.



**Complexity:** Building the minimal DAG is linear time [21], and decompression (unfolding the DAG back into a tree) is also O(*N*) for *N* output nodes. Navigational queries (e.g. following parent/child pointers) on the DAG are slightly complicated by shared subtrees (a node can have multiple parents in the DAG). With additional indexing, one can support basic queries in *O*(log *n*) time on a DAG [3]. In practice, DAG compression is very fast and simple, making it attractive for applications like just-in-time compression of syntax trees or common subexpression elimination. It is most suitable when exact subtree repetition is expected – for example, in abstract syntax trees or expression trees with common subexpressions, in data with copy-pasted XML fragments, or in tries/automata where identical sub-structures occur. If the data has mostly *structurally unique* subtrees, DAG compression yields little to no size reduction [24] (though it still removes pointer overhead if one counts that, which succinct methods do more optimally). DAG compression can be seen as a baseline: it never makes things worse, and is *never too far from optimal* for any tree structure, but it often can be improved upon by more powerful methods described next.


## Entropy-Based (Statistical) Tree Compression



Entropy-based methods compress trees by encoding the tree's structural information and labels using probabilistic models and coding (like Huffman or arithmetic coding), aiming for space close to the information-theoretic minimum. Instead of looking for large repeated subtrees, these methods exploit statistical regularities (frequencies of labels, correlations between labels and structures). One prominent example is the approach by Ferragina *et al.* (2005, 2009) who introduced the concept of **$k$-th order entropy of a tree** and a compression transform called **XBWT** [25]. The $k$-th order label entropy, $H_k$, generalizes the entropy of a string to tree contexts: roughly, it measures how predictable a node’s label is given the labels of its $k$ ancestors [26]. Ferragina *et al.* proposed a Burrows–Wheeler style transformation for labeled trees (XBWT) that linearizes the tree labels in a way that groups similar contexts, then applies entropy coding. They proved that the tree’s labels can be encoded in about $|T|\cdot H_k(T)$ bits (plus lower-order terms) for an *n*-node tree $T$ [25]. In other words, the compressed size approaches the *$k$-th order entropy* of the label sequence [25]. This is asymptotically optimal: it achieves compression proportional to the information content of the labels. (The tree’s shape is handled separately by encoding the topology, as described below.) In practice, a small additional overhead (e.g. compression boosting adding ~1% of *n* bits) may be needed to fully achieve the entropy bound [27].



For the **tree structure (topology)** itself, entropy coding can be applied if the distribution of node degrees is non-uniform. A binary or ordinal tree can be encoded as a sequence of parentheses or degree indicators. It is known that *any* $n$-node unlabeled binary tree can be represented in $2n$ bits (this is the number of bits in the well-known *succinct* representation, which is optimal if all shapes are equally likely). However, if in a particular dataset some node degrees occur more frequently than others (e.g. many unary nodes), one can compress the shape below $2n$ bits by using shorter codes for more frequent degree patterns. Jansson *et al.* (2006) formalized a notion of **zero-order entropy of tree shape** (based on node degree frequency) and showed that assuming a degree distribution, the tree’s bracket representation can be encoded in less than $2n$ bits proportional to that entropy [28]. In fact, by encoding the tree in a degree-aware way (e.g. DFUDS encoding with statistical compression), one can **beat the 2·*n* bit barrier** for storage of an unlabeled tree shape [28].



**Complexity:** Entropy-based compression often involves sophisticated transformations (like XBWT, which requires a depth-first traversal and sorting akin to a Burrows–Wheeler transform). The algorithms are typically linear or near-linear in *n* (for instance, Ferragina’s method uses suffix-array-like techniques to achieve linear or $O(n \log n)$ time). These methods can be more computationally heavy than simple DAG or grammar heuristics, due to the use of sorting or arithmetic coding. Decompression requires decoding the statistical codes and inverting the transforms, generally linear time in the output size. The key advantage of entropy-based compressors is that they **guarantee a compressed size close to the information-theoretic minimum** for the given model (e.g. within a few percent of $n H_k$ or of the degree-entropy). This makes them very effective for trees that do not have large identical substructures but have skewed label distributions or high locality (for example, an XML tree where certain tags or patterns are very common). In such cases, grammar or DAG methods might not find large repeats to merge, but entropy coding will still compress the frequent labels or common structural patterns (like many nodes with one child) by using fewer bits per occurrence. On the other hand, if a tree has huge exact repeats, entropy coding alone won’t be as compact as grammar-based methods that can collapse repeats into one occurrence – though entropy coding could be combined with dictionary methods. In practice, Ferragina *et al.* integrated their compressed tree representation into an index (XBzip) and demonstrated good performance on XML data [29]. A downside is that performing arbitrary tree navigational queries on a purely entropy-compressed representation is non-trivial – usually one needs to augment it with additional structures (e.g. rank/select supports) which can increase space or query time [30]. Thus, entropy compressors are often used when **maximal compression** is needed (e.g. storing massive trees for archival or transmission), or as a complement to succinct data structures, rather than for in-memory query-intensive use on their own.


## Top-Tree Compression (Top DAG)



**Top-tree compression** is a relatively recent approach that combines ideas from DAG compression and grammar compression. Introduced by Bille *et al.* (2013/2015), it uses a data structure called a **top tree** (a hierarchical clustering of the tree) to expose repetitive patterns that are not necessarily full subtrees at the same root [31]. The compression algorithm recursively splits the tree into clusters and identifies repeats among those clusters. The result can be represented as a **top DAG**, a DAG of clusters that represents the original tree. This method exploits both repeated subtrees *and* repeated *structures* that are more complex (e.g. a pattern of siblings or an “internal repeat” where a tree fragment occurs in multiple contexts) [31]. Essentially, top-tree compression can detect similarities that classical DAG compression would miss, while still yielding a structured representation amenable to fast navigation.



A key theoretical result is that top-tree compression is **never worse than DAG compression by more than a logarithmic factor**, and can be exponentially better in the worst case [32][33]. For instance, consider again a long chain of identical labels: DAG compression cannot shorten it, but top-tree compression will recognize the repetitive pattern along the chain and compress it to O(log *n*) size (much like a grammar would) [34]. In general, Bille *et al.* showed their method achieves near-optimal worst-case compression: for a tree of size *n* over an alphabet of size σ, the top-tree compressed form is at most about $n/(\log n)^{0.19}$ in size in the worst case [35] (for constant σ). This was later improved: recent research by Lohrey *et al.* (2017) presented a *linear-time* algorithm to construct a top DAG of height $O(\log n)$ whose size is $O(n/\log_\sigma n)$, which is asymptotically optimal [36]. In simple terms, top-tree compression can often reach the information-theoretic limits of compression (n/ log n behavior) while never doing much worse than the minimal DAG (only a logarithmic blow-up in the worst scenario) [36][32].



**Complexity:** The original top-tree compression algorithm by Bille *et al.* was polynomial-time but practically unoptimized (their work focused on proving the existence of a good compressed form and fast query support, leaving open the question of practical performance [37]). However, the follow-up work achieving size-optimal top DAG compression does so in **linear time** O(*n*) [36], making the approach feasible. Decompression from a top DAG is similar to expanding a hierarchical clustering: one can recursively expand clusters in O(*N*) total time for *N* output nodes (essentially linear time, since each original node will be reproduced once). One of the attractions of top-tree compression is that it supports **fast navigation** on the compressed tree. Bille *et al.* demonstrated that basic navigational operations (parent, i-th child, etc.) can be supported in *O*(log *n*) time on the compressed representation [38]. This is achieved by the hierarchical clustering structure: each navigation step may require “zooming in” one level in the top DAG, hence the log factor corresponding to the height of the cluster tree. In summary, top-tree compression offers a **balance** between DAG and grammar methods: it adapts to a wider range of repeats than DAG compression (capturing patterns that are not identical subtrees) with strong theoretical compression guarantees, while still allowing relatively efficient query operations. It is suitable for cases where a tree has a lot of repetitive **structure** that is not trivially identical. For example, it has been applied to compress *tries* (prefix trees) of dictionaries, where similar branching patterns occur in different parts of the trie even if the subtrees are not identical; top-tree compression of tries significantly reduces size while supporting fast lookups [39]. In highly structured data (like XML with recursive patterns or systematic variations), top-tree methods can shine. Although still emerging in practice, experiments show that a tuned top-tree compressor can run faster than grammar compressors (e.g. six times faster than TreeRePair in one implementation) at the cost of a somewhat larger output (about 50% bigger than TreeRePair’s in that test) [40][41]. This suggests that with further engineering, top-tree compression could become a practical alternative when both compression and direct usability are priorities.


## Succinct Tree Representations



A **succinct tree representation** uses space close to the information-theoretic lower bound (the entropy of the structure) without applying ad-hoc compression techniques to repeated patterns. Succinctness is about *bit-optimal encoding* of the tree topology (and labels) while still supporting constant-time navigation. For an unlabeled static tree with *n* nodes, there exist encodings using **2·*n* + o(*n*) bits** that support operations like parent, child, subtree size, etc., in O(1) time [42]. Jacobson’s balanced parenthesis encoding (1989) and later improvements by Munro and Raman are examples achieving this space bound [43]. Here 2·*n* bits is essentially optimal because it equals the information content of an arbitrary binary tree on *n* nodes (Catalan number ~4^n possibilities). For labeled trees, one must also store the labels of *n* nodes. Storing labels naïvely takes *n* log σ bits (for σ possible labels). Succinct structures aim for **n log σ + O(n)** bits total for labeled trees [29], which is only a lower-order overhead above the raw label information. Ferragina *et al.* (2009) achieved such a representation (n log σ + O(n) bits) for labeled trees along with an indexable structure, calling their implementation **XBzip** [29]. Succinct representations typically separate the concerns of shape and labels: the shape is encoded in 2n bits (for unlabeled) or slightly less if using entropy of degrees [28], and labels are stored in a compressed array (e.g. using Huffman or plain array if no compression). The overall structure often allows constant-time *rank/select* queries on bitvectors to navigate the tree.



**Complexity:** Building a succinct representation is usually O(*n*) or O(*n* log *n*) depending on the support structures. For example, constructing the bit vector of parentheses is linear, and preparing rank/select structures can be done in linear or linearithmic time. Many succinct tree libraries can construct in practice in near-linear time. Decompression (recovering an explicit pointer-based tree or tree traversal order) is straightforward: one can iterate through the bit encoding and output nodes, which is O(*N*) for *N* nodes. The hallmark of succinct structures is that they allow one to *avoid* decompression altogether – algorithms can work directly on the bit-encoded tree, answering queries in constant or logarithmic time. Succinctness is **not focused on reducing the tree size below its information content**, so unlike the other compression methods, a succinct tree’s size does not drastically shrink if there are big repeats. In the worst case of no repeats, grammar or DAG compression would also produce around *n* symbols/nodes of output, so succinct is of the same order, just with a smaller constant factor (bits vs pointers). The big advantage is that succinct trees guarantee a near-optimal space usage for **any** tree without needing to detect repeats, and they support *fast random access*. This makes them ideal for applications like *suffix trees* or *suffix tries*, where one needs to store a massive tree (e.g. for genome sequences or large text indexing) in memory and still answer queries quickly. Compressed suffix tree implementations often use succinct trees to reduce space from O(*N* log *N*) bits (naïve) to O(*N*) bits, which is a huge saving for large *N*. Succinct trees are also used in in-memory XML processing when fast queries are needed and the data is not extremely repetitive. However, if the data is *highly repetitive*, purely succinct storage (at ~2n + n log σ bits) will be larger than a specialized compressor that takes advantage of those repeats. In such scenarios, combining approaches can be beneficial (e.g. applying grammar compression and then encoding the grammar’s output succinctly [16]). In summary, succinct representations are the method of choice when one wants **predictable, near-minimal space** and **constant-time operations**, while tree-specific compression (grammar, DAG, top-tree, entropy) can achieve greater reduction in space at the cost of slower navigation or more complex algorithms, especially when there is substantial redundancy to exploit.


## Comparison and Suitability of Methods for Different Tree Types



Each class of tree compression algorithm has different strengths, and their suitability varies with the type of tree data and usage requirements:


* **Compression Ratio:** Grammar-based and top-tree compressors usually achieve the highest compression on highly repetitive or self-similar trees, since they can merge patterns that are not exactly identical. They can reduce tree size exponentially in the presence of recursive or repetitive structures [34][6]. DAG compression is more limited, only collapsing identical subtrees, but it is simple and guarantees at least some compression whenever there are duplicate subtrees (and never worse than no compression). Entropy-based methods excel when there are no large repeats but the label/structure distribution is skewed – they squeeze out statistical redundancy, approaching the entropy bound of the data [25]. Succinct encoding does not reduce *information* redundancy at all; it only removes pointer overhead. Thus, in terms of sheer size, succinct trees might be larger than other compressed forms if the tree has a lot of redundancy. For example, an XML file with many repeating tags and subtrees could be much smaller under TreeRePair or top-tree compression than in a succinct representation. On the other hand, if a tree is essentially random (no repeats, labels uniformly random), grammar or DAG methods won’t compress it much either, and succinct representation will be very close to optimal (since there’s no compressible pattern).
* **Time Complexity and Performance:** All methods discussed have linear time *worst-case* compression and decompression algorithms (or close to linear). DAG compression is the simplest and fastest to perform (one pass with hashing or union-find of subtrees) [21]. Grammar compressors like TreeRePair are also linear time [13], but with larger constants and more complex operations. Entropy compressors might require building auxiliary structures (like suffix arrays for XBWT) and using arithmetic coding, which can make them slower in practice. The latest top-tree compression algorithms run in linear time [36], though the constants may be high due to complex clustering logic. In terms of query speed on the compressed data, succinct trees are unmatched – they support constant-time navigation by design [42]. DAG and grammar compressed trees typically need *O*(log *n*) time for navigation (the log factor comes from traversing pointers into shared or generated structures) [38][12]. Top-tree compressed trees also allow *O*(log *n*) time navigation, as shown by Bille *et al.* [38]. Entropy-compressed trees usually require decompression or additional heavy indexes for navigation, making random access slower unless extra space is spent to support it [30]. So if **fast, repeated querying** of the tree is required (as in an index or an interactive application), succinct structures or carefully indexed DAG/grammar forms are preferable. If one is doing one-time compression for storage or transmission, then maximizing compression ratio (via grammar/top-tree or entropy coding, or combinations thereof) takes priority.
* **Use Cases and Tree Types:** For **XML trees**, which often contain repeated element structures and many repeated labels, grammar-based methods (like XML-specific grammar compressors [9][10]) and entropy methods (which compress common tag names and nested patterns [25]) have been successfully applied. DAG compression can also be useful if entire subtrees repeat (e.g. identical records), and succinct XML representations exist for fast querying at the cost of larger size. In practice, XML compressors often combine strategies (e.g. XMill separates text values from structure for entropy coding; other tools use DAG or grammar for structure). **Suffix trees** and **tries** (very large trees used for indexing strings) benefit from succinct representations due to their huge size – compressed suffix trees based on succinct encoding require O(*N*) bits instead of O(*N* log *N*) and support suffix queries efficiently. There is active research on applying grammar or top-tree compression to tries (e.g. top-tree compression of tries by Ferragina *et al.*) to reduce them further [39], especially if the dataset (like a dictionary or genomic database) has repetitive patterns. For **binary trees** such as decision trees or computational trees, the best approach depends on the data: if the tree is *deep and repetitive* (like a recursively defined structure or a highly unbalanced chain with repeating labels), grammar or top-tree compression will drastically reduce it (whereas a DAG won’t help for a repetitive chain) [24][34]. If the binary tree is an irregular or unique structure (no large repeats), a succinct representation is often ideal to store it compactly with fast access. In scenarios like storing many **similar parse trees** or **expression trees**, grammar compression can find shared patterns across the tree ensemble, and DAG can identify common subexpressions. Entropy coding might compress the frequency of certain node types (e.g. operator nodes vs operand leaves) if biased.



In summary, there is no one-size-fits-all:


* **DAG compression** is fast and simple, best when exact subtrees repeat frequently; it’s a good default that never harms and can be augmented with other techniques.
* **Grammar-based methods** achieve superb compression on repetitive structured data (common in XML, JSON records, etc.), at the cost of more complex compression and slower navigation.
* **Entropy-based methods** approach the theoretical minimum size on any data by leveraging statistical redundancy; they are valuable when every bit counts or when patterns are subtle (frequency-based rather than copy-based redundancy).
* **Top-tree compression** straddles a middle ground, capturing complex repeats with strong theoretical guarantees and moderate query efficiency – useful for richly structured but query-intensive applications.
* **Succinct representations** guarantee near-optimal space for arbitrary trees with lightning-fast queries, making them ideal for large-scale data structures like index trees or any application where consistent performance is critical and the data cannot be assumed repetitive.



Often, practical systems will *combine* these techniques: for instance, one might compress large repeated subtrees via a DAG or grammar, then apply entropy coding to the remaining data (labels or small-scale patterns), and finally store the result in a succinct form for efficient access. The choice of algorithm ultimately depends on the characteristics of the tree data (repetitiveness, label distribution, size) and the requirements (maximum compression vs. query speed vs. implementation complexity), as supported by the research findings cited above.

question: What data structures are commonly used to solve the Range Minimum Query (RMQ) problem?

# Data Structures for the Range Minimum Query (RMQ) Problem


## Definition and Applications of RMQ



A **Range Minimum Query (RMQ)** on an array asks for the position of the minimum element in a sub-array defined by indices (l, r) [1]. Formally, given a static array $A[1 \dots n]$ of $n$ comparable values, an RMQ returns $\text{argmin}_{k \in [l,r]} A[k]$, i.e. the index of the minimal element in $A[l \dots r]$ [1]. For example, if $A = [0,5,2,5,4,3,1,6,3]$, then RMQ(3,8) returns 7 because $A[7] = 1$ is the smallest value in the sub-array $A[3..8] = [2,5,4,3,1,6]$ [2]. RMQ is typically considered on a static array (no insertions or deletions), where queries are answered *on-line* (the queries are not all known in advance) [3].



RMQ structures are fundamental and have numerous applications. For instance, RMQ is closely tied to the **Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)** problem on trees: LCA queries can be reduced to RMQ queries and vice versa [4]. In fact, Gabow, Bentley, and Tarjan (1984) showed that LCA on a tree can be transformed in linear time to an RMQ problem on an array, implying both LCA and RMQ can be solved in $O(1)$ query time with linear preprocessing [4]. RMQs are also a key tool in string processing; for example, the **Longest Common Prefix (LCP)** of any two suffixes of a string can be found via an RMQ on the LCP array of the string’s suffix array [5]. More generally, efficient RMQ data structures are used in exact and approximate string matching algorithms [6] (e.g. in Lempel–Ziv text compression and suffix array construction) and in various graph algorithms [7]. This breadth of applications makes RMQ a widely studied query problem in computer science.


## Offline RMQ Techniques (Reduction to LCA and Cartesian Trees)



One straightforward offline strategy is to precompute answers for *all possible queries* and store them in a lookup table. In principle, one can fill an $n \times n$ table $B$ where $B[i,j] = \min(A[i..j])$ for every $1 \le i \le j \le n$. Then any RMQ is answered in $O(1)$ by a simple table lookup [8]. However, this **naïve approach** is impractical because it requires $\Theta(n^2)$ time and space to precompute and store all answers [9].



A more efficient offline solution uses a reduction to the **Lowest Common Ancestor** problem via **Cartesian trees**. The **Cartesian tree** of array $A$ is a binary tree obtained by treating $A$ as the inorder traversal of a tree that satisfies the heap property (each node’s value is ≤ the values in its subtree) [10]. This tree can be built in linear time using a stack-based algorithm, and it encodes the range minima of $A$. Specifically, it can be shown that for any two positions $i$ and $j$ in the array, the lowest common ancestor of the corresponding nodes in the Cartesian tree has a value equal to $\min(A[i..j])$ [10][11]. Thus, an RMQ query on $A$ can be answered by an LCA query on the Cartesian tree. By preprocessing the tree for constant-time LCA queries, we obtain an RMQ data structure with **$O(n)$ preprocessing time** and **$O(1)$ query time** (using linear space) [12]. This optimal approach was first described in 1984 by Gabow, Bentley, and Tarjan (and independently by Harel and Tarjan) [12]. It reduces the RMQ problem to LCA, then applies an LCA algorithm that runs in $O(1)$ per query (e.g. via Euler tour and ±1 RMQ on the depth array) to achieve constant query time.



*Figure:* Example of a Cartesian tree constructed for an array $A = [8,7,3,20,2,17,5,21,11,12]$. Each tree node corresponds to an element of $A$, and the tree has the min-heap property. An RMQ query on $A$ from index 6 to 10 (subarray $[17,5,21,11,12]$) is answered by the LCA of the nodes at positions 6 and 10 in the Cartesian tree. In this example, the nodes at indices 6 and 10 have values 17 and 12, and their lowest common ancestor has value 5 – which is exactly the minimum value in $A[6..10]$. This illustrates that RMQ results correspond to LCA queries on the Cartesian tree [10][11].



Another offline approach to RMQ is the **block decomposition technique** (often attributed to Fischer and Heun). This method divides the array into small blocks of size $s = O(\log n)$ and precomputes RMQ answers *within* each block, as well as a top-level structure for RMQs *across* blocks [13][14]. All possible queries on a block of size $s$ are precomputed and stored (one can use each block’s Cartesian tree to enumerate queries), which takes $O(s^2)$ time per distinct block shape [[15]([[17]([[32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=,the%20range%20of%204%20s)))]. Crucially, there are not too many distinct block “shapes” because blocks with the same relative order of elements have isomorphic Cartesian trees. In fact, the number of possible Cartesian tree shapes on $s$ items is the $s$th Catalan number, which grows as ~$4^s/s^{3/2}$ [16]. For $s = O(\log n)$ this is polynomially smaller than $n$, so storing precomputed answers for each unique block shape is feasible [[15]([[17]([[32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=,the%20range%20of%204%20s)))]. The block minima themselves are stored in a separate array, and a sparse table (or other structure) is built on this array to answer queries that span multiple blocks [18][13]. Overall, this yields an **$O(n)$ space** structure that answers queries in **$O(1)$ time**: a query is resolved by (a) looking up the precomputed answer for the suffix of the left block and the prefix of the right block, and (b) an RMQ on the array of block-minima for the fully covered blocks in between [19][20]. This two-level scheme achieves constant-time queries after linear-time preprocessing, matching the optimal complexity in theory.



It is worth noting that if all queries are known in advance (true **offline** query processing), one can solve the queries without building a persistent data structure at all. One such method is known as **“Arpa’s trick”** in competitive programming: it processes the array and queries using a disjoint set union (DSU) structure. The idea is to iterate through the array and use a union-find data structure to gradually “uncover” elements, while answering any queries whose range minimum becomes determined at that point. With careful ordering (processing array values from smallest to largest or scanning indices from one end), this method can answer $Q$ queries in about $O(n + Q)$ time in total [21]. The DSU-based approach provides another way to achieve linear preprocessing and query time *on average*, but it only works when queries are batched beforehand and is not applicable to truly online scenarios [21]. Nonetheless, it demonstrates that knowing all queries can sometimes enable simpler solutions that avoid heavy data structures.


## Online RMQ Data Structures (Segment Trees, Sparse Tables, etc.)



For **online queries** (answered in arbitrary order on a static array), several classic data structures can be used to support efficient RMQs after an initial preprocessing phase:


* **Segment Tree:** A segment tree is a balanced binary tree built on the array where each node stores the minimum of a segment of $A$. It can be constructed in $O(n)$ time and uses $O(n)$ space [22]. Once built, each RMQ can be answered in $O(\log n)$ time by traversing $O(\log n)$ tree nodes (each covering roughly half the remaining interval) [22]. Segment trees are a flexible structure; they not only answer RMQ queries efficiently, but also support updates to the array (each update in $O(\log n)$) if a dynamic scenario is considered [22]. The downside is the $O(\log n)$ query time, which, while fast, is slower than the $O(1)$ achievable by other static methods. Still, segment trees are widely used in practice due to their ease of implementation and versatility.
* **Sparse Table:** The sparse table method achieves **$O(1)$ query time** by preprocessing many overlapping ranges. It constructs a lookup table `st[j][i]` that stores the index of the minimum element in the subarray of length $2^j$ starting at $i$ [[23]([[24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=As%20in%20the%20solution%20above%2C,2))]. This table has $O(n \log n)$ entries and can be filled in $O(n \log n)$ time using dynamic programming relations [[23]([[24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=As%20in%20the%20solution%20above%2C,2))]. Once built, any query range $[l,r]$ can be answered by splitting it into two overlapping intervals of length $2^k$ (where $2^k \approx r-l+1$). The answer is the minimum of the two precomputed intervals that cover $[l,r]$, which can be retrieved in constant time [25]. Thus, sparse tables use more memory (on the order of $n \log n$) but give constant query time [26]. They are optimal for static arrays in terms of query speed and relatively straightforward to implement. The trade-off is the potentially heavy preprocessing cost and memory usage for large arrays, due to the $n \log n$ table size.
* **Square Root Decomposition:** This is a simpler heuristic approach that lies between segment trees and sparse tables in performance. The array is divided into blocks of size about $\sqrt{n}$; one computes an array of block minima, and also precomputes prefix minima within each block. To answer RMQ$(l,r)$, one considers at most one partial block at the start, one partial block at the end, and all full blocks in between [19]. The minimum for the partial blocks is found by a linear scan of those blocks (which takes $O(\sqrt{n})$ in the worst case), while the minimum for the full blocks in the middle is precomputed (by looking up the minimum of the corresponding block-minima array, which can be done in constant time with another layer of preprocessing, or in $O(\sqrt{n})$ by scanning if not preprocessed) [18]. In typical implementations, this yields **$O(\sqrt{n})$ query time** with **$O(n)$ preprocessing**. The advantage of sqrt-decomposition is its simplicity – it uses only arrays and simple loops – but its query performance is worse than segment trees for large $n$ (since $\sqrt{n}$ grows faster than $\log n$) [27]. It can still be effective for moderate array sizes or when extremely simple code is desired.



In summary, segment trees and sparse tables are the most common **online RMQ** structures. A segment tree offers a good balance of $O(n)$ space, fast construction, and $O(\log n)$ queries (and it handles updates), whereas a sparse table uses more preprocessing to achieve $O(1)$ queries on static data [22][26]. Other structures exist (like binary indexed trees for prefix minima, or Cartesian trees as an implicit structure), but those either do not generalize well to arbitrary RMQ or are subsumed by the above approaches. For static arrays, the sparse table is often the go-to choice when queries are extremely frequent and space is available, while the segment tree (or even sqrt-decomposition) is chosen for its simplicity and flexibility when a slight increase in query time is acceptable.


## Trade-offs: Preprocessing Time, Query Time, and Space Complexity



Different RMQ solutions exhibit different trade-offs between one-time preprocessing cost, per-query time, and memory usage. The ideal structure depends on the context (number of queries, array size, memory limits, etc.). The following summary compares common approaches and their complexities:


* **Naive full table:** Precompute every possible range minimum in an $n \times n$ table, taking $O(n^2)$ time and space. Query time is $O(1)$ by direct lookup [8]. (This approach is rarely feasible except for very small $n$ due to its quadratic cost.)
* **Segment tree:** Build in $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space; answer each query in $O(\log n)$ time [22]. This is efficient for moderate $n$ and supports dynamic updates, at the cost of a logarithmic query time.
* **Sparse table:** Preprocessing takes $O(n \log n)$ time and space, after which queries are $O(1)$ [26]. This method excels when the query count is very large and memory is not a bottleneck, providing constant-time lookups.
* **Sqrt decomposition:** Precompute block minima in $O(n)$ time and space; queries run in about $O(\sqrt{n})$ time in the worst case [27]. It uses simple logic and is faster to set up than a sparse table, but its query performance is suboptimal for large arrays.
* **Optimal static RMQ (Cartesian tree + LCA or Fischer-Heun):** Preprocessing in $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space yields $O(1)$ query time [28]. This category includes the Cartesian tree + LCA approach and block-decomposition methods discussed earlier. It achieves the theoretical optimum, but as noted, the implementation complexity and constant factors are higher than for simpler methods.



In terms of *space* complexity, all of the above (except the naive method) use linear space in the size of the array, albeit with different constants (e.g. a segment tree might use ~4n space for tree nodes; a sparse table uses ~n log n entries; the Fischer-Heun structure uses about 3n entries for tables plus some auxiliary arrays). There are also **succinct RMQ structures** that further reduce space (covered in a later section). Generally, achieving faster queries requires more preprocessing and/or space. For example, going from $O(\log n)$ query time (segment tree) to $O(1)$ query time (sparse table) costs an extra factor of $O(\log n)$ in preprocessing and storage [[23]([[24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=As%20in%20the%20solution%20above%2C,2))][26]. Likewise, the fully optimal $O(1)$ query structures use sophisticated preprocessing to encode range minima information in linear space. The choice of data structure thus depends on the particular trade-off that best fits the problem constraints – if queries are extremely numerous, a heavy preprocessing may be worth it; if memory is tight, one might opt for a structure with smaller space footprint but slightly slower queries, etc.


## Theoretical Optimality vs. Practical Performance



Theoretically, the RMQ problem can be solved with **optimal time and space**: linear preprocessing and constant query time. This big-O optimality was achieved by the mid-1980s in research literature [12]. However, data structures with optimal asymptotic bounds are not always the best choice in practice. One reason is that constant factors and real-world considerations (like memory access patterns) play a significant role for realistic array sizes. The simplest optimal methods (e.g. the Cartesian tree + Euler-tour LCA method) involve multiple layers of abstraction and additional arrays (for depths, Euler indices, etc.), which can introduce overhead. As a result, many practitioners prefer simpler structures like segment trees or sparse tables for typical use-cases, even if they are slightly suboptimal in theory, because they tend to be easier to implement correctly and have good constant-time behavior in practice [28]. The segment tree’s $O(\log n)$ query time, for example, is often fast enough for $n$ up to the millions, given modern CPU speeds and the fact that its memory access pattern is relatively cache-friendly. A sparse table has $O(1)$ queries, but its $O(n \log n)$ space can be significant and cause cache misses; if $n$ is not extremely large or queries not extremely many, the benefit of $O(1)$ vs $O(\log n)$ may not offset the higher preprocessing cost.



Another practical consideration is implementation complexity. As noted in competitive programming resources, the fully optimal RMQ solutions are among the most complex to code and debug [28]. In a contest or rapid development scenario, one might choose a segment tree (which can be written quickly from memory) over a tricky bit-level algorithm that achieves $O(1)$ queries. The **Farach-Colton and Bender** Cartesian tree method or the Fischer–Heun block method are rarely implemented in contests due to their code length and intricacy, despite their optimal performance [28].



That said, research and engineering efforts have shown that with careful optimization, the theoretically optimal approaches can be made very fast in practice. For example, Fischer and Heun’s 2n-bit structure (described below) was refined by Ferrada and Navarro (2016) and by Baumstark *et al.* (2017) to significantly improve practical performance [29][30]. Baumstark *et al.* report that their tuned implementation of a succinct RMQ index is up to 3× faster on real-world benchmarks than prior implementations [31]. This indicates that the gap between theory and practice can be narrowed with careful low-level optimizations (such as using efficient bit operations, reducing recursion depth, etc.). Still, for everyday purposes, the simpler data structures often suffice and can even be faster for moderate input sizes. In summary, while **theoretically optimal RMQ structures exist, one should weigh their constants and coding complexity against simpler alternatives**, especially in competitive programming or practical software where development time and typical input sizes are considerations [28].


## Recent Developments and Advanced Structures



Beyond the classic approaches, there have been advances in **hybrid and succinct data structures** for RMQ in the research literature:


* **Succinct RMQ structures:** A *succinct* data structure uses space close to the information-theoretic minimum. For RMQ, it’s known that one can encode all answers using about $2n$ bits (since an array’s Cartesian tree has $C_n$ possible shapes, where $C_n$ ~ $4^n/(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\pi})$ is the $n$th Catalan number, whose binary logarithm is about $2n$) [[15]([[17]([[32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Range_minimum_query#:~:text=,the%20range%20of%204%20s)))][33]. Fischer and Heun (2007/2011) were the first to achieve a *2n + o(n) bit* index for RMQ with constant query time [34]. Their structure stores a binary encoding of the Cartesian tree plus auxiliary tables, and it can answer queries without needing the original array values [34]. Subsequent work by Navarro and Sadakane (2014) and others optimized the space-time trade-offs: for example, one result achieves $O(1)$ queries with $2n + O!\Big(\frac{n}{\log^c n}\Big)$ bits for some constant $c$ [35]. In 2020, a lower bound was proved showing that any data structure that achieves $O(1)$ query time must use at least $2n + o(n)$ bits of space (in the cell probe model) [36]. In other words, roughly $2n$ bits is the minimum space for constant-time RMQ, vindicating the optimality of the succinct structures. These succinct solutions are important in memory-critical applications (like compressed text indexes) but involve advanced techniques like bitwise *rank/select* operations and are generally more complex to implement than classical structures.
* **Hybrid approaches (rank/select and recursion):** Ferrada and Navarro’s 2016 method is an example of a hybrid RMQ solution [29]. Their approach reduces an RMQ query to a combination of simpler operations: it represents the array in a binary **bitvector** form and uses fast bit tricks. Specifically, they transform RMQ into queries on two bitvectors (supporting rank/select queries in constant time) and one smaller RMQ on a *reduced array* of size $o(n)$ [29]. They introduce a structure called a **range min-max tree** to recursively answer RMQs: the original array is reduced in size by sampling minima at certain intervals, and queries get split between direct bitvector computations and a recursive query on the smaller array. This hybrid of bit-level operations and a recursive RMQ achieves very fast queries in practice, by leveraging the highly optimized bit operations on modern CPUs. Baumstark *et al.* (SEA 2017) improved this design further [30]: they used only two levels of recursion and replaced the final recursive structure with a simple sparse table for the base case [30]. They also provided a custom-tailored *select* operation on bitvectors to speed up queries [30]. These refinements brought consistent speedups, making their implementation the fastest known RMQ solution at the time, outperforming previous ones by up to 3× on standard benchmarks [31]. This line of work shows how combining ideas (succinct encodings, recursion, and classical tables) can lead to both theoretically optimal and *practically* efficient solutions.
* **$O(1)$ query with sub-linear extra preprocessing:** Another notable advanced structure is the **sqrt-tree** (square root tree) method. This technique, which lies in between a segment tree and a sparse table, achieves *constant-time queries* with sub-linear extra overhead on preprocessing. In a sqrt-tree, the array is hierarchically decomposed: we first split $A$ into $\sqrt{n}$-sized blocks and build a top-level structure on the $\sqrt{n}$ block minima (like a segment tree or another layer of decomposition), and we apply this recursively for a couple of levels. By choosing the block sizes in a decreasing geometric progression, one can attain $O(1)$ query time with about $O(n \log\log n)$ preprocessing time and space [37]. The sqrt-tree essentially reduces the query problem to a few small RMQ lookups on tiny blocks (handled by table lookup) and a couple of higher-level RMQs on much smaller arrays (handled by a sparse table or another round of decomposition). The result is an extremely fast query (only a handful of operations) and near-linear preprocessing. The drawback is that this method is quite complex to implement and usually not warranted unless $n$ is extremely large [38]. It is of theoretical interest as a different route to optimal RMQ (in fact, it gives $O(1)$ queries with *o(n)* extra space beyond the array by trading a tiny factor in preprocessing time).



In conclusion, the RMQ problem has a rich array of solutions ranging from simple and practical to theoretically optimal and highly engineered. Classic data structures like segment trees and sparse tables provide robust baselines for most purposes. For those needing absolute speed or space efficiency, advanced techniques (Cartesian trees with LCA, block decomposition, succinct encoding, etc.) are available and backed by a body of research proving their optimality [12][36]. The choice of approach depends on the constraints and goals: whether one prioritizes ease of implementation, query throughput, or minimal memory. Ongoing research continues to refine RMQ structures, for example by improving constant factors, adapting them to different models (parallel, external memory [39], dynamic scenarios), and integrating them into broader applications like suffix array construction and graph processing. The RMQ problem thus remains a classic example of how theoretical computer science results can translate into practically useful tools for a variety of computational tasks.
