# Coverage Motion Planning Algorithms for Floor-Cleaning Robots


## Introduction



Coverage Path Planning (CPP) is the problem of determining a path that allows a robot to pass over all points in a target area (ensuring no spots are missed), while avoiding any obstacles [1]. For floor-cleaning robots like autonomous vacuum cleaners and scrubbers, CPP is a core capability – the robot must **systematically cover the entire floor area** to clean effectively. Over the years, many algorithms have been developed for coverage planning, ranging from simple predefined patterns to advanced AI-based methods. This report surveys major categories of coverage motion planning algorithms and discusses their performance in terms of coverage efficiency, adaptability to environment complexity/dynamics, real-time feasibility, and practical use in consumer vs. industrial robots. Key algorithm families include: **(1)** classical pattern-based methods, **(2)** heuristic graph/search-based methods, **(3)** sampling-based planners, **(4)** optimization-based approaches, and **(5)** learning-based approaches. We cite peer-reviewed research to highlight the strengths and limitations of each approach.


## Classical Coverage Algorithms



Classical methods rely on simple predetermined patterns or behaviors to achieve coverage. They often do not require a detailed map *a priori* and were popular in early or low-cost cleaning robots due to their simplicity. Common classical strategies include **random bounce**, **spiral paths**, and **boustrophedon (zigzag) sweeps**:


* **Random Bounce (Random Walk):** The robot moves in a straight line until it encounters an obstacle, then turns at a random angle and continues. This stochastic strategy eventually covers the area given enough time [2]. It is extremely simple and robust to unknown environments (the robot can operate without a map or localization). However, random walking is *inefficient*: it tends to cover some areas multiple times and leave others temporarily untouched, requiring a long time to achieve full coverage [3]. Studies have noted that random bounce methods often take the longest to cover an area completely, especially compared to systematic patterns [3]. Despite low efficiency, many early consumer vacuums used random bounce due to limited sensing/computation, sometimes achieving ~85–95% coverage in a given timeframe by sheer repetition.
* **Spiral Path:** In a spiral strategy, the robot starts at a point and gradually expands its path outward in an outward spiral (or inward from the perimeter) to cover a circular area. Spiral coverage is useful for covering open areas or “spot cleaning” a localized spill. For example, a robot might spin outward from a starting position, ensuring a dense spiral path that overlaps slightly to guarantee no gaps. Spirals are often combined with other behaviors: e.g. a robot might do a spiral when it finds a large open space. This pattern is more systematic than random motion, but in a complex room with obstacles, a single spiral cannot cover everything – the robot will need to perform multiple spirals in different sections or switch to another mode when an obstacle is encountered. A known algorithm that employs spiral motions is the **Backtracking Spiral Algorithm (BSA)** [4], which drives the robot in a spiral and backtracks when it hits obstacles or boundaries. Spiral methods reduce redundant passes compared to random motion, but still may overlap paths significantly and require careful handling of obstacles (often by switching to another mode like wall-following when an obstacle is hit).
* **Boustrophedon Path (Zigzag Sweeping):** The term “boustrophedon” refers to a back-and-forth pattern (like plowing a field) that systematically sweeps a region in parallel lines [5]. In robotics, **Boustrophedon Cellular Decomposition** is a classic algorithm that divides the free space into simple cells and then covers each cell with straight-line sweeps [6]. The robot moves in a straight line across a cell until it reaches the boundary, then shifts over and sweeps back in the opposite direction, repeating in a zigzag manner (akin to a lawnmower pattern). This approach guarantees complete coverage of each cell with minimal overlap, aside from necessary overlaps at the turns. Choset’s seminal work (2000) introduced boustrophedon decomposition for coverage of known spaces [7], using critical points to split the area into cells that can be covered by back-and-forth motions. **Figure 1** below illustrates a boustrophedon coverage path: obstacles partition the space into subregions (cells) and the robot executes a systematic zigzag path in each cell, indicated by the blue lines.



*Figure 1: Example of a **Boustrophedon coverage path** in a room with obstacles. The environment is divided into subregions (separated by red lines), and the robot follows a back-and-forth sweep in each cell (blue path) to cover all free space [8][9].*



Boustrophedon patterns are highly **coverage-efficient** in structured environments – they avoid needless revisiting of areas and ensure all reachable space is covered exactly once [5]. They do require the robot to localize itself and maintain alignment of its sweeping lines; in practice this can be done if the robot has a map or can follow straight lines reliably. Many modern floor cleaners implement some form of zigzag coverage when operating in open rooms. One limitation is handling irregular obstacles: the space must be decomposed such that each cell is obstacle-free. The original algorithm assumed a static environment known in advance, but later implementations allow on-the-fly cell splitting when new obstacles are detected. Overall, classical patterns (zigzag, spiral, etc.) are **easy to execute in real time** (very low computational load) and tend to work well in simple or moderately cluttered spaces. Indeed, some consumer cleaning robots combine these modes – e.g. a device might follow walls around a room, then perform zigzag lines in the interior, and occasionally use spirals or random bounces in tight spots [3]. These hybrid approaches leverage the reliability of simple behaviors to approximate full coverage.


## Heuristic-Based Methods (Graph and Search Algorithms)



Heuristic-based coverage planners use graph representations or search strategies (often on a grid map) to decide the robot’s path. These methods typically assume an approximate map (e.g. an occupancy grid) and then apply *path planning algorithms* or simple rules to achieve coverage. They are more “intelligent” than blind random motion, but not necessarily globally optimal – they use heuristics to guide the robot efficiently. Two common examples are **grid-based search (e.g. Wavefront, A*)** and **greedy coverage strategies**:


* **Grid Wavefront and Lawn-mower Search:** One straightforward heuristic approach is to treat the floor as a grid of cells and perform a systematic sweep or search over that grid. The **Wavefront algorithm** is a classic grid-based method where a breadth-first search (BFS) flood-fill is used from a starting cell to generate a spanning tree that covers all reachable cells [10]. Essentially, the robot conceptually “waves out” from the start, visiting neighboring cells in layers. This yields a coverage path that is akin to a lawnmower pattern on the grid, ensuring every cell is eventually visited. Wavefront assumes a static environment and a known grid; it is efficient for simple, rectangular or grid-aligned areas [10] but can struggle with irregular obstacles (it may do excessive detours or require backtracking if dead-ends are reached). Many *zigzag coverage routines* on grids are effectively implementing a wavefront or lawnmower pattern – these are heuristics because they don’t explicitly optimize a cost, but they aim for a reasonable path that covers all free cells.
* **A* and D* Search for Coverage:** Graph search algorithms like **A*** (A-star) and **D*** (Dynamic A-star) can be adapted for coverage path planning. A* is typically used to find shortest paths between two points, but for coverage we can use it to repeatedly plan paths to cover *multiple targets*. For example, one heuristic strategy is: at each step, plan an A* path to the nearest *unvisited* area (or frontier) and mark it covered, repeating until all areas are covered. Song and Gupta (2018) propose an online coverage algorithm called “A*-CPP” that uses A* searches to incrementally cover unknown space [11]. D* extends A* for dynamic environments – it can replan efficiently when obstacles move or new areas become accessible. A cleaning robot with a map can plan an optimal route to cover one region, then dynamically update the plan if it encounters a blockage, using D* to adapt in real-time [12]. These search-based methods **improve efficiency** over random or naive sweeps by always moving toward an uncovered area via a near-shortest path. However, they still can produce some redundant travel because each new target is chosen myopically (greedily). In practice, a greedy A* coverage will cover everything but not necessarily in the absolute minimum distance – it trades optimality for computational speed and simplicity. Importantly, these graph-based algorithms require a grid representation; as grid resolution increases for accuracy, the computational cost rises and may become impractical [13]. Thus, there is a balance between map granularity and real-time feasibility.
* **Greedy and Frontier-Based Coverage:** Another heuristic approach is **greedy coverage**, where the robot always moves to what it perceives as the “most urgent” or nearest unexplored area. One common strategy in unknown environments is **frontier-based exploration**: the robot identifies frontier cells (the boundary between known free space and unknown space) and navigates to them to expand the covered region. This is often used in mapping robots [14] and inherently results in full coverage as the robot explores all frontiers. The greedy nature means the robot might not plan an optimal global route, but it is *adaptive* – it responds to newly discovered space in real-time. Frontier-based methods have been shown effective for simultaneously mapping and covering an area [14]. Other greedy rules include “always follow the left wall until you can't, then move to the next unclenaed spot” or “go to the closest dirty (uncovered) spot”. These simple rules can yield reasonable coverage but might get the robot stuck oscillating if not designed carefully (e.g. repeatedly toggling between two nearby targets). Overall, heuristic methods like A*, D*, wavefront, and greedy exploration are **faster and more adaptable** than purely predefined patterns – they can handle complex layouts by reasoning on a grid or graph. Many consumer robots that build maps (using SLAM) employ such methods: they create a floor map and then plan a series of paths to systematically cover each region, often dividing the space into sectors then covering each sector one by one (which can be seen as a heuristic decomposition). The **Complete Coverage D*** algorithm is one example from research that adapts a graph search for full coverage [15], demonstrating how classical path planners can be modified for the coverage task.


## Sampling-Based Algorithms



Sampling-based motion planning algorithms like **PRM (Probabilistic Roadmaps)** and **RRT (Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees)** are well-known in robotics for pathfinding in complex spaces, especially high-dimensional configuration spaces. In the context of floor cleaning (a mostly 2D coverage problem), sampling-based approaches are less common, but researchers have explored them and their variants for coverage path planning:


* **Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) for Coverage:** A PRM planner works by randomly sampling points in the free space and connecting them into a network (roadmap) of feasible paths. Traditionally, PRMs are used to plan *a path* between start and goal; to use PRM for coverage, one can sample points such that they uniformly cover the area, then plan a route that visits all those points. Essentially, the problem reduces to ensuring the roadmap's nodes are dense enough to represent the area, and then finding a route through all nodes (which becomes a graph covering or traveling salesman problem). PRMs are typically **offline** (they assume a known static map) [16]. They are efficient for high-dimensional problems, but for a simple floor plane a random roadmap is not obviously better than a grid decomposition. However, PRM-based methods could be useful in very complex environments where a grid would be too large; the PRM naturally concentrates samples in open areas and around obstacles. One could then use a heuristic or optimization to traverse the PRM graph covering all edges or nodes. Some research has combined PRM with heuristics to ensure complete coverage – for instance, generating waypoints via PRM and then ordering them for coverage. The challenge is that PRM alone doesn’t guarantee systematic coverage (it might leave gaps if samples are sparse), so it must be combined with a strategy to fill in any uncovered spots. In general, PRM is **fast at finding feasible paths** in cluttered spaces [16], which can help a robot navigate from one region to another during coverage.
* **Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT) for Coverage:** RRT is another sampling-based planner that incrementally grows a tree from the start point, rapidly covering the space by extending towards random samples. RRT can be used in an *online* manner, continually extending the tree as the robot moves [17]. For coverage, one idea is to bias the RRT’s sampling to unexplored areas so that the tree will eventually span the free space (this relates to exploration algorithms). RRTs excel at finding paths in complex, obstacle-rich environments and can adapt to changes by regrowing branches, which makes them promising for *dynamic or unknown environments* [18]. For example, an **Exploration-RRT** variant has been proposed that integrates exploration objectives into the RRT’s sampling to cover space efficiently. One advantage is **real-time feasibility**: RRT can run quickly and expand the search frontier without computing a full map – useful if the robot is discovering the environment as it cleans. However, like PRM, a basic RRT does not inherently ensure complete coverage; it might randomly miss some nook or cranny unless guided. Researchers often use RRT to generate intermediate waypoints or a skeleton path and then have a secondary process ensure all areas off that skeleton are cleaned. **Hybrid approaches** have emerged, for example a **Hybrid-RRT* algorithm** that combines grid-based methods with RRT to handle both open areas and complex obstacles [19]. Overall, sampling-based algorithms bring strengths in navigating complex, high-dimensional or dynamic spaces, but they typically require augmentation to guarantee 100% coverage. They are more common in academic research on coverage of complex structures (e.g., coverage for UAVs in 3D space or robots with complex kinematics) rather than in everyday floor robots. Floor-cleaning tasks are largely 2D and structured enough that simpler planners often suffice, but sampling methods provide a toolkit for cases where randomness in planning can help escape local minima or handle unpredictable changes.


## Optimization-Based Approaches



Optimization-based coverage planning treats the coverage task as an optimization or search for an *optimal route* that covers the area, often subject to constraints. This category includes **formulations like MILP (Mixed-Integer Linear Programming)**, other mathematical programming methods, and continuous optimization techniques. The goal is usually to minimize some cost (path length, time, energy) while covering all required area. In essence, this is similar to the **Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)** or **graph covering problems**, which are known to be NP-hard for arbitrary environments [20]. Indeed, complete coverage in a known environment can be NP-hard, so exact optimization is computationally expensive [21][20]. Still, several approaches exist:


* **MILP and TSP-Based Formulations:** Researchers have formulated coverage planning as a MILP, where binary variables represent whether certain cells or waypoints are visited, and linear constraints ensure all areas are covered exactly once. This can yield an *optimal coverage path* for small instances, but solving MILPs for large environments is generally intractable without simplifications. For example, a MILP model can decide the order in which to visit a set of sub-areas or rooms to minimize total travel distance [22]. Tang and Ma (2023) present a mixed-integer programming model for multi-robot coverage that optimally allocates areas and ordering, but they rely on efficient heuristics to solve it for larger instances [23]. In single-robot scenarios, one might partition the space into cells (via grid or decomposition) and then use MILP or integer linear programming to solve a minimal Hamiltonian path that covers all those cells [20]. The result is theoretically the shortest possible route that covers everything – an **optimal coverage path**. However, because the problem is NP-hard, these exact methods scale poorly; they may work for a floorplan with, say, a handful of rooms, but not for a complex building with dozens of obstacles without additional heuristics. **Heuristic optimizers** (like genetic algorithms, discussed below) are often used as an alternative to pure MILP, to get near-optimal solutions faster. Optimization approaches are most feasible in *static, known environments (offline planning)*, such as an industrial setting where the floor layout is given and one can compute a route overnight if needed, then have the robot execute it repeatedly.
* **Convex Decomposition and Coverage:** In some cases, coverage can be approached with convex optimization by leveraging geometry. For instance, one can decompose the environment into **convex regions** (using methods like trapezoidal decomposition) and then plan simple back-and-forth trajectories in each region. The decomposition itself might be achieved via algorithms that solve for convex polygonal partitions. The advantage is that within a convex cell, the robot can move in straight lines without needing to navigate around obstacles. While the partitioning step might not be formulated as a convex *problem* per se (it’s more combinatorial), once you have convex cells, optimizing the path within each (minimizing turns, for example) can be done with continuous optimization. Some research has looked at optimizing the sweep direction within each cell to minimize coverage time (this can be set as an angle optimization problem and solved by evaluating a cost function, sometimes convex) [24]. Another example is optimizing the **placement of back-and-forth tracks**: if the robot’s tool has a certain width, one can model the coverage as parallel strips and use optimization to decide the strip orientation for minimal passes. These are usually convex or quasi-convex problems. Overall, convex optimization in coverage appears in *sub-problems* (like optimal lawnmower lane orientation, or sensor sweep optimization) rather than the whole coverage tour problem (which is discrete).
* **Meta-Heuristic and Evolutionary Algorithms:** A subset of optimization-based methods are those using evolutionary or swarm intelligence algorithms – e.g. **Genetic Algorithms (GA)**, **Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)**, **Ant/Bee Colony Optimization**, etc. These are not exact solvers but heuristic optimization techniques that can find good (if not provably optimal) coverage routes. For example, a GA can encode a sequence of waypoints or room visitation order as a “chromosome” and evolve a population of solutions to minimize total path length [25]. PSO or Ant-Colony methods can similarly explore the solution space by mimicking natural processes (swarms or foraging behavior) [26][27]. These methods have been applied to CPP especially for complex or high-level planning – for instance, optimizing the path for a drone to cover a set of survey points, or optimizing multi-robot task allocation for coverage. In floor cleaning, one might use GA to determine an efficient sequence to cover multiple rooms or zones. The advantage of meta-heuristics is that they can handle large search spaces and complex cost functions (even incorporating things like battery constraints, time windows, etc.). The downside is they don’t guarantee optimality and can be computationally heavy, though with modern computing they can often produce a good solution in reasonable time. In practice, one might run a GA offline to plan the cleaning route for a building, then load that route into the robot. This is more relevant to industrial or professional settings (where a supervisor could compute a route). For consumer robots, such heavy optimization is rarely done on the device, but cloud-based path optimization is a possible future scenario.



In summary, optimization-based approaches strive for **maximum coverage efficiency** (minimal overlap and travel) by solving a global planning problem. They perform best when the environment is known and static, and when computation can be done off-line or with powerful processors. They are **less adaptable in real-time** to changes – if something in the environment changes (a new obstacle, moved furniture), the optimal plan might need re-computation from scratch. Some algorithms incorporate buffer in their plans or quickly recompute sub-parts if blocked, but generally these methods assume a predictable environment. Thus, in dynamic or unknown settings, pure optimization is often combined with reactive methods (or one falls back to heuristic methods if the optimal plan fails). Industrial cleaning robots in structured environments can leverage optimization to reduce operation time (saving energy and labor) – e.g., an automated scrubber for a warehouse might compute an optimal coverage route that minimizes redundant passes [28]. In contrast, consumer robots typically do not solve MILPs on the fly; at most they might use a simple iterative algorithm to plan the next “room” to clean in an efficient order.


## Learning-Based Approaches



With advances in AI and machine learning, there is growing interest in using learning-based methods for coverage planning. These include **Reinforcement Learning (RL)** – where a robot learns a coverage policy through trial and error optimization – and **Imitation Learning (IL)** – where a robot learns from demonstrations of good coverage behavior. Learning-based approaches promise greater adaptability, as the robot can *learn to handle complex scenarios* that might be hard to script with classical algorithms.


* **Reinforcement Learning for Coverage:** In an RL framework, the robot is typically placed in a simulation of an environment and learns to navigate to maximize a reward function tied to coverage. For example, the reward might give positive feedback for covering new floor area and penalize revisiting already cleaned spots [29]. Using deep RL (with neural network policies), robots have been trained to perform complete coverage in maze-like environments and to handle obstacles in adaptive ways [30]. Recent research demonstrates that actor–critic methods (like A2C, PPO) can learn coverage strategies that are effective even with random obstacle layouts, adjusting the path on the fly to go around obstacles while minimizing missed spots [30]. The key advantage here is **adaptability**: RL policies can be very flexible in dynamic or complex environments. Unlike a fixed algorithm that might get stuck, a learned policy can, in theory, generalize to novel situations by virtue of its training. For instance, an RL-trained cleaner might implicitly learn behaviors such as wall-following, zigzagging in open areas, and systematic room-to-room transitions without being explicitly programmed to do so – it discovers these because they lead to higher reward (complete coverage) [29][31]. One study showed that a deep RL agent could achieve coverage comparable to classical methods while automatically adjusting to new obstacle placements, something traditional planners struggle with unless reprogrammed [30]. That said, RL approaches require extensive training (often in simulation) and careful reward design. If the reward doesn’t capture the true goal (e.g., if it over-penalizes overlaps, the robot might take risky paths and miss spots), the learned behavior may be suboptimal. There’s also a **sim-to-real gap**: policies trained in simulation might not perform well on real robots due to differences in sensors or dynamics. Researchers are working on techniques to transfer learned policies to real robots for coverage tasks [32], but it remains an active area. So far, most RL-based coverage solutions are experimental. They show that a learned agent can be **as efficient as heuristic planners** and significantly more **robust to unforeseen changes**, since it can react based on its state observations and learned value function [31].
* **Imitation Learning and Guided Learning:** Imitation Learning involves teaching the robot by example – for coverage, one could collect trajectories from human operators or from a very good algorithm, and then train a policy to imitate those. This can speed up learning compared to pure RL, because the policy doesn’t have to stumble upon a good strategy – it is shown one from the start. For instance, an expert trajectory that follows an optimal boustrophedon pattern could be used to train a neural network controller via behavior cloning. More advanced is **Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL)**, where the robot’s policy tries to generate trajectories indistinguishable from expert demonstrations. This has been applied to coverage as well: for example, **GAIL was used to guide a coverage robot’s policy to converge close to expert behavior while using RL** [33]. The combination of imitation and reinforcement (often called **learning from demonstration**) can yield a high-performance policy that covers like an expert and fine-tunes itself further via RL. One paper demonstrated using GAIL that a robot could learn to cover maps at high speed, by imitating an expert’s efficient path and then refining with its own trial-and-error [33]. Learning-based methods also allow incorporating complex sensor data (like camera input) to make decisions, potentially enabling **semantic coverage** (prioritizing certain areas) or recognizing when an area is truly clean.



In practice, **learning-based approaches are just beginning to appear in deployment**. Most consumer or industrial floor robots do not yet rely on end-to-end learned policies for coverage – they use classical or heuristic planners as described earlier. The reasons include the difficulty of training robust policies and verifying their behavior (important for a product that must reliably not get stuck or miss spots). However, learning methods are very promising for *adaptive coverage*: for instance, a future robot could learn the layout of your home and optimize its cleaning pattern over time, or adjust its strategy if it senses the floor is dirtier in some spots (spending more time there). Already, some vacuum robots use machine learning for tasks like dirt detection or room classification, and it’s plausible that reinforcement learning will be integrated for path planning once the reliability issues are solved. In summary, learning-based algorithms offer **high adaptability and the potential for intelligent decision-making** in coverage planning. They can handle complex dynamics (moving obstacles, changing environments) better than any fixed algorithm by learning a policy for those situations [31]. The trade-off is the significant **computational load in training** (which is usually done off-board or offline) and the need for large amounts of training data or simulation. At runtime, however, a learned policy (a neural network forward pass) can be very fast – thus meeting real-time constraints easily once deployed. The research community has shown that RL agents can outperform some classical methods in challenging scenarios [34][31], so we can expect more integration of learning in coverage robots moving forward.


## Performance and Practical Considerations



In evaluating these diverse algorithms for floor-cleaning robots, we consider several performance aspects: **coverage efficiency**, **adaptability to environment complexity/dynamics**, **real-time feasibility**, and **suitability for consumer vs. industrial deployment**. Different algorithms excel on different fronts, so the choice often depends on the use case:


* **Coverage Efficiency:** This refers to how thoroughly and quickly the robot can cover the area, ideally minimizing redundant coverage (overlap) and missed spots. Classical zigzag (boustrophedon) and spiral methods generally have good efficiency in open, static areas – for instance, a boustrophedon pattern *systematically covers without unnecessary overlap* [5], achieving near-100% coverage in an orderly way. Random bounce, by contrast, is inefficient, often revisiting areas many times; its efficiency improves over long durations, but in a fixed time it may only cover ~80–90% of the area due to its erratic path. Heuristic graph-based methods like wavefront and A* yield **high coverage rates with moderate overlap** – they plan shorter routes than random motion, but might still overlap a bit when navigating around obstacles or returning to previously visited zones. Optimization-based approaches aim for the theoretical **optimal (minimal) path length** to cover everything, thus highest efficiency (minimal overlap) by design. Studies framing coverage as an optimal routing problem confirm that these methods can reduce path length significantly compared to heuristics [21]. However, in practice, approximations or suboptimal solutions are used for large problems, so there’s some gap. Learning-based approaches can achieve good efficiency if trained well – an RL agent can learn to avoid redundant moves and cover systematically. For example, a learned policy might internally figure out a sweeping strategy nearly as good as boustrophedon, and one study noted that the RL algorithm optimized coverage path in presence of obstacles, reducing wasteful motions [30]. That said, if not carefully trained, an RL robot might exhibit quirky behavior that reduces efficiency (like favoring one side of a room). In summary, for pure efficiency in a static known environment, an optimization-planned path is hard to beat. For unknown or dynamic settings, a combination of systematic sweeping and reactive planning (which many heuristic methods provide) tends to ensure high coverage with acceptable extra distance.
* **Adaptability to Complexity and Dynamics:** Adaptability is crucial for real-world cleaning – the robot should handle cluttered furniture layouts, multiple rooms, and moving obstacles or changes (like people in the space or doors opening/closing). Classical algorithms have mixed adaptability. Random walk is *highly adaptive* in the sense that it doesn’t require any model – it will keep bouncing around new obstacles – but it has no intelligence, possibly missing narrow alcoves for a long time or failing to specifically target remaining dirty spots. Boustrophedon and similar require a known or sensor-detected map; if the environment changes (say a new obstacle appears), a naive boustrophedon path might not account for it and could leave an area uncleaned or necessitate a restart. There are online versions (like Spiral-STC and sensor-based zigzag) that can adapt to obstacles by locally modifying the path [35] – these have better adaptability, allowing coverage to continue around unexpected obstacles at the cost of some re-planning or backtracking. Heuristic methods like D* and frontier exploration are explicitly designed for changing environments: D* will replan around new obstacles in real-time [12], and frontier methods naturally go wherever new space opens up. Thus, these are **adaptable to both complex static layouts and dynamic changes**. Sampling-based planners, especially RRT, are also quite adaptable: RRT can quickly re-explore a space if something changes, since it builds a new tree with the latest information. They shine in *complex environments* with many obstacles, as they can weave through complicated spaces without needing an exhaustive grid – making them suitable for highly cluttered scenarios. Optimization-based plans are usually the least adaptable *at runtime*: if the environment does not exactly match the model (e.g., unforeseen obstacle or an area becomes inaccessible), the optimal plan might be invalid. The robot then either has to fall back on a simpler method or recompute an optimization (which is slow). Some advanced approaches create robust optimal paths or periodically re-solve a MILP with updated info, but this can be computationally expensive. Learning-based methods tend to be **very adaptable** *if* they have been trained on the kinds of variations present. An RL policy can handle dynamic obstacles by observing them and learning to navigate around while continuing coverage [31]. For instance, an RL-trained cleaner could learn to recognize when a path is blocked and choose a different route without explicit reprogramming – something demonstrated in simulations [30]. However, if the scenario is far outside its training (say a type of obstacle or layout it never saw), it might generalize poorly. Overall, heuristic and learning methods currently offer the best adaptability for unknown or dynamic conditions, which is why they are popular for home robots that must deal with everyday changes (chairs being moved, humans present).
* **Real-Time Feasibility (Computational Load):** Floor-cleaning robots typically have limited processing power (especially battery-operated consumer models), so algorithms must be efficient enough to run on-board in real time. Classical strategies are excellent in this regard – they require almost no computation (just simple reactive logic or predetermined patterns). A robot can easily execute random bounce or spiral behaviors on a tiny microcontroller. Even boustrophedon (if the map is known) just involves following preset waypoints; if the map is unknown, a sensor-based zigzag involves local decisions that are low-cost. Heuristic graph-based methods introduce more computation: e.g., running A* on a grid map or doing BFS for wavefront. But modern vacuums that create a grid map (with perhaps tens of thousands of cells) can still run A* or BFS in fractions of a second on their onboard processors – these algorithms are polynomial-time and practical for moderate grid sizes. D* for dynamic re-planning is also efficient (it reuses previous search results), which is why it’s used in robotics for real-time navigation. Sampling-based methods like RRT are generally very fast, as they perform simple operations per sample; a basic RRT can run in real time and replan quickly, although if extremely high coverage precision is needed, the number of samples might grow and slow things down. Optimization-based methods are the most computationally intensive. Solving a MILP optimally can take hours for large instances. In a real robot, one would not attempt to solve a big MILP on the fly. Instead, either a simplified problem is solved (small area, short horizon) or one uses precomputed plans. Some vacuum robots may do a bit of TSP solving to decide the order of rooms to clean, but this is usually done with heuristics or simplified models. If a cleaning robot were to use a full optimization approach, it would likely compute the plan off-line (perhaps in the cloud or during an idle period) and then just execute it. Learning-based methods have an interesting profile: **training** a deep RL model is extremely computationally heavy (often requiring GPUs and many hours of simulation), but **execution** of a trained policy is very light. A neural network policy can output control actions in milliseconds on small hardware. So if a policy is pre-trained, the robot can run it in real time with little effort, making decisions on the fly. The catch is if the robot needs to continue learning or adapting online, that could be expensive. In most proposals, the heavy training is done beforehand. Therefore, learning-based controllers can be quite feasible on-board for real-time operation (just as face recognition or other learned tasks run on mobile devices now). In summary, *all the surveyed methods can be made to run on a robot with the right design*, but classical and heuristic algorithms are by far the easiest on computation, sampling-based and learned policies are moderate, and full optimization is typically offloaded or done only for small-scale problems.
* **Consumer vs. Industrial Deployment:** The requirements and constraints in consumer (home) robots versus industrial/commercial cleaning robots can differ, leading to different algorithm choices. **Consumer robots** (like Roomba and its competitors) prioritize low cost, simplicity, and robustness in unknown home environments. Early models famously used random bounce and simple heuristics (like wall-following and spirals) because they had limited sensing and no mapping [3]. This worked for small homes, though it was not the most time-efficient. Newer high-end models now incorporate mapping (using cameras or LiDAR) and plan systematic coverage – often grid-based or zigzag patterns – to ensure faster, more thorough cleaning. For example, iRobot’s later Roomba models and many competitors create a floor plan and then execute a back-and-forth coverage of each room. They essentially shifted from “classical random” methods to **heuristic graph-based** methods as processing and sensing capabilities improved. Consumer robots also face very dynamic environments (pets, kids, etc.), so adaptability is valued: this is achieved through bump sensors (for reactive avoidance) and, more recently, AI that can recognize and avoid hazards (like cords or pet waste). However, advanced methods like MILP or RL are not yet explicitly common in mass-market products – partly due to reliability and partly because the simpler methods are “good enough” when combined with a bit of smarts (the difference between a 95% coverage and 99% might not justify a complex AI if the simpler method already satisfies customers). **Industrial and commercial cleaning robots** (such as autonomous scrubbers for warehouses, airports, or offices) can leverage more sophisticated planning. These robots often operate in larger, more structured environments (long corridors, large open halls) where a *global plan* can greatly optimize efficiency (saving hours of operation). They also usually have access to a predefined map (e.g., a facility map) or can be driven once manually to create a map. In such cases, *optimization-based approaches* become attractive: the robot can compute or be given an optimized coverage route that minimizes time and battery usage. Industrial robots also might coordinate multiple units (multi-robot coverage) to clean huge areas; this scenario benefits from optimization (task allocation, partitioning the area) and has been addressed with MILP and other algorithms in research [36][37]. Additionally, because industrial robots are expensive and often maintained by professionals, one can afford more powerful computing (even cloud connectivity) to plan paths. We see that in industry, *safety and predictability* are also crucial – a deterministic planned route might be preferred over a learning-based unpredictable policy. That said, some industrial machines have begun to use machine learning for navigation and obstacle detection. In terms of algorithm choice: **structured environments with repetitive tasks** (like a warehouse that needs cleaning every night) favor planning a repeatable optimal path (even if it takes some computing time once), whereas **unstructured or changing environments** (a busy retail store with different layouts each day) favor adaptive heuristic or learning approaches.



Finally, we note practical constraints like **battery life** apply to both consumer and industrial robots. Some algorithms explicitly incorporate these – e.g., planning coverage such that the robot can return to a dock when battery is low [38]. Industrial cleaners often have bigger batteries and can cover more in one go; consumer robots often need to recharge mid-mission. Modern consumer robots handle this by mapping which areas are left, returning to dock, then resuming where they left off – this is essentially a heuristic solution to a constrained coverage problem (some research treats it formally [38]).



In conclusion, there is no one-size-fits-all algorithm for coverage – rather, successful floor-cleaning robots use a *hybrid of methods*. Simpler classical patterns ensure robustness and low cost, heuristic planners add efficiency when maps are available, optimization can be leveraged for strategic planning in static settings, and learning-based techniques are emerging to provide greater autonomy and adaptability. Ongoing research and development continue to refine these algorithms, making robots ever more efficient at keeping our floors clean [39].

# Evaluation Metrics for Human–Robot Communication Quality



Evaluating the quality of human–robot communication requires a multi-faceted approach. Researchers assess not only the technical correctness of linguistic exchanges, but also task outcomes, user experience, social dynamics, and multimodal coordination. Below, we organize key metrics into several categories and describe each, including how they are measured, relevant contexts, and supporting research findings.


## 1. Linguistic and Dialog Metrics



Effective human–robot communication starts with robust language interaction. **Speech Recognition Accuracy** is a fundamental metric, reflecting how well the robot understands human speech. It is typically quantified by the percentage of words correctly recognized or by the Word Error Rate (WER), which computes the edit distance between the spoken input and the robot’s transcription [1]. High speech recognition accuracy is crucial in voice-command scenarios and dialog systems; for example, a recent HRI system reported a speech recognition WER of ~22% in realistic settings [2], indicating room for improvement in noisy, real-world contexts. Alongside understanding user speech, the **naturalness** of the robot’s own speech and dialog behavior is evaluated. Naturalness is usually measured via user ratings or Mean Opinion Scores, asking how “human-like” or fluid the robot’s speech and responses sound. It is especially relevant in conversational robots or social robots where an unnatural tone or phrasing can disrupt the interaction. Closely related is **dialog fluency** – the smooth, timely flow of conversation without awkward pauses or interruptions. Fluency can be assessed subjectively (e.g. users rating how fluent or “non-awkward” the interaction felt) and objectively (e.g. measuring response latencies and interruptibility) [3]. For instance, Chao and Thomaz (2010) had participants rate aspects of a human–robot dialog, finding that an adaptive turn-taking system was rated as less awkward and more natural than a baseline system [3]. In task-oriented dialogs, fluency also relates to **turn-taking efficiency** – robots that anticipate user actions and minimize human idle time are seen as more fluent team partners [4]. Overall, high linguistic performance (accurate speech recognition, natural-sounding speech synthesis, and fluent turn-taking) is associated with more successful and satisfying human–robot communications [3][4].


## 2. Task Performance Metrics



Beyond the dialog itself, it is critical to measure how well the human–robot team accomplishes their intended tasks. **Task success rate** (or task completion rate) is a primary metric – it is the proportion of goals or tasks that are completed correctly by the human–robot pair. This is measured simply by logging outcomes (success vs. failure) across trials. A high success rate indicates effective communication of instructions and coordination. For example, in a search-and-rescue HRI scenario, a performance metric might be the number of victims found by a robot under human guidance, minus any penalties for errors [5]. Complementing success, the **error rate** captures how often misunderstandings or mistakes occur. Errors can include misinterpreted commands, task failures, or safety infractions. They are typically counted per task or per unit time. A low error rate is especially important in safety-critical contexts (e.g. surgical robots or autonomous driving) where communication errors can have serious consequences. **Task completion time** (or efficiency) is another key metric: how long it takes for the human–robot team to finish a given task or interaction. This is measured with timestamps or timers and is relevant in any context where efficiency matters – from industrial assembly lines to service robots in busy environments. Shorter completion times often indicate more efficient communication and coordination. However, speed must be balanced with accuracy; hence researchers often consider both time and success rate together. Indeed, a large survey of HRI studies found that *task performance outcomes* and *task timing* were among the most frequently reported objective measures in evaluations [6]. These metrics are context-dependent – for instance, in collaborative manufacturing, metrics like throughput or idle time may be used, while in assistive robotics, one might measure the percentage of tasks the robot can autonomously handle versus needing human intervention. Overall, task performance metrics provide a concrete gauge of how communication quality translates into real-world results [7][6].


## 3. User-Centered Metrics



From the human’s perspective, the quality of communication is reflected in their experience, attitudes, and perceived effort. **User satisfaction** is a broad metric encompassing the user’s overall contentment with the interaction. It is usually measured through post-interaction questionnaires or rating scales (e.g., asking users to rate their satisfaction or enjoyment on a Likert scale). High user satisfaction indicates that the communication was effective and met the user’s needs or expectations. In conversational settings, new scales like the HRI Conversational User Enjoyment Scale have been proposed to quantify how enjoyable a human–robot conversation is [8]. Another crucial human factor is **trust**. Trust in a robot means the user’s willingness to rely on the robot’s actions and recommendations. Trust is especially relevant in scenarios where the robot operates with some autonomy (such as assistive robots, autonomous vehicles, or military robots) and the human needs to decide how much to delegate. To measure trust, researchers often use validated psychometric scales – for example, the **Trust Perception Scale-HRI** (Schaefer, 2016) or similar surveys developed for human-automation trust [9]. These instruments typically ask users to agree or disagree with statements like “I am confident in the robot’s abilities” or gauge trust on multiple dimensions (reliability, predictability, etc.). Higher trust scores have been correlated with greater acceptance and smoother cooperation in HRI [9]. Alongside trust, users form judgments about a robot’s **perceived intelligence and competence**. This is often measured by questionnaire items (e.g., from the Godspeed Questionnaire Series) that ask how intelligent, knowledgeable, or capable the robot appeared [10]. Such perceived intelligence metrics are relevant in educational robots or any context where the robot provides information or makes decisions – a robot that communicates clearly and correctly will be rated higher in intelligence, which can improve user adherence to its guidance [10]. Another user-centered aspect is **workload** – the mental and physical effort a user must expend during the interaction. If communicating with the robot is confusing or the user must constantly adapt, the workload is high, indicating poorer communication quality. Workload is commonly measured by the NASA Task Load Index (TLX), a standardized questionnaire that yields a workload score based on mental demand, effort, frustration, etc. [11]. In HRI studies, NASA-TLX is often used to compare interfaces (e.g., voice commands vs. manual control) to ensure that adding the robot does not overburden the human. Ideally, an effective human–robot communication reduces user workload by making interaction intuitive. In summary, user-centered metrics like satisfaction, trust, perceived intelligence, and workload are typically gathered via surveys and interviews, and they capture the human’s subjective evaluation of the communication. These metrics are validated by extensive use in HRI research – for instance, trust and usability-related ratings consistently rank among the top reported measures in HRI experiments [12].


## 4. Emotional and Social Interaction Metrics



Human–robot communication quality is also judged by how well the robot handles the social and emotional dimension of interaction. One set of metrics involves **emotion recognition** – the robot’s ability to detect and appropriately respond to human emotions (via facial expressions, voice tone, body language, etc.). The accuracy of an emotion recognition system is measured by comparing the robot’s detected emotion to a ground truth (often the human’s self-report or an expert labeling). In research studies, this is expressed as classification accuracy or F1-score for various emotion categories. High accuracy means the robot can correctly infer if a person is happy, sad, frustrated, and so on. This is vital in contexts like therapeutic or companion robots, where the robot must tailor its behavior to the user’s emotional state. Modern HRI systems achieve around 80–90% emotion recognition accuracy using multimodal sensors [13]. For example, one study reported a humanoid robot recognizing human facial emotions with about 80% accuracy during live interaction [13]. Beyond recognition, robots are also evaluated on **emotional expression** – whether the robot can convey emotions in a way humans understand (through facial displays, tone of voice, etc.). This is often measured by asking users if they can correctly perceive the robot’s intended emotion, or by recognition rates of the robot’s expressions.



Another important social metric is **engagement**. Engagement reflects how involved and attentive the human is during the interaction, which in turn indicates that the communication is compelling and effective. Engagement can be measured in several ways. Subjectively, researchers use self-report questionnaires like the User Engagement Scale to ask participants how absorbed or interested they felt [14]. Objectively, engagement can be inferred from behaviors such as eye contact frequency, body leaning, or response times. In studies with children or other populations where surveys are not feasible, observational coding (e.g. counting how often a person initiates interaction with the robot, or time spent focused on the robot) is used as an engagement metric [14]. High engagement is relevant in educational and entertainment robots – for instance, a tutoring robot should keep students engaged to facilitate learning. Closely related to engagement is **rapport**, the mutual positive connection and harmony in communication. In long-term or social interactions (such as a robot therapist or a peer-like companion robot), building rapport with the human is a marker of quality communication. Rapport is typically measured through specialized questionnaires administered to users, which gauge aspects like how comfortable, understood, and “in sync” they felt with the robot. Recently, researchers have developed a Connection-Coordination Rapport (CCR) scale – an 18-item instrument to quantify human–robot rapport [15]. Such scales ask users about trust, empathy, and ease of communication with the robot, among other factors. A high rapport score indicates the robot was able to establish a social bond, leading to more natural and effective interaction. In contexts like healthcare or caregiving, high rapport can correlate with better outcomes (e.g. patients following the robot’s exercise recommendations due to a trusting relationship).



These emotional and social metrics are supported by HRI research emphasizing that effective communication is not purely about information exchange but also about social connection. For example, studies show that people feel significantly more **engaged** with a robot that establishes mutual eye contact (mutual gaze) compared to one that does not. Similarly, a robot that appropriately responds to a user’s emotional cues (e.g., offering encouragement when the user is frustrated) tends to be rated as more likable and trustworthy [[16]([[19](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2020.532279/full#:~:text=%E2%80%A2%20Emotional%20expression%20of%20robots%3A,2018%3B%20Rossi%20and%20Ruocco%2C%202019))][17]. Therefore, emotional recognition, user engagement, and rapport are key quality indicators, especially for social robots and any scenario where long-term human–robot relationships are expected.


## 5. Multimodal Interaction Metrics



Human communication is inherently multimodal – we combine speech with gestures, gaze, facial expressions, and more. Likewise, human–robot communication quality is evaluated by how well the robot can interpret and synchronize multiple modalities. One important metric here is **gesture interpretation accuracy**. Many robots are equipped with vision systems to recognize human gestures (hand signals, body movements) as part of the interaction. The accuracy of gesture interpretation is measured by the percentage of gestures correctly recognized or classified by the robot’s system, often validated against a labeled dataset or human observer’s coding. High gesture recognition accuracy is critical in contexts like collaborative manufacturing or household robots where users may point at objects or use hand signs to give commands. State-of-the-art systems report very high accuracy for recognition of predefined gestures – for instance, an HRI platform using both a Leap Motion sensor and an armband achieved around 95–97% gesture classification accuracy in lab tests [2]. Such metrics demonstrate that the robot can reliably “understand” the physical gestures accompanying or replacing speech.



Another multimodal aspect is **gaze coordination**. This refers to the robot’s ability to coordinate its eye movements or camera orientation with the human’s gaze and attention. Metrics for gaze coordination include the frequency of **mutual gaze** (moments when both human and robot are looking at each other’s face), the accuracy of **gaze following** (how often the robot correctly looks at the object the human is referencing or looking at), and timing metrics such as gaze response latency (how quickly the robot meets the human’s gaze or shifts gaze appropriately). These are often measured through video analysis or eye-tracking: for example, counting the percentage of time the robot maintains eye contact when appropriate, or how many times the robot’s gaze aligns with the human’s pointing gestures. Gaze coordination is especially relevant in conversational and collaborative tasks. A robot that looks at a person when they speak and shifts gaze to objects to signal attention will feel more natural to interact with. Research has shown that timely mutual gaze from a robot can increase users’ feelings of engagement and connection. In practical terms, a metric like *mutual gaze rate* (how often mutual eye contact is achieved per minute) could be used to quantify this aspect; higher rates (within comfortable limits) generally signify better social attunement. Additionally, designers examine **multimodal alignment** – whether the robot’s speech, gesture, and gaze work in concert. For example, if a robot says “Pick up that cup” while nodding or directing its eyes toward the cup, the alignment between verbal and nonverbal cues can be evaluated (often by task success or user understanding in response to the combined cue). Misalignment (such as the robot’s gaze not matching its spoken referent) would be noted as a communication quality issue.



In sum, multimodal metrics assess how well robots handle the richness of human communication channels. High performance in gesture recognition and gaze coordination leads to more natural, efficient interactions – e.g., fewer misunderstandings and faster task execution when using pointing, and greater user comfort due to appropriate eye contact. These metrics are supported by numerous studies in HRI and social robotics that emphasize the importance of nonverbal behavior: a review of multimodal HRI interfaces noted significant improvements in user experience when speech input was combined with accurate gesture and gaze interpretation [2][18]. As robots continue to integrate multiple sensors (cameras, microphones, depth sensors), evaluation of these multimodal communication metrics remains a crucial part of assessing overall interaction quality.




---



Each of the above metric categories provides a different window into communication quality. In practice, HRI researchers often employ a **balanced scorecard** of metrics from all these categories to get a comprehensive evaluation [6][12]. For example, in an experiment with a social robot, one might simultaneously measure speech recognition accuracy (to ensure instructions are understood), task success rate, user trust and workload via questionnaires, emotion recognition accuracy, and observe gaze behaviors – painting a holistic picture of the interaction. Using peer-reviewed, validated metrics (such as standardized questionnaires and well-defined performance measures) ensures that results are reliable and comparable across studies. As the field of human–robot interaction matures, these metrics help researchers and designers identify weaknesses in communication (e.g., a robot might achieve tasks quickly but score low on user trust, indicating a need to improve transparency or predictability). Ultimately, the goal is to improve these metrics in unison, creating robots that not only *hear and act* correctly, but also *connect* with humans in a natural, effective, and trustworthy manner [10][[16]([[19](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2020.532279/full#:~:text=%E2%80%A2%20Emotional%20expression%20of%20robots%3A,2018%3B%20Rossi%20and%20Ruocco%2C%202019))].
