sections.text:
# Common UI Design Patterns in Sense-Making, Information Organization, and AI Writing Tools


## Visual Layout Patterns



**Sidebars and Multi-Pane Layouts:** Many sense-making and knowledge tools use sidebars or multi-pane designs to organize content and navigation. A sidebar (typically a vertical column on one side) can present a menu of sections, folders, or tool modes while the main pane shows the primary content. This layout helps flatten the information hierarchy by giving users simultaneous access to multiple categories or views [1]. For example, a note-taking app might have a sidebar list of notebooks/tags and a main editor panel. This pattern keeps context readily available without overwhelming the main workspace. By dedicating persistent space for navigation or secondary information, sidebars support quick mode switching (e.g. between a document view and an outline or reference material) – a common requirement in sense-making scenarios.



**Card-Based Interfaces:** The “card” UI pattern groups related information into discrete, flexible containers – visually resembling index cards or tiles [2]. Many modern organization tools (project boards, digital whiteboards, note apps) use card-based layouts to break complex information into manageable chunks. Each card might represent an idea, data point, or task; users can rearrange or stack cards, reflecting relationships at a glance. Card UIs are inherently modular: they allow dragging cards around to reorganize priority or flow, and often adapt to different screen sizes easily (cards can wrap or scroll). The card metaphor also invites *progressive disclosure* of detail – a card might show a title or summary, with full details revealed on click. By segmenting content into cards, interfaces like Trello or Notion help users focus on one unit of information at a time while maintaining a broader overview of all items.



*A timeline-based interface (from the LifeLines prototype) showing an overview of a patient’s record on a single screen with multiple timelines and event icons. Such visual timelines help users grasp temporal patterns and access details efficiently.* Timelines are a prevalent layout for sense-making tools that involve temporal data or narratives. **Timelines and Chronologies:** A timeline arranges information along a horizontal time axis, which is invaluable for understanding sequences, trends, and duration. In investigative analysis or journalistic sense-making, for instance, events can be plotted in chronological order to reveal cause-effect patterns. The classic *LifeLines* system demonstrated how a one-screen timeline overview of personal history (with each facet of a record shown as a line, and events as icons) can “facilitate spotting anomalies and trends” while allowing direct access to details [cs.umd.edu][cs.umd.edu]. Timeline views leverage humans’ natural ability to reason about time visually; they make it easy to see overlaps (e.g. two projects running concurrently) or intervals with no activity. Interactive timeline UIs often support zooming or filtering – a design following Shneiderman’s mantra “overview first, zoom and filter, details-on-demand” (a form of progressive disclosure). By giving a temporal *overview*, timeline layouts help users build a mental model of the data’s evolution before diving into specifics. They are common not only in dedicated sense-making apps, but also in note-taking and writing tools (for example, a writer might use a timeline to plot story events or a researcher to organize historical data). The visual alignment of items in time can reveal patterns that might be missed in a static list or narrative form.



**Hierarchies and Networks (Nested Organization):** Organizing information in nested hierarchies (tree structures) is a time-tested approach found in everything from file systems to outliner apps. Many knowledge management tools provide an outline or notebook hierarchy, letting users create nested categories and sub-items (for example, a notebook containing sections, pages, and sub-pages). Hierarchies impose a parent–child order that can be useful for top-down thinking and logical grouping. They also naturally enable progressive disclosure: nodes can be collapsed to hide detail or expanded to show it. However, strictly hierarchical organization can be limiting – an idea placed under one category might belong in others too, and deep hierarchies can hinder finding things. To address this, modern tools often combine hierarchies with *network* structures like tags or links. **Tags** allow assigning multiple labels to an item, effectively placing it in multiple categories at once. Research in personal information management has found that tagging systems enable “multiple mappings, supporting diverse categorizations and offering greater flexibility” than rigid folders [5]. The flip side is that too many tags or links can introduce complexity or cognitive load if not managed [6]. Many note-taking applications now feature a global **graph view** – a network of nodes (notes) and edges (links) – in addition to any hierarchical arrangement. This visual network affords a sense of how pieces of information connect, beyond tree-based parent-child relations. It taps into spatial organization (discussed later) by letting users see clusters of related notes. In fact, the resurgence of such **hypertextual** linking in “tools for thought” is a key trend: researchers observe that modern note-taking practices heavily use bidirectional links to revisit and reuse ideas, echoing the early hypertext vision of Memex and NoteCards [7]. In summary, effective UIs for organizing information often blend structured hierarchies (for clarity and navigation) with flexible network relationships (for cross-cutting connections), giving users multiple pathways to arrange and find their knowledge.


## Interaction Mechanisms


### Direct Manipulation and Drag-and-Drop



Direct manipulation is a fundamental interaction style in which users act on visible objects rather than through abstract commands. Drag-and-drop (DnD) is a prime example: users can grab an item (a note card, a file, a concept node) and physically move it to another location or category. This mechanism is intuitive and leverages our spatial and muscle memory – aligning with the principle that interfaces should allow *physical actions* instead of complex syntax [8]. Many sense-making tools encourage users to **drag items into clusters or sequences** to form meaning (e.g., grouping related evidence on a canvas, reordering slides or ideas). In knowledge organization, one might drag a note into a folder or onto a tag to classify it. The benefit is immediacy: feedback is usually instantaneous (e.g., the item appears in the new list or changes color to indicate it’s been categorized), which reinforces the feeling of *direct engagement* with the data. Usability research stresses that clear signifiers (visual cues that an item is draggable) and continuous feedback (seeing the item move, highlighting drop targets) are critical for DnD interactions [9]. When designed well, drag-and-drop can be very efficient—consider how quickly users can rearrange a kanban board by dragging cards, compared to manually editing some list order. However, designers must also provide accessible alternatives (keyboard or menu commands) for those who cannot or do not discover the drag gesture. Overall, DnD and similar direct manipulation techniques make the interface feel *tangible*, which is especially powerful in creative sense-making where users benefit from a hands-on, trial-and-error approach to organizing thoughts.


### Tagging and Interlinking



**Tagging** is a lightweight mechanism to annotate items with keywords, enabling flexible organization and retrieval. It became popular in early web tools (like Delicious for bookmarks) and is now ubiquitous in note-taking and productivity apps. Unlike moving a note into a single folder, tagging allows one item to belong to multiple categories (for example, an article note could be tagged `#machine-learning` *and* `#policy`). This many-to-many classification mirrors how our brains categorize things and supports serendipitous finding (you might browse everything tagged `#policy` and stumble on that article even if you filed it under `#machine-learning`). Empirical studies have shown the value of this flexibility – tags “support diverse categorizations,” though they also come with a cost of potential overhead in managing many labels [5]. From an interaction standpoint, tagging often happens via a text box or an autocomplete dropdown; some UIs also allow *dragging an item onto a tag* (a blend of DnD with tagging). Closely related to tags is the idea of **interlinking** information items. In personal knowledge bases and sense-making environments, users create explicit links between notes or concepts (akin to hyperlinks on the web). For instance, while writing, you might [[link]] a piece of text to another note, or in a research tool, connect two idea nodes with an arrow labeled with a relationship. This turns a set of notes into a network of knowledge. Such interlinking is essentially user-generated associative tagging (each link is like saying “this is related to that”). It’s a key mechanism in hypertext systems and has seen a renaissance with bi-directional linking in tools like Roam Research. By following links, users can navigate their knowledge non-linearly, which strongly supports sense-making – as Vannevar Bush envisioned, it creates “trails” of thought. Recent research on scholarly knowledge work finds that hypertext-style linking patterns help in “revisiting and reusing existing/past ideas” during sensemaking [7]. To make linking fluid, UIs provide affordances like wiki-style syntax, drag-selection of text to create a link, or context menus suggesting relevant links. Some AI-assisted tools even suggest links automatically (blurring into AI mechanisms) by analyzing content. In sum, tagging and linking empower users to impose *meaningful connections* on information beyond strict hierarchical placement, and the UI’s job is to make creating and traversing those connections as easy as jotting a margin note or drawing a line on paper.


### Annotation and Highlighting



Annotation refers to adding one’s own notes or marks to information – a practice long carried from paper margins into digital interfaces. In sense-making scenarios, annotation is how users externalize their thinking about source materials. For example, an intelligence analyst might highlight excerpts of reports and attach comments about their significance, or a student might annotate a research article with summaries and questions. Modern UIs support annotation through features like inline highlights (with different colors to signify themes), comments or footnotes attached to specific text, and even free-form ink or sketches on touch devices. The act of **highlighting** key text or data points serves as a filtering mechanism: it makes important information stand out visually, which later helps in synthesis (all highlights can be reviewed in one place, or aggregated into a summary). **Sticky notes** or comment threads in the margin allow users to layer interpretations without altering the original content, maintaining context. From an interaction perspective, creating an annotation should be lightweight (e.g. click and type, or a quick shortcut) so it doesn’t interrupt the flow of reading/thinking. Many sense-making tools (like PDF readers, data analysis environments, etc.) also allow tagging or linking within annotations, combining these mechanisms for richer semantics (for instance, tagging a comment with `#assumption` vs `#evidence`). Research has consistently found that annotation helps engagement and comprehension – effectively, it’s an active reading strategy that makes the interface a two-way medium (not just consuming information but conversing with it). For UI design, a challenge is how to display annotations without cluttering the interface. Common solutions include popovers (show note on hover/click), side panels listing all annotations, or toggling annotation visibility. In collaborative knowledge tools, annotations become a communication channel – multiple users can highlight or comment and then resolve or reply, which turns sense-making into a shared, interactive process. Overall, supporting annotation is crucial in these domains because it embeds the user’s insights directly into the workspace, making the interface not just a tool for viewing information but a canvas for *interpreting* it.


### Conversational Prompts and AI Assistance



The rise of AI writing tools and other AI-assisted interfaces has introduced *conversation* as a new mode of interaction in productivity software. Instead of purely interacting through direct manipulation or structured forms, users can now give **natural language prompts** to the system. For example, in an AI writing assistant, a user might literally *ask* the tool, “Summarize these notes into a draft introduction,” or instruct, “Rephrase this paragraph to sound more formal.” The interface for this is often a chat-like prompt box or a command bar. This mechanism draws on the familiarity of messaging UIs, but under the hood it’s sending the prompt to an AI model. One advantage is approachability – users can express what they want in their own words, which lowers the barrier to using complex functionality (you don’t have to find the right menu or learn a macro language). However, it also poses challenges: users may not know the *scope* of the AI’s abilities or how to phrase requests optimally. Therefore, AI-infused tools are adopting design patterns to guide prompt interactions. Common approaches include **prompt templates or examples** (suggesting questions the user can ask), **interactive parameters** (sliders or toggles for tone, length, creativity level to accompany a prompt), and **immediate feedback** on prompts (like showing a preview of what the AI will do, or highlighting parts of the input it considered). The interaction is often iterative: the user gives a prompt, the AI responds with a suggestion, and then the user may refine or follow up. This iterative loop is essentially a form of **mixed-initiative interaction** – a concept in HCI where both human and computer can take turns steering the task. As Horvitz (1999) noted in his principles for mixed-initiative UIs, the system should be designed to **allow the user to guide, refine, or correct the AI’s actions** and not act autonomously in a vacuum [10]. For instance, after an AI generates text, the interface might allow the user to highlight a portion and say “elaborate on this point” or “cite a source for this,” giving the user agency to direct the next step. Another emerging pattern is **in-situ AI suggestions**: rather than the user always prompting, the system can proactively offer help (like a ghost text in place as you write, or a sidebar saying “I found 3 related references, want to see them?”). This needs to be handled carefully to not distract or annoy; progressive disclosure is relevant here (the AI can hint subtly and only expand if asked). In summary, conversational and prompt-based interactions turn the interface into a two-way dialogue, which is powerful for complex tasks (writing, coding, analyzing data) – but the UI must manage this dialogue so that it remains transparent what the AI is doing and under the user’s control. Done right, it feels like *collaborating* with an assistant rather than using a rigid tool.


## UI Design Principles in These Tools


### Progressive Disclosure for Complexity Management



Tools for thought often pack a lot of functionality – from layering multiple views (notes, calendars, graphs) to advanced AI actions – so applying **progressive disclosure** is key to prevent overwhelming users. Progressive disclosure is a design technique that defers or hides advanced features and information until they are needed [11]. In practice, this could mean that a note-taking app starts with a clean, simple interface for writing, and only shows options like “link to existing note” or “open graph view” when the user explicitly wants to do those things. Similarly, an AI content generator might present a single text box to begin with, but offer more detailed controls (tone, audience, outline tools, etc.) in an “Advanced” panel or after an initial draft is produced. By staging the interaction, the UI stays **focused on the primary task** – as an example, Google’s basic search page is minimal, while the advanced search is tucked away for those who need it [12]. The goal is to make the experience feel *simple for novices* yet *empowering for experts*. Techniques to achieve this include collapsible sections (accordions), step-by-step wizards for complex tasks, hover/tooltips for extra options, and sensible defaults that cover common cases. Progressive disclosure also aligns with human cognitive limits: it presents “bite-size” information or choices at any given time [13], reducing cognitive load and confusion. In sense-making tools, one might see this principle in something like a visualization dashboard – initially, it might show a default view of data, with filters and parameters hidden under a “refine results” drawer that the user opens when needed. In knowledge management, an app might hide rarely used commands (like importing/exporting data, bulk editing tags) under secondary menus. Importantly, progressive disclosure is *not* about dumbing down the software; it’s about **sequencing** the interaction. As Nielsen Norman Group describes, it “helps novice users avoid mistakes and saves them time” by not showing everything at once [14], while still letting power users delve deeper in subsequent steps. Ultimately, applying this principle leads to cleaner interfaces where users can concentrate on sense-making or writing, with confidence that the more powerful tools are there – just one click away – when their workflow requires it.


### Spatial Organization and Visual Grouping



Spatial organization is a core principle behind many sense-making and note-taking interfaces: it leverages the human brain’s strong spatial memory and pattern recognition abilities. The idea is to arrange information visually (in two or even three dimensions) such that *where* something is located and *what* is near it carry meaning. Research has shown that using 2D spatial layouts for documents or icons can take advantage of users’ innate ability to remember locations and spatial relationships [15]. For example, consider a digital whiteboard for brainstorming: a user might place all finance-related ideas on the top-left, and marketing ideas on the bottom-right. Later, they’ll often recall “I put that note in the top-left cluster” – effectively using spatial memory to organize retrieval. Interfaces like mind maps, concept maps, and tools like Miro or FigJam explicitly encourage spatial grouping: users draw nodes and can place them anywhere on an infinite canvas, drawing connecting lines. This freedom allows people to impose a structure that might not be strictly hierarchical but is *visually logical* to them (perhaps grouping by theme, chronology, or any conceptual dimension). An early landmark in HCI, **Data Mountain**, demonstrated that letting users arrange web page thumbnails on a 3D inclined plane led to improved finding of saved pages, compared to a traditional list – it “was designed specifically to take advantage of human spatial memory” and indeed showed measurable benefits over the browser’s Favorites menu [16]. The principle extends to simpler UIs too: even the arrangement of panes or cards on a dashboard can use spatial cues (for instance, a timeline at the bottom to imply chronology, a notepad on the side to imply peripheral jotting). **Visual grouping** is closely related: elements that are grouped (by proximity, or enclosed in a container) are perceived as related. Good interfaces for complex information use grouping to create *regions of meaning* – e.g., a cluster of related nodes on a graph, or a colored background behind notes that belong together. Users often do this grouping themselves in flexible tools (by literally moving items together, or by drawing shapes around them). By honoring spatial organization, design can also support *multiple working strategies*: one person might prefer a spatial canvas to arrange research notes (externalizing the mental model), while another uses an outline – some advanced tools let you toggle between an outline view and a spatial view of the same data, acknowledging both preferences. In summary, spatial organization principles in UI design recognize that “where” things are is as important as “what” they are, especially in cognitive tasks – the interface becomes not just a medium for display, but a physical landscape of the user’s thought process.


### Multimodal Inputs and Outputs



We are no longer limited to keyboard and mouse. Modern sense-making and writing tools increasingly embrace **multimodal interaction** – allowing users to use voice, touch, stylus, gestures, and even gaze in combination. The rationale is to match the interface to natural human communication channels: as one article quipped, people “speak, gesture, and move in a powerful flow” in normal life, so our interfaces should accommodate a similar richness [17]. In practical terms, a multimodal note-taking tool might let a user *dictate* a quick note via speech while on the go, and later use pen or touch on a tablet to draw a concept diagram linking that note to others. Or consider an analytics dashboard where a user can ask a question verbally (“Show me sales trends for last quarter”) and then refine the displayed chart with touch gestures (zoom, filter by region). By supporting multiple inputs, interfaces can be more accessible (different users have different strengths or disabilities) and more efficient (sometimes speaking is faster than typing, or a quick sketch explains a concept better than text). An early study in this domain by Oviatt et al. found that combining speech and pen inputs can improve robustness and user satisfaction for map-based tasks, as users naturally like to say “put a red X here” while circling on a map – something purely voice or purely touch alone wouldn’t handle as gracefully [17]. In sense-making, multimodal output can also play a role: e.g., auditory cues can signal trends in data (sonification) while visualizations show details, or haptic feedback can guide attention to a certain part of an AR display. The design principle is to let modalities *complement* each other – each mode doing what it’s best at. Voice is great for quick commands or dictation, pen is great for spatial layout and annotation, touch is intuitive for direct object manipulation, and keyboard is precise for text entry and shortcuts. A challenge in multimodal interface design is keeping interactions seamless: the user should feel they are using one coherent tool, not juggling separate systems. That involves fusion in the UI – for instance, if a user says “this” while circling an item with the pen, the system must fuse those into one intent (selecting the item being circled). Fortunately, advances in sensor and recognition tech are making this easier. For tools focused on thought and creativity, multimodal interfaces open up new workflows: imagine brainstorming by talking through ideas (captured and transcribed live), arranging those idea cards with a swipe of your hand on a large screen, and writing details with a keyboard – all in one session. The net effect is to reduce the friction between the user’s mind and the tool: you use whatever mode of expression is most natural at each moment, and the system responds accordingly. This flexibility can be empowering, especially when dealing with complex, fluid tasks like sense-making and writing.


## Unique Affordances of AI-Integrated Interfaces


### Co-Creation and Mixed-Initiative Interaction Patterns



When AI is integrated into user interfaces for creative and analytical work, it shifts the interaction model from *user-tool* to *user-AI collaboration*. This introduces unique affordances – and demands new design patterns – to support **co-creation**. In a co-creative UI, the system is not just a passive instrument; it contributes suggestions, content, or actions that the user can then build upon. A classic example is an AI writing assistant that can generate a draft paragraph for the user, who then edits it and perhaps asks the AI to try again or continue the next paragraph. The interface thus becomes a collaborative workspace between human and AI. One key affordance here is the ability to **negotiate control and initiative**. Neither the human nor the AI should dominate the interaction; instead, there’s a back-and-forth. From a design standpoint, this is often achieved by explicit controls for the user to invoke AI assistance (buttons like “Rewrite this” or “Suggest an idea”), combined with the AI’s ability to make proactive suggestions at opportune moments (like autocompletion or a subtle prompt, “Need help?”). It’s crucial that the human can *always override or guide* the AI – ensuring the human’s agency is preserved. As early as 1999, HCI researchers like Horvitz emphasized designing for a “mixed-initiative approach” where the user can refine or redirect the automated services, rather than the system acting autonomously without user input [10]. In practical terms, UIs implement this via features like **editable AI outputs** (the user can post-edit whatever the AI generates, with changes feeding back into the AI’s understanding), **feedback mechanisms** (thumbs-up/down on suggestions to tell the AI if it was helpful, which might tune future suggestions), and **constraints** (letting the user set boundaries, e.g. “don’t use jargon in the summary” or “keep the explanation under 100 words”).



There are emerging UX patterns specific to co-creation. One is treating the AI as a *partner with a role*. For instance, some writing tools portray the AI as a character or a specialist (“Your AI Editor” persona) to set expectations about the style of help it provides. Another pattern is **scaffolding the collaboration**: research prototypes have tried varying how much structure to impose on human-AI co-writing. In a study of co-writing with language models, different “scaffolding” levels (from very open-ended, where the AI just waits for prompts, to highly structured, where the UI guides the user through a sequence of subtasks with AI help) were explored to see what users prefer [18][19]. The insight is that *different users and tasks call for different collaboration styles*. Indeed, recent findings show that writers have personal preferences for how the AI should assist at various stages: e.g., *content-focused* writers (like researchers) want idea generation help but insist on controlling phrasing, whereas others might be happy letting AI draft and then focus on editing for voice [20][21]. This suggests UIs should offer adaptable co-creation modes – perhaps a slider between “AI does more” vs “AI does less,” or distinct “brainstorm” versus “polish” modes for the AI assistant.



Designing co-creative interactions also involves new feedback and *metacommunication* from the AI. Because the AI is contributing creative content, the user needs ways to understand and manage those contributions (which leads into the transparency topic below). Some co-creative systems employ **session histories or diffs** to show what the AI added versus what the user wrote, so the user can track contributions. Others let the AI explain its suggestion (e.g., an AI designer tool might say it placed an element in a layout “because it creates balance” – a form of the AI expressing design rationale). A framework called **COFI (Co-Creative Framework for Interaction design)** has been proposed to categorize these kinds of interactions, emphasizing that the design space is broad – from AI taking initiative to user taking initiative, and everything in between [22]. The takeaway is that co-creative interfaces work best when they feel like a **conversation between two agents** working towards a common goal. The user should feel the AI’s contributions are helpful ideas from a collaborator, not impositions, and the UI should provide affordances for the user to instruct, interrogate, or correct the AI as naturally as they would with a human collaborator.


### Transparency of AI Behavior and Explanations



AI-powered features can be powerful, but they are often a “black box” – the reasoning behind a suggestion or action may be opaque. This is why **transparency** and **explainability** have become critical design considerations in AI-infused interfaces. Transparency means giving the user insight into the AI’s state, capabilities, or decision process. For example, when an AI writing assistant suggests a factual sentence, a transparent design would provide citations or indicate the source from which that info was drawn. If an AI analytical tool categorizes an email as important, it might highlight the keywords that led to that classification. The goal is to help the user build a correct mental model of what the AI is doing, so they can trust it appropriately (or catch its mistakes). Studies show that when AI “agents” communicate their reasoning or uncertainty, users tend to have more calibrated trust and better team performance with the AI [23]. For instance, if a chatbot assistant displays a confidence score or says “I’m not very sure about this answer,” users can judge how much to rely on it, much like a human team member expressing doubt.



Conversely, lack of transparency can mislead users. People might overestimate an AI’s abilities simply because it presents output in a very fluent or authoritative way. There is evidence that many users already harbor **flawed mental models** about AI like large language models – some think, for example, that if the output is grammatically polished, it must be correct, or they may assume the AI “understands” and reasons like a human [24]. Such misconceptions can lead to over-reliance or misuse, like trusting wrong information or expecting the AI to do tasks beyond its design. To combat this, UI designers incorporate explanation features. Common approaches include: **visual explanations** (e.g., highlighting the words in a prompt that influenced the AI’s response, or showing weights in a recommendation), **on-demand justifications** (“Why did you suggest this?” buttons that make the AI produce a rationale or show relevant data), and **behavioral transparency** (the AI discloses when it’s switching strategies or if it has taken an autonomous action on the user’s behalf). Even simple cues help – for example, differentiating AI-generated content from user-generated (perhaps with a slight background shade or an icon) can remind users to critically evaluate those parts. In AI writing tools, we now see features that label AI-written text or require a human review before text is finalized, acknowledging that the AI’s output is a draft, not gospel.



Another aspect of transparency is setting the *expectation* upfront about what the AI can or cannot do. Guidelines for human-AI interaction advise designers to **make the system’s capabilities and limits clear** early on [25]. Practically, this might mean an onboarding message that explains, say, “This assistant can help with brainstorming and grammar suggestions, but it may not have up-to-date factual information.” Some interfaces also dynamically remind users of limitations, like if a user asks something out of scope, the system says “I’m sorry, I wasn’t trained on that topic.” Transparency also ties into accountability and ethics – for sensitive domains (medicine, finance), showing the provenance of AI outputs (data sources, last update of the model, etc.) is important so that professionals can verify and take responsibility for final decisions.



The challenge in designing for transparency is to provide *useful* explanations without overwhelming or confusing the user. There’s ongoing research into what types of explanations people actually understand and find helpful. A rule of thumb is to match the explanation to the user’s needs: an end-user might just need a simple highlight or a confidence bar (“70% sure”), whereas a developer user might want a full decision tree or attention visualization. Interfaces might implement a **tiered disclosure of explanations** – a one-sentence summary rationale by default, with the option to “show more” detailed technical info if the user wants. Lastly, transparency features should be carefully evaluated because they can backfire if done poorly (e.g., a placebic explanation that is just a rephrasing of the output can create *illusion* of transparency without actually aiding understanding [26]). When done right, however, transparency turns the AI from an inscrutable oracle into a teachable, predictable partner. It engenders trust not by blind faith, but by clarity and openness, which is crucial as AI becomes embedded in the tools we use to think and create.


## Emerging Trends and Research Directions



**AI-Augmented Sensemaking and “Intelligent” Knowledge Management:** A clear trend is the deep integration of AI capabilities into sense-making and organization tools. Large language models (LLMs) and similar AI are being used not just for writing assistance, but as general research and synthesis aids. This means future UIs will increasingly feature AI-driven operations like automatic summarization of documents, intelligent search that can answer conceptual questions (not just keyword match), and even proactive discovery of connections in your data. Recent HCI research points out that LLMs are now employed as *computational tools with new interfaces and abilities for working with data*, aiding in tasks like data collection, synthesis, and sense-making [27]. For example, we’re seeing early versions of “smart” note-taking apps that can ingest a heap of your raw notes and then generate a coherent outline or concept map, or that you can query in natural language (“What were the main findings in all my journal reading notes last week?”). Another development is AI-assisted **knowledge base linking**: some tools can suggest links between your notes or tag new notes with relevant existing tags using semantic analysis. Over time, one can imagine a kind of *AI research assistant* living in these tools – one that not only responds to direct prompts but continuously helps organize and surface insights from the information you have. The design challenge and direction for research here is how to integrate these AI features without taking away the user’s sense of ownership or without cluttering the workflow. The vision is that AI becomes a *cognitive amplifier*, handling rote tasks (like aggregating data or performing routine transformations) and providing insight pointers, while the human focuses on interpretation and decision-making.



**Resurgence of Networked Thinking (Hypertext Reborn):** The notion of hypertext – non-linear, interlinked information – is experiencing a revival through modern “tools for thought,” and this is influencing UI design trends. Knowledge management tools are moving away from strictly hierarchical file-folder models toward graph-oriented, networked models. This resonates with early hypertext systems (like Bush’s Memex or Engelbart’s NLS), but now with better interface technology and AI support. Researchers observe that the *recent resurgence in hypertextual note-taking* (as seen in apps like Roam, Obsidian, Logseq) opens up **new design opportunities for augmented sensemaking** [7]. Future interfaces will likely expand on visual graph representations of knowledge, allowing users to literally see their second brain of notes as a constellation of interconnected ideas. Features like **backlink management** (seeing all notes that link to the current note) and **graph filtering** (highlighting only certain types of connections) are becoming standard. We may also see more temporal and semantic dimensions added – imagine a 3D view where one axis is time (when notes were created) and another is grouping by tag or topic, essentially a *spatiotemporal knowledge map*. There’s also a push towards making hypertext more collaborative: multi-user graph-based knowledge bases where teams can build and navigate a shared network of ideas. This raises research questions around navigational aids (how to prevent getting “lost in hyperspace”), visualization techniques for large graphs, and the interplay of structure versus serendipity. In short, the emerging trend is embracing the complexity of knowledge by not forcing linear structures, instead giving users UIs to weave a web of information – a web that AI might help maintain by suggesting new threads (links) and highlighting patterns in that web.



**Conversational and Invisible Interfaces:** With AI becoming more capable of understanding natural language and context, we see a trend toward interfaces that *disappear* into a conversational agent or that integrate into existing communication channels. For example, instead of clicking through menus to set up a data visualization, you might simply tell a chatbot interface what you need (“Compare the sales of product X and Y over the last 5 years in the Americas”) and it generates the chart for you. This concept extends the **prompt-based interaction** discussed earlier – envisioning the primary interface as a dialogue. Already, products like Notion are adding conversational query features for databases, and Microsoft’s “Copilot” initiative is bringing chat-driven commands into Office apps. The long-term direction is a kind of *ubiquitous AI assistant* that is present across your tools, so the UI challenge is to blend this seamlessly: sometimes you still want the direct manipulation (to tweak that chart by hand), but other times letting the AI fetch or transform information via a quick ask is more efficient. The research direction here includes improving the AI’s understanding of context (it should know what data you have and what you might be referring to without extremely explicit instructions) and making the conversational agent feel trustworthy and integrated. It also includes multimodal conversation – maybe you ask a question by voice while looking at a visualization, and the answer highlights on the chart itself. The boundary between “the interface” and “the assistant” will continue to blur. Designers will need to ensure that this doesn’t turn into a disempowering experience (where the AI does stuff and the user has no idea how or why). Transparency and good dialogue design (confirmations, summaries of actions taken, etc.) will be critical, as will the ability to *fall back* to manual control if the conversation isn’t achieving the desired result.



**Human Agency, Authenticity, and Ethical Considerations:** As AI-driven tools become prevalent, a significant emerging focus is ensuring they align with human intentions and ethical norms. One concern raised in the context of AI writing tools is that they might inadvertently homogenize content or steer it in unintended directions – potentially threatening the authenticity or originality of the user’s work [28]. Emerging design research is grappling with how to keep the user’s voice and goals front and center. One direction is developing interfaces that **highlight AI contributions** (so authors can review and decide if those really fit their voice) or even tools that *coach* users to retain their style (for instance, alerting “This sentence is very different in tone from your usual writing – was it intended?” if an AI wrote it). Another aspect is **user agency** – providing users with control over the AI’s influence. This could mean sliders for how conservative or creative the AI’s suggestions should be, or the ability to easily undo AI actions (e.g., a global toggle to turn off all AI-written sentences). Researchers are also exploring *frameworks for responsible AI interaction*: for example, how to handle biases that the AI might introduce in organizing information or suggesting content. If an AI assistant in a note-taking app keeps prioritizing certain sources or ideas (perhaps reflecting biases in its training data), the interface should allow the user to notice and correct that (maybe by visual diversity indicators or a setting to widen the scope of suggestions). Privacy is another ethical dimension – these tools often work by learning from the user’s data, so giving users transparency and control over what data is used (and how it’s stored) will be increasingly important. In collaborative environments, there’s an emerging question of attribution: if an AI contributes to a shared knowledge base or a document, how do we log that? Future UIs might maintain an “authorship log” that clearly marks which content came from whom (human or AI) in a version history. All these considerations point to a broader trend: **human-centered AI design**. The frontier of research is not just making AI more powerful, but making the *interaction* with AI more aligned with human values like trust, understanding, and empowerment [29]. We can expect new guidelines (building on works like Amershi et al.’s 18 guidelines [30]) and possibly industry standards that shape how AI features are presented in UI – much like we have standards for usability, we might get standards for *AI usability* and ethics (e.g., requiring that any AI-generated content is disclosed to users, or that critical decisions have a human-in-the-loop).



**Immersive and Spatial Computing for Sensemaking:** Looking a bit further, the maturation of AR/VR and spatial computing technologies is poised to influence UI design for knowledge tools. Researchers in information visualization and sensemaking are already exploring “immersive analytics,” where analysts put on a VR headset and literally arrange data in a 3D space around them, or use augmented reality to annotate physical documents and spaces with virtual sticky notes. The intuition is that immersion and embodiment could amplify cognitive abilities – by engaging more senses and allowing more **spatial manipulation**, people might detect patterns or form memories better. Early studies have shown promise, like using VR to analyze social networks or timelines where you can “walk” through the data. As hardware becomes more lightweight (e.g., AR glasses), future knowledge workers might have persistent spatial layouts of their information floating around their office or room. This brings UI challenges: designing interfaces that are no longer on a flat screen but intertwined with the user’s environment. Gestural interaction, voice commands, and even gaze/eye-tracking will become primary input modes in these contexts (making multimodal design even more crucial). The UIs will need to address fatigue (both cognitive and physical – nobody wants to wave their arms endlessly) by smartly anchoring data in space and allowing quick reorientation or summary views. Collaborative sensemaking could also be revolutionized: imagine a remote team all “present” in a virtual room filled with their shared data, each person represented by an avatar, manipulating the info together in real-time. This is an active research direction, pulling together HCI, data vis, and AI (for example, AI could manage the layout in 3D or highlight anomalies for the team). While mass adoption of fully immersive UIs may be a few years away, the design concepts are already informing today’s tools – for instance, spatial grouping on 2D canvases is a step toward spatial 3D arrangement; and features like infinite canvas with zoom (Prezi style navigation in 2D) mimic flying through an information space. We can expect gradual progression: more use of spatial metaphors, more fluid navigation (beyond scrolling – like zoomable UIs, which have been studied in HCI as well), and incremental introduction of AR features (perhaps viewing your notes on a physical wall via projection or glasses) as intermediate steps.



In conclusion, user interface designs for sense-making, information organization, and AI-assisted writing are rapidly evolving. They build on classic principles – visual layouts that ease cognitive load, interactions that feel natural and empowering – while incorporating cutting-edge AI and embracing new paradigms of human-computer collaboration. Peer-reviewed research is actively informing these designs, from foundational studies on how timelines aid understanding [cs.umd.edu], or how spatial memory can be harnessed [16], to contemporary investigations into human-AI co-writing dynamics [20] and transparency techniques for AI assistants [23]. The common thread is designing interfaces that augment human intellect: helping us externalize thoughts, find patterns, and create in partnership with our tools. As emerging trends take hold – AI becoming a creative partner, knowledge bases becoming living graphs, and interfaces potentially expanding into our physical reality – the principles of good UX (clarity, feedback, consistency, flexibility) will remain our guide. The coming years will likely bring hybrid interfaces that are part notepad, part conversation, part visualization space. The challenge and excitement for designers and researchers is ensuring these remain *human-centered*, enabling users to achieve deeper insight and creativity without losing their sense of control or clarity. By grounding designs in both proven patterns and new empirical research, we can develop tools that truly enhance our sense-making and creative capabilities in the age of AI.

# Investigating EVM for Different Modulation Schemes


## What is Error Vector Magnitude (EVM)?



**Error Vector Magnitude (EVM)** is a key metric that quantifies the modulation accuracy of a digital communication signal. It measures the difference (as a vector in the I/Q plane) between the received symbol and the ideal constellation point where that symbol *should* be. In essence, EVM expresses **“the difference between the expected complex voltage value of a demodulated symbol and the value of the actual received symbol.”** [1] A lower EVM means the received symbols are closer to their ideal locations, indicating a higher-quality signal, whereas a higher EVM denotes greater deviation (errors) due to noise or impairments [2].



 [3] *Illustration of EVM on a constellation: The red dot is a received symbol and the blue circle is the ideal constellation point. The black arrow represents the error vector between the received and ideal symbol.*



In practice, EVM is typically reported as a **root-mean-square (RMS)** value of these error vectors over many symbols, often expressed as a percentage of the signal reference amplitude or power [4]. For example, an EVM of 0% means a perfect signal (no error between received and ideal points), whereas an EVM of 5% means that, on average, the received symbols are about 5% away from their ideal locations in the I/Q plane [5]. EVM incorporates both amplitude and phase errors, making it a comprehensive indicator of signal quality (unlike raw bit error rate which is just pass/fail) [6]. It is widely used in standards (WLAN 802.11, LTE, 5G, etc.) as a compliance metric to ensure transmitters keep distortions and noise under control [7][3].


## Calculating EVM: General Formula and Normalization



The calculation of EVM follows a general procedure that is **common to all modulation types** (M-PSK, QPSK, M-QAM, etc.), with appropriate normalization. The typical steps are:


1. **Demodulate the signal** to obtain the received symbol values (constellation points) from the waveform [8].
2. **Determine the ideal symbol values** for the intended constellation (the target points for each transmitted symbol). Usually the constellation is normalized to a reference scale (explained next).
3. **Compute the error vector for each symbol**, which is the difference between the received symbol and its ideal constellation point: ek=rk−dke_k = r_k - d_kek​=rk​−dk​, where rkr_krk​ is the k-th received symbol and dkd_kdk​ is the corresponding ideal symbol [9]. The magnitude of this error vector is ∣ek∣=(ℜ{ek})2+(ℑ{ek})2|e_k| = \sqrt{(\Re\{e_k\})^2 + (\Im\{e_k\})^2}∣ek​∣=(ℜ{ek​})2+(ℑ{ek​})2
​ [10].
4. **Calculate the RMS error** over all $N$ symbols: one common formula is


EVMRMS  =  1N∑k=1N∣ek∣2Pref ,\text{EVM}_\text{RMS} \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N |e_k|^2}{P_\text{ref}} } \,,EVMRMS​=Pref​N1​∑k=1N​∣ek​∣2​
​,

where $P_\text{ref}$ is the reference signal power used for normalization [11]. In many definitions, $P_\text{ref}$ is taken as the **average symbol power** of the ideal constellation [12][13]. This essentially yields the ratio of the mean error power to the mean signal power.
5. **Express as a percentage or in dB**: The EVM is often reported as a percentage: EVM% $= \text{EVM}*\text{RMS} \times 100%$ [4] (or in dB, as $20\log*{10}(\text{EVM}_\text{RMS})$). For instance, if the RMS error vector is 0.05 (i.e. 5% of the reference amplitude), the EVM is 5%. This normalization allows EVM specs to be compared across different signal powers and modulation formats [12][14].



**Normalization is crucial.** To use a *general EVM formula for all modulation types*, we must define a consistent reference power. A common choice – and the one implicit in many standards – is to normalize such that *the mean squared amplitude of the constellation is 1* (or some fixed value) [12]. In other words, the **average power per symbol** of the ideal constellation is set as the reference for EVM calculation [15][16]. This way, EVM measures the error relative to the average symbol power, and the formula becomes applicable to **any modulation scheme** (BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, etc.) on an equal footing [14]. Research from NIST emphasizes this approach: *“normalization...enable[s] direct comparison of EVM for a given average power level per symbol between modulation types.”* [14] In fact, when this normalization is applied, the definition of EVM **“stands for multi-modulation systems”** uniformly [17][12].



It should be noted that different normalization methods exist, and one must be consistent. Some instruments allow EVM to be referenced to the **peak constellation power** instead of the average. For example, normalizing to the peak (the highest-power constellation point) will yield a different numeric EVM than normalizing to the average power [18]. (Peak normalization often matters for modulation formats like PAM or APSK.) In most cases for QAM/PSK, RMS (average power) normalization is used because it yields a meaningful percentage of average signal power [19]. **Crucially, when comparing EVM values across measurements or modulation types, the same normalization reference must be used** to avoid confusion [20]. For consistency, the discussion below assumes the standard RMS (average power) normalization unless stated otherwise.


## Applicability of a General EVM Formula to M-PSK and M-QAM



Given the above normalization, **the same EVM formula is appropriate for M-ary PSK (including QPSK) and M-ary QAM**, with only minor considerations. The definition of EVM as “RMS of error vectors normalized to signal power” is inherently modulation-agnostic [12][21]. In other words, whether the signal is BPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM or 64-QAM, we compute the error vectors and average them in the same way. The difference lies in what the reference power $P_\text{ref}$ is, but if we consistently use the *average symbol power* of each constellation, the EVM calculation treats all modulations fairly. Research confirms that with the proper normalization, *“the mean square amplitude of all possible symbols in the constellation of any modulation scheme is one”*, and thus the EVM formula yields a comparable measure of error across different modulations [12][11].



In practical terms, using a single general equation (like the one given above) for all modulation types is the **right approach**, as long as you normalize appropriately for each constellation. A respondent on a technical forum summarized this well: *“The EVM can be calculated for different types of modulation by using different normalization methods. For example, the average power normalization method is commonly used for QAM modulation, while the peak power normalization is used for PAM.”* [19] In our context, sticking to average power normalization across M-PSK and M-QAM means the “general EVM formula” effectively works for all. Experimental validation by NIST also showed that after applying the standard normalization, measured EVM results **line up consistently across BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, etc.**, enabling direct comparison [21].



That said, one nuance is that constellations with **multiple amplitude levels** (like QAM or APSK) inherently have a higher peak-to-average power ratio. If one were to normalize to the *peak* signal amplitude instead, the EVM values would scale accordingly (since the reference would be larger). For example, Keysight notes that for 64-QAM, referencing EVM to the peak constellation point introduces a constant offset (~3.7 dB in that case) in the SNR vs EVM relationship [22][23]. However, these are just different ways of measuring the same thing – the underlying error vectors remain the same. The industry trend, as reflected in standards like IEEE 802.11 and LTE, is to report EVM as a percentage of average signal power, making the metric uniformly applicable to any modulation format [14].


## EVM vs. Eb/No: Expected Behavior for MPSK and MQAM



Because EVM fundamentally measures the ratio of error power to signal power, it has a **direct relationship to the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)**. In an AWGN-limited system (noise only, no other impairments), the **RMS EVM is essentially the inverse of the SNR (per symbol)**. In fact, if EVM is normalized to average signal power, one can show that (for Gaussian noise)



EVMRMS≈1SNRlinear ,\text{EVM}_\text{RMS} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{SNR}_\text{linear}}} \,,EVMRMS​≈SNRlinear​
​1​,



or equivalently SNR (linear) $\approx 1/(\text{EVM}_\text{RMS}^2)$ [24]. This makes intuitive sense: a higher SNR (less noise) means the error vectors are smaller relative to signal amplitude, yielding a lower EVM. For example, an EVM of 10% corresponds to an SNR of roughly 20 dB, whereas an EVM of 1% corresponds to about 40 dB SNR [24]. This inverse-square relationship holds regardless of modulation format, **provided SNR is defined on the same basis** (here, per symbol or per constellation point).



**EVM vs. Eb/No curves** – If we plot EVM (y-axis) against $E_b/N_0$ (x-axis) for different modulation schemes, we should expect all curves to trend downward as $E_b/N_0$ increases (since higher $E_b/N_0$ means higher SNR). However, the curves will not completely overlap for different modulations when using $E_b/N_0$ on the x-axis, because $E_b/N_0$ accounts for energy per bit, and different modulations carry a different number of bits per symbol. At a given $E_b/N_0$, a higher-order modulation (with more bits per symbol) has a higher *symbol* energy $E_s = E_b \log_2 M$. This means for the same $E_b/N_0$, a 16-QAM signal (M=16, 4 bits/sym) actually has a 6 dB higher *symbol SNR* than a QPSK signal (M=4, 2 bits/sym), because 16-QAM’s symbols carry 4 bits of energy, not 2. As a result, at equal $E_b/N_0$, the **raw EVM** (error relative to average symbol power) of 16-QAM will be lower than that of QPSK or BPSK. In quantitative terms, if $E_b/N_0$ is fixed, EVM scales roughly as $1/\sqrt{E_s/N_0}$, and since $E_s/N_0 = (E_b/N_0)\cdot\log_2 M$, we have:


* EVM $\propto 1/\sqrt{\log_2 M}$ at a given $E_b/N_0$ (approximately).



For example, at the same $E_b/N_0$, a QPSK signal (2 bits/sym) will show about $\sqrt{2}\approx1.414$ times higher EVM than a 16-QAM signal (4 bits/sym), because the 16-QAM’s symbol SNR is doubled for the same bit-SNR. Similarly, 64-QAM (6 bits/sym) would exhibit even lower EVM at the same $E_b/N_0$ (its symbol SNR is 3 times that of QPSK for equal $E_b/N_0$). This explains why **higher-order modulations require lower EVM (stricter transmitter quality) to achieve comparable bit error performance**. The constellation points in 64-QAM are much closer together than in QPSK, so to maintain low BER, the noise (and distortion) must be very small relative to the average signal power (hence a low EVM). Indeed, it is well documented that to get the same BER, 16-QAM needs about 6–7 dB higher SNR than QPSK, and 64-QAM needs another ~6 dB beyond that [25]. Correspondingly, the acceptable EVM levels tighten as modulation order grows. For instance, one set of example EVM targets for different modulations (assuming a low BER target) is: **BPSK ≈ 10%**, **QPSK ≈ 5%**, **16-QAM ≈ 1.5%**, **64-QAM ≈ 0.75%** [26]. While the exact numbers depend on the standard and context, the trend is clear – higher-order schemes demand lower EVM.



It’s important to note that **the general shape of EVM vs. $E_b/N_0$ is similar for all modulation formats** – roughly a monotonic decrease that flattens out at high SNR (where EVM approaches the residual noise floor or other impairments). If thermal noise dominates, EVM (in dB) will increase linearly as SNR (in dB) decreases, essentially mirroring the inverse relationship. In fact, when plotted on a log-log scale, EVM vs. $E_b/N_0$ would appear as parallel curves for different modulations, separated by a horizontal shift corresponding to the $\log_2 M$ factor. This was demonstrated in theoretical studies which showed that after proper normalization, EVM is *“equivalently useful as signal-to-noise ratio”* as a performance metric [27][24]. In other words, EVM can be used interchangeably with SNR to predict performance, regardless of modulation, once we account for how $E_b$ relates to $E_s$.



**In summary**, using a consistent EVM formulation across M-PSK, QPSK, and M-QAM is not only possible but standard practice. The key is choosing a normalization (usually average symbol power) that puts all modulation schemes on equal footing. Under AWGN conditions, EVM provides a direct gauge of effective SNR, and thus its behavior as a function of $E_b/N_0$ is predictable and similar across modulation formats – decreasing roughly as noise is reduced. Higher-order modulations yield lower EVM at the same $E_b/N_0$ (due to their higher $E_s$), but they *require* that lower EVM (higher SNR) to maintain integrity, which is why specifications for 64-QAM, for example, demand very small EVM percentages. Overall, the **general EVM formula is accurate and appropriate for all these modulation types** as a universal measure of signal quality, as confirmed by both theoretical analyses and experimental validations [21][24].

* R. A. Shafik *et al.*, “On the Extended Relationships Among EVM, BER and SNR as Performance Metrics,” *ICECE 2006*.  [11][24]

I would like to fully understand the different stages of data processing carried out, as well as the reasoning and hypotheses behind them.
