# Beyond the Nyquist Limit: Frequency Domain Information Beyond Sampling Constraints


## Introduction to the Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem



The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem is a fundamental result that links a signal’s frequency content to the required sampling rate for lossless digitization. In essence, if a continuous signal is **band-limited** (no spectral content above some maximum frequency *f<sub>max</sub>*), it can be perfectly reconstructed from evenly spaced samples as long as the sampling frequency *f<sub>s</sub>* is at least twice that maximum frequency [1]. This minimum rate *f<sub>s>=2f<sub>max</sub>* is known as the Nyquist rate. Sampling at or above this rate prevents **aliasing**, a distortion where high-frequency components masquerade as lower frequencies in the sampled data [[2]([[37](https://home.strw.leidenuniv.nl/~por/AOT2019/docs/AOT_2019_Ex13_NyquistTheorem.pdf#:~:text=Any%20signals%20that%20contain%20frequencies,signal%2C%20and%20are%20called%20undersampled))]. In practical terms, the theorem guarantees that *a bandlimited signal with no content above B hertz is completely determined by samples spaced 1/(2B) seconds apart*, meaning a sample rate above 2B Hz captures all information [3]. When these conditions are met, one can *perfectly reconstruct* the original analog signal from its discrete samples (e.g. via sinc interpolation) without loss of fidelity [4]. This theorem underpins most modern data conversion: for example, audio signals capped at 20 kHz require ~40 kHz sampling, and imaging sensors must satisfy spatial Nyquist criteria relative to scene bandwidth to avoid aliasing.


## Theoretical Limitations of Nyquist-Based Sampling



While Nyquist-Shannon provides a *sufficient* sampling condition, it comes with important limitations. **Strict band-limiting** is assumed: if a signal contains frequencies above the Nyquist frequency (half the sampling rate), those components become irretrievably “mixed” into lower frequencies in the sampled data [5]. In other words, any signal content beyond *f<sub>s</sub>/2* is **indistinguishable from an alias at a lower frequency** once sampled [6]. Classical reconstruction filters will faithfully recover the aliased component rather than the true high-frequency content [7]. Thus, for an arbitrary signal, the Nyquist criterion is effectively a hard limit – trying to capture a higher-frequency band without increasing *f<sub>s</sub>* will result in lost information or aliasing errors. Moreover, the theorem requires the signal to *truly have zero energy beyond* *f<sub>max</sub>*; real-world signals are often not perfectly band-limited (for example, sharp transients or edges have infinitely wide spectra), so in practice one uses analog **anti-alias filters** to attenuate out-of-band components before sampling [8]. Even then, **critical sampling** (at exactly 2B) leaves no margin for filter roll-off or transition bands, which is why systems typically sample above the theoretical minimum.



Another limitation is that Nyquist’s condition does not directly address signals that are not baseband (i.e. centered at 0 frequency) or those with *gaps* in their spectrum. The standard theorem assumes a contiguous band from 0 to B Hz; if a signal instead occupies disjoint bands, uniform sampling at 2B may be overkill. In 1967, Henry **Landau** generalized the theory, showing that for multi-band signals the **average sampling rate** must be at least twice the total occupied bandwidth (the Landau rate) for perfect reconstruction [9]. Notably, Landau’s result assumes prior knowledge of which spectral bands are occupied – a constraint that classical Nyquist sampling avoids by demanding a high enough rate to cover the worst-case band. In summary, the theoretical stance is that **without additional assumptions**, one cannot obtain frequency information beyond the Nyquist limit: attempting to do so leads to ambiguity and aliasing. However, if signals have special structure or if clever non-uniform sampling schemes are used, these classical limits can be circumvented by exploiting that additional information [10]. This insight opens the door to “beyond Nyquist” strategies described next.


## Modern Signal Processing Techniques Beyond Nyquist



Over the past two decades, researchers have developed new sampling and reconstruction techniques that **go beyond the classical Nyquist paradigm** by leveraging prior knowledge or signal structure. These methods relax the requirement of uniform high-rate sampling, allowing recovery of high-frequency or wideband information from fewer samples or at lower rates. Key approaches include **compressed sensing**, **sub-Nyquist sampling** (including non-uniform or multi-rate schemes), and **super-resolution techniques** in imaging and spectroscopy. Each of these exploits some form of sparsity or redundancy to beat the usual sampling limits.


### Compressed Sensing



**Compressed sensing (CS)** is a framework that bypasses Nyquist’s strict rate requirement by assuming the signal is sparse or compressible in some basis. Instead of uniformly sampling at twice the max frequency, CS acquires a smaller number of more general linear measurements and then uses computational algorithms to reconstruct the signal. The seminal work of Candès, Romberg, Tao and Donoho (circa 2006) showed that if a signal has only *K* significant coefficients in some domain, it can be recovered from on the order of *K* log(*N*) measurements (<< *N*, the Nyquist number of samples) under appropriate conditions. In other words, **sampling “inefficiently” at the Nyquist rate is not necessary when the signal itself contains far less information than a full band-limited signal**. For example, **Baraniuk et al. (2010)** demonstrated an analog system called the *random demodulator* that acquires a sparse wideband signal using a sampling rate much lower than the Nyquist rate [11][12]. In their setup, a continuous-time signal of bandlimit *W* (Hz) but containing only *K* dominant frequency components is first randomized (mixed with a pseudonoise sequence and integrated) and then sampled at a rate proportional to *K log(W/K)* rather than *W*. Simulations showed that **O(**K** log(*W*/K)** samples per second were sufficient to stably reconstruct the signal – an “exponentially lower” rate than the usual Nyquist frequency *W* [12]. The trade-off is that reconstruction is no longer a simple sinc interpolation; one must solve a **nonlinear inverse problem** (often via convex optimization or greedy algorithms) to recover the sparse spectrum from these compressed measurements [13]. In effect, compressed sensing trades off sampling *density* for signal *assumptions* and computation. Numerous studies have since validated that by **exploiting sparsity, one can sample beyond the Nyquist limit in the sense of requiring far fewer samples than traditional uniform sampling** [14]. This principle has been applied in various domains – for instance, sparse astronomical signals, neural recordings, and imaging – showing that high-frequency information can indeed be recovered from surprisingly undersampled data, as long as the signal has a sparse representation and sufficient signal-to-noise ratio.


### Sub-Nyquist and Non-Uniform Sampling



This category includes strategies that deliberately depart from uniform sampling to harness additional freedom in capturing high-frequency content. **Non-uniform sampling** (e.g. jittered or irregular sample timing) can decorrelate aliasing components, making it possible to disentangle high-frequency signal content that would alias under uniform sampling. In fact, when data are not sampled uniformly, the classical Nyquist frequency no longer cleanly applies – the aliasing manifests in more complex ways rather than a single folding frequency [15]. This complexity can be exploited: for example, certain periodic non-uniform sampling schemes allow estimation of signal components beyond the normal Nyquist limit. One result (Mishali & Eldar, 2009) showed that a **multi-coset sampling** strategy – sampling using several interleaved periodic sub-sequences – can exactly recover multiband signals at an **overall rate far below the Nyquist rate**, provided the number of channels and their offsets are chosen appropriately [16]. The signal is effectively “spread” across multiple low-rate streams, and a specialized reconstruction algorithm (often involving spectral sparse recovery) is used to identify and reconstruct the occupied bands. Eldar’s group built a hardware prototype called the **Modulated Wideband Converter (MWC)**, which multiplies the analog input by pseudorandom waveforms and lowpass-filters the result before sampling. This system was shown to perfectly recover sparse multiband signals **using sampling rates orders of magnitude smaller than Nyquist**, under certain provable conditions [17][18]. In essence, the MWC and related architectures perform an analog pre-conditioning (modulation and mixing) that *folds* high-frequency content down into baseband in a randomized fashion, allowing a digital algorithm to sort out the contributions.



Importantly, these sub-Nyquist methods rely on knowing that the signal only occupies a fraction of the spectrum (though the exact frequencies may be unknown). In line with Landau’s theory, if the total occupied bandwidth is, say, 10% of the full range, one only needs to sample on the order of 10% of the Nyquist rate (plus some overhead) to capture all information [9]. The **“Xampling”** framework (short for compressed sampling) formalized by Eldar and colleagues encapsulates this idea of **analog signal acquisition at an information-rate, not at the highest frequency**. Non-uniform sampling can also be used in other creative ways: for instance, using **dithered sampling intervals or multiple asynchronous samplers** can turn a single-tone high-frequency signal into a set of disparate alias copies that can be solved for the true frequency. Research has shown that even a **single high-frequency sinusoid above Nyquist can be identified** by using two or more carefully designed non-uniform sampling sequences and fitting the data to a sinusoidal model [19]. In summary, by choosing sampling patterns wisely (e.g. multi-channel, time-varying, or random sampling), one can **extend the effective bandwidth** capture of a system without increasing the nominal sampling rate – albeit at the cost of more complex reconstruction. These techniques have enabled new frontiers like wideband spectrum sensing for radio communications at a fraction of conventional ADC rates [20].


### Super-Resolution in Imaging and Spectroscopy



“Super-resolution” refers to a class of techniques aimed at exceeding classical resolution limits, whether in the spatial domain (imaging) or frequency domain (spectroscopy). In the context of imaging, digital sensors impose a Nyquist limit in space (half the sampling frequency corresponds to one pixel’s period). **Super-resolution imaging** algorithms seek to recover scene detail finer than the sensor’s pixel grid by using multiple observations or prior knowledge. A common approach is **multi-frame super-resolution**: by capturing a burst of low-resolution images with slight sub-pixel shifts (e.g. due to hand tremor or controlled dithering), one effectively samples different alignments of the high-frequency scene content [21]. Each image on its own is aliased (high spatial frequencies beyond the pixel Nyquist appear as moiré/aliases), but since the aliases differ between frames, they can be “inverted” to recover the true high-frequency detail. For example, Google’s smartphone cameras use a handheld burst super-resolution algorithm that merges multiple RAW images to produce a final image with roughly **double the linear resolution of the native sensor** [21]. The key is that the scene is assumed static and the motion between frames provides diversity; collectively, the frames contain spatial frequency information that no single low-res image had. Techniques like **pixel super-resolution (PSR)** explicitly address the lost high frequencies by modeling how the sensor integrates light over each pixel and then solving an inverse problem to estimate sub-pixel details [22]. In experimental settings, researchers have demonstrated that combining 4 or 8 shifted images can reconstruct an image with frequencies beyond the original Nyquist limit (up to the new effective sampling rate), consistent with theoretical limits that about a 2× gain is possible from purely shift-based super-resolution [23].



In **spectroscopy** and other 1D frequency analysis, super-resolution often refers to resolving spectral features more finely than the standard Fourier limit (which is tied to the observation time or sampling rate). One powerful class of methods are **parametric spectral estimation algorithms** like Prony’s method, MUSIC, or ESPRIT, which assume the signal consists of a few distinct sinusoidal components. These methods use algebraic techniques (e.g. eigen-decompositions of a covariance matrix) to locate spectral lines with precision far beyond the FFT bin width, effectively achieving frequency resolution better than 1/T (T = signal duration). For example, the MUSIC algorithm can pinpoint closely spaced frequencies that would appear as one broad peak in a conventional spectrum, by exploiting the low-dimensional signal model. Similarly in optics or chemistry, if a spectrum has only a handful of narrow peaks, compressed sensing reconstruction can yield a high-resolution spectrum without needing an exceedingly long time record. A recent study in computational spectroscopy noted that **Nyquist constraints make long time signals necessary for high frequency resolution**, but techniques like compressed sensing and MUSIC can dramatically reduce the required sampling duration by assuming a small number of spectral excitations [24][25]. In practice, this has enabled *spectral super-resolution* where one can discern spectral lines or “molecular fingerprints” beyond what the nominal time-bandwidth product would suggest. For instance, in **ultrafast laser spectroscopy**, researchers achieved real-time measurement of molecular absorption features beyond the normal Nyquist frequency by randomly modulating the time delays between pulses and applying compressed sensing reconstruction [[26]([[33](https://phys.org/news/2024-04-molecular-fingerprint-nyquist-frequency.html#:~:text=,the%20femtosecond%20excitation%20pulses%20randomly))]. The molecular response in their experiment is sparse (only certain resonant frequencies contribute), which allows the use of far fewer probing points in time than a uniform Nyquist-rate scan would require [27]. The result is faster acquisition of a broad spectrum without sacrificing resolution, effectively breaking the trade-off between frequency resolution and measurement time.



In summary, super-resolution techniques – whether in spatial imaging or frequency analysis – **rely on additional information or assumptions** (like multiple shifted views, sparsity of spectral components, or known point-spread functions) to **surpass the direct Nyquist limit** of a given sampling grid. They do not violate physical laws; rather, they cleverly extract more information by making the inverse problem better-posed through prior knowledge.


## Practical Applications and Experimental Validation



Many of these beyond-Nyquist approaches have moved from theory into practice, demonstrating real-world feasibility in a range of domains. Below are several notable applications and experimental validations:


* **Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI):** Medical MRI was an early adopter of compressed sensing to accelerate scans. Lustig *et al.* showed that by undersampling *k*-space (the spatial frequency domain) randomly and using sparse-image reconstruction, one can achieve high-quality images with far fewer samples than the Nyquist criterion would require. For example, dynamic MRI sequences have been reconstructed from a sampling rate *4× lower than Nyquist* with minimal loss, using randomized acquisitions and nonlinear CS reconstruction [28]. In one case, a cardiac imaging scan that would normally be limited to ~3.6 frames per second (at the Nyquist rate) was successfully reconstructed at **25 fps** from the same data acquisition time by exploiting compressive sampling and image sparsity [29]. Such CS-MRI techniques (often achieving 4–8× acceleration) are now implemented on clinical scanners, enabling faster imaging or higher resolution scans without increasing hardware sampling rates.
* **Cognitive Radio and Wideband Spectrum Sensing:** Sub-Nyquist sampling makes it possible for radios to monitor very wide frequency bands without high-rate ADCs. The modulated wideband converter (MWC) developed by Mishali and Eldar is one example that was built and tested for spectrum sensing. It allows a cognitive radio to detect occupied frequency slots in a broad spectrum (GHz of bandwidth) by sampling each channel at only a few tens of MHz [20]. This works because the radio spectrum at any given time is sparse (many channels are inactive), so the signal consisting of several disjoint active bands can be perfectly recovered from the low-rate samples. The MWC prototype demonstrated reliable detection of signals while sampling at a rate orders-of-magnitude below the conventional Nyquist rate for the entire band [30][20], validating that such analog sub-sampling front-ends can perform in practice.
* **Ultrasound Imaging:** Ultrasound machines traditionally require very high sampling rates (several times the carrier frequency of the ultrasound, often 20–40 MHz) on many channels to do beamforming for high-resolution images. Recent research led by Eldar’s group introduced **compressed ultrasound** techniques that drastically reduce this requirement. By using fewer analog-to-digital channels and sub-Nyquist sampling on each (combined with advanced Fourier-domain beamforming algorithms), they produced ultrasound images with the *same resolution* as the full-rate system while acquiring **~142× less data** [31]. In vivo experiments demonstrated that high-contrast, high-detail B-mode images can be reconstructed from significantly sub-sampled data [32]. This paves the way for portable ultrasound devices that consume less power and bandwidth by only sampling the necessary information and reconstructing the image via sparse recovery methods.
* **Optical Super-Resolution Microscopy:** In microscopy, methods like STORM, PALM, and STED have broken the classical diffraction limit, but there are also sampling-related super-resolution techniques. One example is **pixel super-resolution in lensless on-chip microscopy**, where multiple intensity-only measurements are combined to recover sample details beyond the sensor pixel grid. Researchers showed that by using phase retrieval and enforcing sparsity or other priors, one can overcome the loss of high spatial frequencies that occurs in direct imaging [22]. Essentially, features smaller than a pixel can be resolved by computationally “filling in” the missing high-frequency components consistent with the measured data. These techniques have been validated in experimental setups, yielding higher resolved images without changing the physical sensor – a testament to going beyond Nyquist in the spatial domain.
* **Spectroscopy and Signal Analysis:** As mentioned, **compressed sensing spectroscopy** has been experimentally realized. A 2024 study demonstrated **real-time molecular spectroscopy beyond the Nyquist limit** by randomly sampling time points in a pump-probe measurement and using CS to reconstruct a high-resolution spectrum [[26]([[33](https://phys.org/news/2024-04-molecular-fingerprint-nyquist-frequency.html#:~:text=,the%20femtosecond%20excitation%20pulses%20randomly))]. This allowed capturing sharp spectral “fingerprints” across a wide bandwidth in a fraction of the time normally required. Likewise, advanced spectral estimation algorithms (e.g. in radar or radio astronomy) are routinely used to detect or resolve components that classical Fourier analysis would consider below resolution or buried in sidelobes. The success of these methods in field experiments (ranging from locating faint stars in telescopic images to identifying closely spaced radar targets) underscores that with the right algorithms, one can extract **frequency-domain detail beyond the direct limits of sampling**.
* **Consumer Photography:** Multi-frame super-resolution has made its way into smartphone cameras for improving digital zoom. As documented by Google’s Pixel phone team, combining a burst of 8–10 raw images (which are individually undersampled/aliased) can yield a final photograph with significantly higher detail than any single image. The technique hinges on the slight hand tremor between frames to sample the scene at inter-pixel offsets [21]. The result is roughly a **2× increase in spatial resolution** (e.g. turning a 12 MP image into a 24 MP effective resolution) without changing the optics or sensor – effectively bypassing the one-photo Nyquist limit by using multiple shifted copies. This has been validated in practice, as the enhanced-detail images have noticeably improved clarity and texture, aligning well with the theoretical expectations of multi-frame alias cancellation [34].



Each of these examples confirms that *with additional structure or processing*, we can indeed obtain frequency-domain information that would be inaccessible under a strict Nyquist regime. The cost is usually extra complexity – either in hardware (for modulators, multiple channels, etc.) or in computation (solving inverse problems) – but the benefit is new capabilities such as faster scans, less data, or higher resolution than was previously thought possible.


## Challenges, Trade-offs, and Limitations of Going Beyond Nyquist



Despite their promise, beyond-Nyquist techniques come with important challenges and trade-offs:


* **Requirement of Signal Structure:** All sub-Nyquist methods assume some prior structure (sparsity, band-limited regions, known signal model, etc.). If the signal does not meet these assumptions, the methods break down. For instance, compressed sensing and super-resolution algorithms typically assume a *small number of significant components*; if faced with a dense or arbitrary spectrum, these methods fail to outperform conventional sampling [25]. In practice, one must verify that the signal is sparse or simple enough (or enforce sparsity via dictionaries) for these techniques to work. Large, complex spectra or images with rich detail are still problematic – there is no magic way to encode an arbitrary high-bandwidth signal into fewer samples without losing information, *unless* that signal is in fact information-sparse.
* **Complex Reconstruction Algorithms:** Unlike ordinary Nyquist sampling (where reconstruction is a straightforward linear filtering operation), beyond-Nyquist schemes rely on heavy-duty computation to recover the signal. Solving an L1-minimization for compressed sensing or a non-linear spectral fitting can be computationally intensive and may require iterative algorithms that are sensitive to tuning. Moreover, these algorithms introduce latency and complexity that may be impractical for real-time systems. As an example, the random demodulator requires convex optimization to recover the sparse spectrum from its measurements [13], and multi-frame super-resolution in imaging involves registration and fusion steps that add processing overhead. The **computational burden** is a key trade-off – we are effectively shifting complexity from the analog domain (fast ADCs) to the digital domain (smart reconstructions).
* **Noise and Robustness:** Pushing sampling below Nyquist often amplifies the impact of noise and modeling errors. When solving an underdetermined system of equations (which is what sub-Nyquist sampling produces), the solution can be extremely sensitive to noise in the measurements. In fact, Landau’s theory notes that sampling exactly at the Landau rate (the minimal required rate) can lead to a markedly poor noise floor or aliasing artifacts if the spectral support is not “nice” (packable) [35]. In other words, there is a **noise-versus-rate trade-off** – going too low in sampling rate (even if theoretically enough measurements exist) can make the inversion ill-conditioned and amplify noise. Many compressed sensing frameworks account for this by collecting slightly more samples than the bare minimum and by incorporating regularization to suppress noise. Nonetheless, high-frequency components that are barely above the noise floor might be lost in a sub-Nyquist system, whereas a full Nyquist-sampled system (with an anti-alias filter) might have preserved them. Robust recovery in the presence of noise and interference remains an ongoing challenge.
* **Hardware and Implementation Complexity:** Implementing these advanced sampling schemes can require sophisticated hardware. For example, the MWC or random demodulator needs analog mixing with high-speed pseudo-random signals, precise timing, and multiple parallel channels – all of which must be calibrated. Jitter or mismatches in the analog components can degrade the theoretical performance. Similarly, multi-camera or moving detector setups for super-resolution introduce synchronization and alignment issues. In short, **system complexity increases**, and with it, potential points of failure. In contrast, the traditional approach of simply sampling faster might, in some cases, be more reliable if technology allows it. There is a practical balance to strike between an elegant sub-Nyquist theory and a real-world implementation that has non-idealities.
* **Limited Generality:** Many beyond-Nyquist techniques are tailor-made for specific scenarios (sparse signals, point sources, etc.). They are not as universally applicable as the Nyquist-Shannon theorem, which works for any bandlimited signal. If the signal’s characteristics change (e.g. a spectrum that was sparse can become fully occupied), a sub-Nyquist system might need to reconfigure or revert to full-rate sampling to avoid information loss. This adaptability adds design complexity. Moreover, “going beyond Nyquist” often *does not scale well*: doubling the number of spectral components or increasing image complexity can dramatically increase the required measurements or the computation time. In contrast, Nyquist sampling scales linearly with bandwidth or image size. Thus, there are diminishing returns if one tries to push these methods into regimes where the signal complexity approaches that of a general signal.



In summary, while it **is possible to beat the Nyquist limit under the right conditions**, one must pay in other currencies: algorithmic complexity, stricter signal models, sensitivity to noise, and hardware sophistication. These trade-offs mean that classical Nyquist sampling is still used as a baseline in many systems, and the newer methods are applied only when the assumptions hold and the benefits outweigh the costs.


## Conclusion and Future Directions



**Is it possible to obtain frequency-domain information beyond the Nyquist-Shannon limit?** The evidence from modern research indicates **yes, but only with the aid of additional information or assumptions**. Techniques like compressed sensing, sub-Nyquist sampling architectures, and super-resolution algorithms have proven that one can reconstruct high-bandwidth or high-resolution signals from far fewer samples than the classical theory would require – in some cases achieving exponential reductions in sampling rate by exploiting sparsity [14]. Practical demonstrations in MRI, radar, communications, and optics have affirmed the feasibility of these approaches, fundamentally extending our reach beyond the prior limits. However, these are not free lunches; the Nyquist criterion itself remains unbroken in the absence of extra prior knowledge. What these methods really do is incorporate side-information (sparsity, spatial shifts, known models) into the sampling process, thereby **reducing the effective degrees of freedom** that need to be measured.



Looking ahead, the field is moving toward *smart sensing* paradigms – integrating analog preprocessing, adaptive sampling, and machine learning to decide when and what to sample. We can expect **future systems to increasingly combine classical and sub-Nyquist approaches**, using high-rate sampling when signals are highly complex, but switching to structure-exploiting compression when possible. The adoption of compressed sensing in commercial MRI and cameras is a bellwether that such techniques are maturing. Nonetheless, many research challenges remain open: how to make sub-Nyquist receivers as robust and real-time as their Nyquist counterparts, how to automatically learn signal structure for optimal sampling, and how to quantify the reliability of reconstructions in mission-critical applications. As one article put it, these advanced methods are still in their **infancy and plenty of theoretical and practical issues remain to be solved**, but they offer a “major opportunity” with substantial potential payoffs [36].



In conclusion, the Nyquist-Shannon theorem is no longer the unquestioned sampling dogma – it is now a *benchmark* that we know can be exceeded under the right circumstances. By embracing techniques that go beyond Nyquist, engineers and scientists can design sensors and systems that are more efficient, higher resolution, and more adaptive. The feasibility has been demonstrated; the task ahead is to refine these methods and extend their range of applicability. In the coming years, we can expect the **Nyquist limit to be routinely pushed aside** in specialized applications, heralding a new era where sampling theory meets intelligent signal models to transcend what was once thought unbreakable.

question: I want to measure the distance between two Bluetooth devices (A Master and a slave) using the corresponding RSSI value. Is there any algorithm or popular approach that maps RSSI values directly to distance?

sections.title: Report
sections.text:
# Estimating Distance Between Bluetooth Devices Using RSSI


## Overview of RSSI and Bluetooth Signal Characteristics



Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) is a measurement of the power present in a received radio signal. In Bluetooth systems (including Bluetooth Low Energy, BLE), RSSI is typically reported in decibels relative to 1 mW (dBm) and generally appears as a negative value (with values closer to 0 dBm indicating a stronger signal). Bluetooth devices can query the RSSI of received packets, making RSSI a convenient proxy for proximity [1]. In theory, as two devices get farther apart, the Bluetooth signal experiences path loss and the RSSI decreases (becomes more negative). This relationship provides the basis for estimating distance: a higher (less negative) RSSI suggests closer proximity, whereas a lower RSSI indicates greater distance.



However, RSSI is an inherently **noisy and variable indicator**. Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, where signals are susceptible to attenuation and interference. The propagation characteristics include **multipath** (signals bouncing off walls or objects and arriving via multiple paths) and absorption (e.g., human bodies and walls can absorb or block signals). As a result, the RSSI at a given distance can fluctuate significantly due to environmental factors. In fact, RSSI-based ranging is “**challenged by non line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions** such as shielding by human bodies and multi-path propagation, particularly in indoor environments” [2]. Obstacles and reflections cause the signal strength to deviate from the ideal distance-based decay, and the measured RSSI “**is not stable and usually fluctuates widely because of multipath effects and signal noise**” [3]. In practice, two devices at the same physical distance might report quite different RSSI values due to these effects. Moreover, different hardware may report RSSI differently (calibration offsets between Bluetooth chipsets can introduce bias). All these characteristics mean that while RSSI is *available* and *correlated* with distance, it is a **noisy distance estimator**, requiring careful modeling or additional processing to use effectively.


## Mathematical Models Relating RSSI to Distance



Several well-known mathematical models relate RSSI to distance. The simplest theoretical model is the **free-space path loss** formula (derived from the Friis transmission equation). In free space (with no obstacles or reflections), the received power decays with the square of distance. In logarithmic terms, this implies *RSSI drops by 20 dB per tenfold increase in distance* (or 6 dB per doubling of distance) in an ideal open environment. The general free-space RSSI-distance relationship can be expressed as:



PRX(d)=PTX+GTX+GRX−20log⁡10(4πd/λ),P_{RX}(d) = P_{TX} + G_{TX} + G_{RX} - 20\log_{10}(4\pi d / \lambda),PRX​(d)=PTX​+GTX​+GRX​−20log10​(4πd/λ),



which simplifies (for given antenna gains and frequency) to an empirical form $RSSI(d) \approx RSSI(d_0) - 10 \cdot 2 \log_{10}\frac{d}{d_0}$ in free space (since the path loss exponent is 2 for ideal line-of-sight) [4]. Here $RSSI(d_0)$ is a reference RSSI at some short distance $d_0$ (commonly 1 m). In more practical terms, many Bluetooth applications calibrate a reference RSSI at 1 meter and then assume a path loss model to estimate distance beyond that.



A more general and widely used model is the **log-distance path loss model** (also called the log-normal model when shadowing is included). This model recognizes that the environment affects the rate at which signal power decays. It introduces a **path loss exponent** $n$ (often denoted $\beta$) to characterize how quickly signal strength attenuates in a given environment. The log-distance path loss model in dB form is:



PL(d)=PL(d0)+10 n log⁡10 ⁣(dd0)+Xg,PL(d) = PL(d_0) + 10\,n\,\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{d}{d_0}\Big) + X_g,PL(d)=PL(d0​)+10nlog10​(d0​d​)+Xg​,



where $PL(d)$ is the path loss (in dB) at distance $d$, and $X_g$ is a Gaussian random variable (in dB) representing shadowing (random variability from multipath and obstacles) [5]. This can be rearranged to predict RSSI: since $RSSI(d) = P_{TX} - PL(d)$, we have



RSSI(d)=RSSI(d0)−10 n log⁡10 ⁣(dd0)−Xg.RSSI(d) = RSSI(d_0) - 10\,n\,\log_{10}\!\Big(\frac{d}{d_0}\Big) - X_g.RSSI(d)=RSSI(d0​)−10nlog10​(d0​d​)−Xg​.



Here $RSSI(d_0)$ is the RSSI at the reference distance $d_0$, and $n$ is the environment-dependent path loss exponent. The term $X_g$ (sometimes called **log-normal shadowing**) is typically zero-mean with some standard deviation $\sigma$ (e.g. $\sigma$ might be on the order of 2–10 dB, empirically measured). The path loss exponent $n$ is **key to modeling different environments**: in free space $n\approx 2$, but in real environments $n$ is higher (or occasionally lower) depending on obstacles and reflections. For example, empirical studies have found typical values such as $n\approx 1.6$–$1.8$ for **indoor line-of-sight** environments (slightly lower than free-space, possibly due to signal guiding effects), $n\approx 2.7$–$3.5$ in **urban outdoor** areas, $n\approx 4$–$6$ for **indoor obstructed** environments (walls, furniture), and around $n\approx 2$–$3$ in a typical **office** environment [4]. These values illustrate how much faster RSSI can decay in cluttered scenarios. By fitting the model (choosing $n$ and possibly a calibrated $RSSI(d_0)$), one can convert a measured RSSI into an estimated distance via the inverse of the above formula:



d^=d0⋅10RSSI(d0)−RSSI(d)10 n,\hat{d} = d_0 \cdot 10^{\frac{RSSI(d_0) - RSSI(d)}{10\,n}},d^=d0​⋅1010nRSSI(d0​)−RSSI(d)​,



ignoring the random $X_g$ term for the point estimate. This log-distance model (sometimes also called a **log-normal** model when $X_g$ is included) is **commonly employed** in RSSI-based ranging [6]. It provides a simple mathematical relation between RSSI and distance and is the basis of many Bluetooth distance estimation algorithms.



It’s important to note that the log-distance model itself is an *empirical* fit – the path loss exponent $n$ and reference RSSI must be determined through measurements or calibration. In practice, one would measure RSSI at one or more known distances and solve for $n$ (e.g., by linear regression on a log-log plot of distance vs signal power). The $X_g$ term captures the fact that even with a calibrated path loss exponent, instantaneous RSSI readings have significant scatter. Some implementations effectively average or filter RSSI to reduce the impact of $X_g$ (noise). When conditions are relatively controlled (line-of-sight, minimal interference), a log-distance model can yield a coarse distance estimate. **However, its accuracy is inherently limited** by the simplifying assumption that distance is the dominant factor affecting RSSI. In complex environments the model can deviate substantially from reality [7][8]. For instance, one study found the correlation between RSSI and true distance to be very weak (essentially “poor” correlation) in early Bluetooth experiments [8]. Even when the model holds on average, instantaneous readings can be off by many dB from the expected value, leading to large distance errors.



Beyond the basic log-distance formula, there are other empirical modeling approaches. Some researchers have extended the model with environment-specific terms – for example, adding fixed attenuation factors for walls or floors (the **multi-wall path loss model**). Others use piecewise or higher-order fits (e.g., a linear fit of RSSI vs distance within a certain range, or different $n$ values in different regimes). In the context of **Bluetooth-based COVID-19 contact tracing**, for example, researchers explored both a *logarithmic* path-loss model and a *linear* model to map RSSI to distance [9][10]. Interestingly, in one large measurement study, a simple linear model (assuming distance is linearly related to measured signal attenuation in the short range of interest) performed *better* than the classic log-distance model for distances up to a few meters [10]. This suggests that the optimal mapping from RSSI to distance is not universal – it may depend on the specific scenario and calibration. In summary, mathematical models like the log-distance path loss model are **popular and simple** approaches to RSSI-based distance estimation, but they rely on empirical tuning and can suffer reduced accuracy in the face of real-world radio irregularities.


## Machine Learning Approaches for RSSI-Based Localization



Given the limitations of analytical models, researchers have increasingly turned to **machine learning (ML)** to improve RSSI-based distance estimation and localization. Machine learning can potentially capture complex, non-linear relationships between RSSI readings and distance by learning from data, rather than assuming a simplified parametric model. There are two major categories of ML approaches in this domain: **fingerprinting methods** and **direct mapping/regression methods**.



**Fingerprinting** is a widely used approach for indoor localization. In a fingerprinting system, an offline training (or “radio map” construction) phase is conducted where RSSI values are recorded at many known locations (or distances). These RSSI signatures (potentially from multiple beacons) form a database. Then, during online use, the current RSSI measurements are compared to the stored fingerprints to find the best match and thus estimate the device’s location. While fingerprinting typically provides a full 2D/3D position estimate, it can also be used in a simpler form to estimate just the distance between two devices (for instance, classifying into “near” vs “far” based on RSSI patterns). **Machine learning** comes into play in the matching and interpolation of fingerprints. Traditional methods use $k$-nearest neighbors or probabilistic matches, but more recent systems leverage ML algorithms (SVMs, neural networks, etc.) to perform the fingerprint matching or regression. In fact, *fingerprinting-based approach is common in Bluetooth localization*, and multiple neural networks have been used as the matching algorithm to construct a positioning solution [11]. Neural networks can take a vector of RSSI values (from multiple transmitters or multiple channel measurements) and output coordinates or a distance estimate, effectively learning the radio map. The advantage of fingerprinting with ML is that it can implicitly account for environmental quirks (multipath, obstacles) by learning from real data. The drawback is the intensive site survey required and the fact that changes in the environment (or moving objects) can degrade the accuracy over time.



Another line of work uses ML for **direct distance estimation** (regression) without an extensive radio map of the entire area. In such approaches, the ML model is trained to output a distance given the RSSI (and possibly other features like RSSI variance, or multiple readings). For example, researchers have trained models using ground-truth distances obtained via more accurate systems (like Ultra-Wideband (UWB) ranging) as labels, and BLE RSSI values as inputs [12][13]. One study uses a subset of smartphones equipped with UWB to collect accurate distance measurements, and trains a **random forest** regression model to predict distance from RSSI; once trained, the model is distributed to other devices to improve their ranging accuracy [12]. Random forests (an ensemble of decision trees) can capture non-linear RSSI-distance relationships and were shown to improve distance estimation performance in that context. In general, classical ML algorithms like Random Forests, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and neural networks have all been explored for mapping RSSI to distance [14]. These data-driven methods often outperform the simplistic log-distance formula, especially when the training data spans the relevant range of distances and environmental conditions. For instance, studies have reported that ML models yield *enhanced accuracy for indoor localization* compared to model-based approaches [14]. As a concrete example, one system achieved a median distance error of about 0.5 m using a learned model (with multiple beacons) in an office environment [15]. Another experiment using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with several anchor nodes achieved localization errors on the order of 0.25 m in a 12×9.5 m room (with four BLE beacons) [16]. These results indicate that with sufficient training data and careful feature processing, machine learning can substantially reduce localization error.



It's worth noting that ML approaches often incorporate **feature engineering and filtering** to handle RSSI’s volatility. Many methods feed not just raw RSSI, but statistics (mean, median, variance of recent RSSI samples) or even sequences of RSSI values into the learning algorithm. Smoothing filters like Kalman filters or particle filters can be combined with ML as well – e.g., using a Kalman filter to pre-process the RSSI time series before input to a learning model, or using sequential models (like an RNN or LSTM) that inherently account for time dynamics. **Hybrid approaches** are common. For example, a short-range positioning design might apply a median filter to RSSI readings to remove outliers, use a moving average to stabilize the signal, and then feed the processed values into a deep neural network [17][18]. Some systems explicitly combine different signal metrics: an example is using both RSSI and the Bluetooth **Angle-of-Arrival (AoA)** (if available through specialized hardware) as inputs to a deep learning model, which can improve accuracy by adding angular information [18][19]. In summary, machine learning approaches for RSSI-based distance estimation range from neural-network-based fingerprinting to regression models trained on calibrated data. These approaches can capture complex propagation effects and often yield better accuracy and robustness than fixed theoretical models, at the cost of requiring training data and higher computational complexity.


## Challenges and Limitations of RSSI-Based Distance Estimation



Despite many advances, RSSI-based distance estimation faces significant challenges and limitations:


* **Multipath and Fading:** Indoors especially, radio signals take multiple paths from transmitter to receiver (reflecting off floors, walls, and objects). The superposition of these paths can cause **fading**, where small changes in position or environment result in large swings in RSSI. This makes the RSSI at any given moment an unreliable indicator of distance. As one paper notes, Bluetooth RSSI in an indoor scenario is **“corrupted due to severely multipath fading,”** producing spurious outlier readings [20]. Even with averaging, multipath can introduce bias (e.g. constructive interference might make the signal seem stronger at some non-intuitive distances).
* **Noise and Interference:** Environmental RF noise and interference from other devices can also perturb RSSI. Bluetooth shares spectrum with Wi-Fi and other 2.4 GHz technologies, so interference can cause RSSI fluctuations. Additionally, the **quantization and variability** in how RSSI is reported (different chipsets, antenna orientations, etc.) introduce noise. The literature emphasizes that RSSI often **fluctuates widely** over time due to these factors [3]. This instability necessitates filtering (e.g., low-pass filters, Kalman filters) to extract a usable distance signal, which in turn introduces lag and smoothing errors.
* **Calibration and Device Variability:** RSSI-distance models rely on calibration (e.g., knowing the transmit power and reference RSSI). In practice, different phones or Bluetooth modules have different antenna gains and RSSI reporting characteristics. A model calibrated for one device pair or one environment might not transfer well to another. For instance, experiments with various smartphones have shown each device has its own RSSI bias and sensitivity, requiring per-device calibration offsets [7][8]. Failing to account for this can lead to systematic distance estimate errors.
* **Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) Obstacles:** When the direct line-of-sight between devices is blocked (by walls, furniture, or human bodies), the RSSI can drop sharply or become more unpredictable. NLOS conditions can cause **shadowing** – a heavy attenuation that is not purely a function of distance. A person standing between two BLE devices, for example, might cause an extra 10–20 dB loss that a simple distance model cannot anticipate. This often leads to gross underestimation of distance (or overestimation, depending on scenario). Research in the context of BLE contact tracing has highlighted body shielding as a major issue: a human body between phones can make a close contact appear as if it were much farther based on RSSI [2]. At the same time, there is some irony with multipath: in cluttered environments, *reflected signals* can sometimes find a way around obstacles. One study observed that Bluetooth **multi-path propagation can partially reduce the effect of body shielding** by providing alternate signal paths in an indoor setting [21]. Even so, the distance estimation in such scenarios becomes highly unreliable.
* **Distance Range and Resolution:** RSSI changes more gradually at farther distances (e.g., going from 1m to 2m might drop RSSI by ~6–10 dB, but going from 10m to 11m might change RSSI by <1 dB in some models). Thus, the *resolvability* of distance from RSSI decreases as distance grows. At close range, small distance differences can produce noticeable RSSI changes, but beyond a certain range, RSSI may saturate near the noise floor. Bluetooth signals also have a finite range (practically a few tens of meters for BLE with typical device power), beyond which RSSI is extremely weak and distance estimation essentially fails. Most algorithms therefore are tuned for a certain distance interval (e.g., 0–10 m).
* **Accuracy vs. Environmental Dynamics:** Changes in the environment over time (people moving, doors opening, furniture rearrangements) can alter the RSSI-distance relationship. An installation that is accurate one day might degrade as the environment changes, unless the system can adapt or recalibrate. This is a challenge especially for fingerprinting approaches – the fingerprint database might need updates – but it also affects model-based approaches since the path loss exponent or reference RSSI might effectively change.



Because of these challenges, RSSI-based distance estimates are often **rough**. Academic studies frequently report errors on the order of a few meters in realistic conditions. For example, early evaluations of Bluetooth RSSI ranging found it had *limited accuracy*, with one study noting that even when usable, the accuracy was limited and not better than a few meters in many cases [8]. Another investigation that collected over 20,000 BLE RSSI samples concluded that *using BLE RSSI for distance estimation is very challenging* without additional information or techniques [22]. In summary, while techniques (filters, models, ML) can mitigate some of these issues, **environmental noise, multipath, and NLOS effects remain the dominant limitations** that prevent highly reliable distance measurements with RSSI alone.


## Accuracy Evaluation and Comparison of Methods



The performance of RSSI-based distance estimation methods can vary widely. Here we summarize and compare the accuracy reported for different approaches:


* **Simple Path-Loss Model:** Using a basic log-distance (or Friis) model with a single RSSI reading generally yields *coarse accuracy*. In open environments, one might achieve errors of 1–2 meters at short range, but in complex environments the error grows. Studies have shown that the error distribution tends to **worsen with distance** – e.g., as distance increases, the spread (variance) of error increases, sometimes dramatically [23]. If the environment is not explicitly calibrated, errors of several meters are common. For instance, using a generic path loss exponent (like $n=2$ or $n=3$) without calibration could easily lead to 5 m or greater error for actual distances of ~10 m [8]. Even with calibration, momentary RSSI fluctuations can cause large instant errors, so often multiple readings are averaged.
* **Filtered/Smoothed RSSI Approaches:** A step up in accuracy comes from filtering RSSI over time and smoothing the distance output. Techniques like taking a **moving average or median filter** over a window of RSSI readings can reduce random fluctuations. One reported algorithm applied a median filter (to reject outlier RSSI values) and then a Kalman filter on the derived distance; it achieved average errors on the order of *0.1–0.4 m* for distances up to a few meters [24]. These impressive sub-meter accuracies, however, were in controlled settings (short ranges of 0.5–3 m, line-of-sight). In more typical conditions, filtering provides some improvement but not a dramatic leap – you might reduce a 4 m error down to 3 m, for example, by smoothing out extreme readings. The **Kalman filter** is commonly used to fuse RSSI measurements over time; it can track a device’s distance by assuming a motion model and updating with RSSI inputs. Such filtering can significantly reduce jitter and accumulated error (one framework found a Kalman filter reduced error by ~8% compared to simpler averaging) [25]. Still, filtering primarily helps with noise and doesn’t fully solve bias from multipath or incorrect model assumptions.
* **Machine Learning and Fingerprinting:** Machine learning models, when well-trained, often show the *highest accuracy* in RSSI-based systems. By learning from extensive data, they capture subtle patterns. For example, a random forest model trained on BLE RSSI (with UWB-measured distances as ground truth) was able to improve distance estimates in an office setting compared to the classical model-based approach [12]. Similarly, neural network-based fingerprinting systems have achieved localization errors around 1–3 m in many indoor scenarios, which is significantly better than uncalibrated RSSI methods [26]. Some recent works with deep learning report sub-meter accuracy: one system combining RSSI with AoA using a deep neural network achieved position predictions with errors well under 1 m in a lab environment [19]. Another study that experimented with various AI models found that an RNN could localize within 0.25 m error (with multiple anchors) [16]. It should be noted that these high accuracies often assume *favorable conditions or multiple signals*. If only a single RSSI stream is used, purely data-driven methods might still struggle when a new environment differs from the training data. **Overfitting** is a risk – a model might perform excellently in the trained environment but poorly elsewhere unless robust features are used.
* **Comparative Findings:** One interesting comparison from a contact-tracing context showed that a **linear model** outperformed a log-distance model for distances ~1–2.5 m when both were individually tuned to the scenario [23]. The linear model yielded smaller error spread, suggesting that for that specific use-case (smartphones carried on the body), the attenuation vs distance was almost linear in the short range of interest. This underscores that no single method is universally best – the “winner” depends on environment, range, and how the method is optimized. Overall, adding **more information** tends to improve accuracy: using multiple anchors (for triangulation), multiple features (RSSI, AoA, etc.), or multiple training examples (fingerprinting) all help constrain the problem compared to relying on one RSSI reading and a simple formula. By contrast, methods that use just a single RSSI measurement and a generic model are the least accurate.



In practical evaluations, a rule of thumb is that raw RSSI-based distance estimates might only be accurate within **a few meters** under real-world conditions [8]. With careful calibration and filtering, one can often get that down to **meter-level accuracy** (1–3 m error). And with sophisticated machine learning or additional signal information, **sub-meter accuracy** is achievable in controlled settings [24][16]. It’s important to stress that these are statistical performance metrics (e.g., median error or RMSE); there will still be outlier cases with larger errors. Therefore, applications that require high reliability often incorporate **error mitigation strategies** – for instance, using proximity classifications (“near” vs “far” thresholding) rather than relying on exact distance, or combining RSSI with other sensors (like using inertial sensors or ultrasonics to cross-validate distance).



**Table 1** (hypothetical summary) illustrates a rough comparison of methods:






| Method | Typical Error (m) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple path-loss (no calib) | 5–10 m (varies) | Large error if environment unknown [8]. |
| Calibrated log-distance model | 2–5 m | After tuning $n$, still limited by RSSI variability. |
| Filtered RSSI (avg/Kalman) | 1–3 m | Reduces noise, moderate improvement [25]. |
| Fingerprinting (RSSI) | ~1–3 m | Requires site survey; 80% within 3 m reported [26]. |
| ML Regression (1 anchor) | ~1–2 m | Trained model on RSSI-distance, moderate complexity. |
| ML + multiple anchors/signals | <1 m | E.g. deep learning with RSSI+AoA, or multiple beacons [19]. |









Overall, **accuracy improves** as methods incorporate more information and processing, from a baseline of a few meters error down toward sub-meter in advanced systems. Yet, even the best RSSI-based methods must contend with the fundamental unpredictability of radio signals. Therefore, a recurring recommendation in research is to combine RSSI with other techniques when high precision is needed, or at least to apply robust statistical or learning-based corrections to counter the well-known challenges of RSSI-based distance estimation [27][28].

# Pulse-Per-Second (1 PPS) Signal Generation in GNSS Receivers


## Introduction to PPS and Its Role in GNSS Applications



A **Pulse-Per-Second (1 PPS)** signal is a sharp electrical pulse output that marks the start of each one-second interval. In GNSS receivers, the 1 PPS is usually a TTL-level pulse (often a few microseconds to a few hundred milliseconds wide) generated every second, aligned with the receiver’s best estimate of an absolute time scale (such as GPS or UTC time). This time pulse serves as a reference marker for timing and synchronization applications. For example, a GNSS-derived 1 PPS is commonly used to synchronize clocks in telecommunications, networks, and scientific instruments, because it provides a reference traceable to atomic clocks onboard satellites [1]. The leading edge of a GPS receiver’s 1 PPS is typically accurate to within tens of nanoseconds of the true UTC/GNSS second tick [1]. By itself, a 1 PPS signal only indicates the second boundaries; it is often combined with a time-of-day message or code to fully specify the current time. In practice, GNSS receivers make the precise timing capabilities of global navigation satellites accessible, allowing users to discipline local oscillators and synchronize distributed systems to better than microsecond or even nanosecond precision.



Beyond general timekeeping, 1 PPS outputs are vital in any application requiring coordinated timing. For instance, they are used to time-tag events, align sampling in distributed sensors, or serve as the reference for generating other frequency signals. Many navigation receivers include a 1 PPS output primarily for coarse synchronization, while specialized **timing receivers** focus on delivering highly stable and accurate 1 PPS for precision time transfer. In all cases, the generation of this pulse is intrinsically tied to how the receiver’s hardware and algorithms maintain a timebase aligned to GNSS time.


## Physical Generation of the PPS Signal in Hardware



Inside a GNSS receiver, the 1 PPS signal is derived from the receiver’s **internal clock**, sometimes called the local time clock (LTC). The receiver’s processor or timing hardware maintains an internal time counter driven by an oscillator (typically a crystal oscillator, TCXO, or OCXO). The GNSS positioning/time solution constantly estimates the offset (bias) between this local clock and the true GNSS time. Using that information, the receiver schedules the 1 PPS pulses in accordance with the GNSS second boundaries. In essence, the 1 PPS output is generated by the local clock, but **disciplined** or steered to match the timing indicated by GNSS [2]. There is no direct hardware connection to the satellite signals for producing the pulse; instead, the GNSS signals are processed to solve for time, and the solution guides the timing of a pulse generated from the receiver’s own oscillator [3]. Physically, a counter or timer in the receiver counts oscillator cycles and triggers a pulse when the count corresponds to an integer second of GNSS time (adjusting for any accumulated offset). The pulse is then driven out on a dedicated pin by a line driver or buffer circuit, producing the TTL-level 1 PPS electrical signal.



Because the local oscillator frequency is rarely a perfect sub-multiple of 1 Hz, there is typically a small **quantization error** in scheduling the pulse. For example, if a receiver’s clock runs at 10 MHz, one tick is 100 ns, so aligning the pulse to the exact GPS second may incur up to ±50 ns of uncertainty depending on how the ticks line up [4]. This effect is known as **sawtooth timing noise**: the 1 PPS may oscillate ahead or behind the true second by an amount up to one clock tick. Studies of dedicated GPS timing boards (e.g. Motorola M12+ or Synergy Systems SynPaQIII) show that their 1 PPS output error is uniformly distributed in a ±50 ns range due to this quantization principle [5][4]. In other words, if the receiver’s timebase runs at 10 MHz, the 1 PPS might jump back and forth within a 50 ns window each second as the timing offset is periodically corrected. Some receivers output a “sawtooth correction” value (in protocol messages) to describe the sub-tick offset of each pulse, allowing external equipment to achieve sub-nanosecond averaging by accounting for this sawtooth error [5][ttcenter.ir]. Physically, the generation involves standard digital hardware (counters, flip-flops, one-shot timers, etc.) to produce a sharp rising edge at the designated moment, and the pulse is then shaped (to desired width/polarity) and driven to the output connector.


## Role of Digitally-Controlled Oscillators (DCOs) and Line Drivers



There are two fundamental approaches to generating a aligned 1 PPS: **(a)** drive the pulse from a free-running oscillator but periodically adjust or “reset” its timing to correct the offset, or **(b)** actively lock the oscillator’s frequency and phase to the GNSS reference so that it runs in sync continuously. A **digitally-controlled oscillator (DCO)** refers to an oscillator whose frequency can be steered via digital control signals (for example, a voltage-controlled crystal oscillator driven by a DAC, or a direct digital synthesizer whose tuning word is set by the processor). In many high-quality GNSS receivers (and GPS-disciplined oscillators), the receiver implements a **digital phase-locked loop (DPLL)** that locks the local oscillator to the GPS 1 PPS timing. Essentially, the receiver measures its clock error relative to GPS time and then gently adjusts the oscillator frequency (via the DCO) to remove both the phase offset and frequency drift. Using this method, the 1 PPS pulses remain in phase with the GPS seconds without needing large abrupt corrections each second [7][8]. In effect, the oscillator is **frequency-locked** to GNSS time so that an integer number of its cycles is exactly one second on average, eliminating the sawtooth jumps. This is how “fancier high-precision receivers” achieve nearly jitter-free pulses [7]. The DCO (or the controlled oscillator) continually disciplines the local clock, and a line driver then outputs the pulse at each second mark with minimal error.



By contrast, simpler or low-cost receivers often do not discipline the oscillator frequency; instead, they let the crystal run at its natural frequency and generate 1 PPS by counting cycles and resetting the count each second based on the latest clock bias estimate. This **“flywheel and reset” method** results in small periodic timing adjustments – effectively nudging the pulse timing by up to one clock tick every second to re-align with GPS time. The result is the aforementioned sawtooth jitter of tens of nanoseconds [5]. The hardware to implement this can be as simple as a microcontroller timer that is reset or a pulse output pin triggered by an interrupt scheduled according to the bias-corrected time. This is sometimes described as using a **line driver with periodic re-initialization**: the output line is driven high at the start of each second as computed by the receiver, and any error in the previous second’s oscillator run time is accumulated and then corrected at the next pulse. While implementation is simpler, the residual timing jitter is on the order of the oscillator’s period (e.g. 20–50 ns for a 20–50 MHz clock) [9].



In receivers employing DCO-based control, the **line driver** still provides the physical output, but the heavy lifting is done by the disciplined oscillator. The receiver effectively creates a phase-lock between its local clock and the satellite system time. This can be implemented digitally: for instance, a DDS (Direct Digital Synthesizer) can serve as a DCO, generating a clock that is numerically steered to match GPS time. A digital PLL monitors the phase of the 1 PPS relative to the GPS second and adjusts the DDS frequency slightly to keep them aligned [8][10]. If the GPS signal is lost, the DPLL can hold the last frequency to free-run the oscillator (holdover mode), and then smoothly re-lock when GPS returns [8]. The advantage of the DCO approach is that it **removes long-term frequency error**, so the 1 PPS does not accumulate phase error and requires only minimal steering. In summary, a line driver provides the electrical interface for the pulse, but a digitally-controlled oscillator (managed by the receiver’s algorithms) often underpins the precise timing of that pulse in high-performance systems.


## Timing Synchronization and Disciplining Using Clock Bias Estimates



Every GNSS receiver solution includes an estimate of the receiver’s **clock bias** (the offset of the local clock from true GNSS time) and often a **clock drift** (frequency error) term. These estimates are obtained through the PVT (Position, Velocity, Time) calculation using satellite signals. The receiver leverages these estimates in a feedback loop to synchronize the 1 PPS output to GNSS time. In practice, this is typically done by a **servo loop or disciplining algorithm** that takes the measured time error (e.g. the difference between the receiver’s last 1 PPS tick and the true GPS second according to the navigation solution) and filters it to control the local oscillator. In a basic receiver with no oscillator steering, the clock bias estimate is used to decide how much to adjust the next pulse’s timing (e.g. schedule it a few nanoseconds earlier or later). More advanced receivers feed the bias (and possibly drift) estimates into a **digital phase lock loop** or even an optimal estimator (e.g. a Kalman filter) to continuously discipline the oscillator frequency [11][12]. The goal is to minimize the time error between the local clock and GNSS.



Classic GPS-disciplined oscillators often use a **PI control loop or Kalman filter** to steer a VCXO based on 1 PPS timing differences. The Kalman approach treats the local clock error as a state (with drift and noise) and uses measurements of that error each second to produce a control signal. Kalman filters have been widely applied in GPS timing for decades [12]. In recent years, modern estimation techniques like **unbiased FIR filters** have been explored as alternatives, offering potentially lower noise and no stability concerns when dealing with non-white or non-stationary noise [ttcenter.ir]. Whether using a simple PLL, a Kalman filter, or a predictive FIR filter, the principle is the same: the receiver continuously refines its knowledge of the clock bias and **disciples the oscillator** to cancel that bias. When properly tuned, this process results in the 1 PPS output staying very close to the true second boundaries, with only minor high-frequency dither remaining (e.g. thermal noise or sub-nanosecond fluctuations).



It is important to note that the intrinsic GPS/GNSS time itself has some uncertainty (on the order of several nanoseconds when averaging many satellites [14]), but this is much smaller than typical local oscillator drift. After removing ionospheric and other errors, GPS time solutions can achieve ~3–5 ns single-sigma precision under good conditions [14]. The dominant source of 1 PPS error in a receiver is usually the local clock and how it’s steered. An *undisciplined* clock will show a random-walk behavior in time error (since the oscillator wanders), whereas a *disciplined* clock will be kept on track. The sawtooth pattern mentioned earlier is a direct artifact of the synchronization method: when the clock bias is reset each second without adjusting frequency, the time error “sawtooths” between corrections [ttcenter.ir]. By disciplining frequency, that sawtooth can be largely eliminated. In summary, GNSS receivers use the estimated clock bias from PVT as feedback — either applying periodic phase corrections or continuously adjusting oscillator frequency — to synchronize the 1 PPS. The specific algorithms (simple averaging, PLL, Kalman, or FIR filters) are chosen to balance stability, noise reduction, and responsiveness in the face of oscillator noise and the inherent limits of GNSS measurement precision [12][ttcenter.ir].


## Comparison of PPS Generation in Different Classes of GNSS Receivers



Not all GNSS receivers are created equal when it comes to timing performance. **Commercial navigation-grade receivers** (such as those found in phones or consumer GPS units) typically use low-cost TCXOs and have update rates of 1 Hz. They will output a 1 PPS that is correct on average but may exhibit tens of nanoseconds of jitter and occasional larger jumps during signal acquisition or if the solution resets. These units usually do minimal or no frequency disciplining – the 1 PPS comes directly from the local clock with only epoch-by-epoch adjustment. For example, a common single-frequency timing module might specify ~±60 ns accuracy (99%) for its 1 PPS [15]. The jitter in such cases corresponds to the internal clock resolution (20–50 ns jitter is common when using a 16.367 MHz or 19.2 MHz clock, for instance) [9]. This level of performance is often sufficient for general synchronization (e.g. keeping a computer clock within a microsecond or so). Lower-end receivers also tend not to provide advanced features like sawtooth correction messages or holdover control; their 1 PPS may wander if the GPS signal is lost.



In contrast, **precision timing receivers** and GPS-disciplined oscillators employ higher-quality hardware and more sophisticated 1 PPS generation. These receivers often include oven-controlled crystal oscillators (OCXOs) or even atomic oscillator options, and they run advanced disciplining algorithms internally. The result is much improved stability and jitter. For instance, modern multi-band timing receivers (tracking multiple constellations and dual frequencies) can achieve time pulse jitter on the order of only a few nanoseconds. A state-of-the-art module like the u-blox ZED-F9T (a multi-band GNSS timing receiver) specifies an output time-pulse accuracy of ±5 ns (1σ) and jitter around ±4 ns [16]. Such performance is orders of magnitude better than older single-band units. One reason is that dual-frequency receivers can correct ionospheric delay and usually have access to more satellites, improving the stability of the time solution. Indeed, tests have shown that dual-frequency GNSS receivers exhibit lower time pulse jitter than their single-frequency equivalents [17]. Additionally, precision timing receivers always discipline their oscillators (often using an internal DCO or by steering an attached OCXO). They may operate in a fixed-position mode to eliminate position uncertainty and focus on time transfer, achieving sub-nanosecond long-term stability relative to UTC (averaging out the short-term jitter).



Beyond these, **scientific and metrology-grade GNSS receivers** (used in laboratories or for geodesy) might integrate with external high-end oscillators. For example, a timing receiver at a national timing lab could be locked to a hydrogen maser or cesium clock; the GNSS 1 PPS is used to gently steer that master clock, or vice versa. In these setups, the 1 PPS generation is part of a larger system (GPS common-view or two-way time transfer) and can achieve timing accuracy at the nanosecond or sub-nanosecond level when averaged [18][[18](https://benthamopen.com/contents/pdf/RPTST/RPTST-2-10.pdf#:~:text=between%20GPS%20time%20and%20UTC,5)%20ns]. However, even a basic commercial timing receiver today (e.g. Trimble, Septentrio, Microchip, or Oscilloquartz models) can meet the stringent requirements of telecom networks (e.g. 5G timing) with < 30 ns absolute UTC error and very low jitter, thanks to GNSS disciplining. As a point of reference, older GPS timing units like the Motorola M12+ had ~50 ns of quantization jitter [4], whereas newer multi-band units have reduced effective quantization to ~8 ns or better (by using higher internal clock rates, such as **128 MHz** in the ZED-F9T, which yields 8 ns resolution) [20].



In summary, **navigation-class receivers** prioritize positioning and use simpler 1 PPS generation with modest accuracy, whereas **dedicated timing receivers** and **scientific-grade systems** employ superior oscillators and control loops to deliver highly stable and accurate 1 PPS signals. The latter often support features like configurable pulse rates, reference frequency outputs (e.g. 10 MHz RF output disciplined to GNSS), sawtooth corrections, and holdover (to keep time even when GNSS is briefly unavailable). This gradation reflects a trade-off: added cost and complexity in hardware for vastly improved timing performance.


## Summary and Conclusions



Pulse-per-second signals from GNSS receivers provide a crucial bridge between satellite system time and local electronics. The **1 PPS output is physically generated by the receiver’s local oscillator** and timing hardware, synchronized to GNSS time by using the clock bias calculated in the navigation solution [2]. In basic implementations, the receiver schedules each pulse based on the latest time solution, effectively re-initializing the pulse timing every second to correct the clock bias. This approach yields a stable average second tick but with a sawtooth-like jitter on the scale of the oscillator’s period (tens of nanoseconds) [5]. More advanced designs incorporate **digitally-controlled oscillators and phase-locked loops** that continuously discipline the local clock to GPS, so that the 1 PPS emerges nearly jitter-free with long-term accuracy traceable to UTC [7][8]. The use of DCOs allows smooth frequency and phase adjustments, avoiding abrupt jumps and enabling holdover during GNSS outages.



We also saw that **filtering and control algorithms** are an integral part of PPS generation. Simple phase-lock loops may suffice for basic GPSDOs, but high-performance receivers often use optimized estimators (e.g. Kalman or FIR filters) to minimize timing error under real-world conditions [12][ttcenter.ir]. These algorithms ingest the measured timing offsets (the clock bias from PVT) and output control corrections to keep the local oscillator in sync with the satellite time signals. The result is that modern receivers can deliver 1 PPS signals aligned to GNSS/UTC within a few nanoseconds or better [16].



In comparing receiver classes, it is evident that **commercial navigation receivers** and **precision timing receivers** differ mainly in oscillator quality and control sophistication. Low-cost units output 1 PPS suitable for millisecond to microsecond-level synchronization, whereas dedicated timing receivers (sometimes called GNSSDOs for GNSS-Disciplined Oscillators) provide nanosecond-level stability and traceability. For applications requiring rigorous timing (e.g. synchronization of telecommunication networks, power grids, or scientific experiments), the investment in a precision GNSS timing receiver is justified by its disciplined 1 PPS performance. On the other hand, for general-purpose devices, the simpler approach still leverages GNSS’s global time to great effect, delivering a 1 PPS that is on average accurate to GPS time within ~100 ns [1] – a remarkable feat considering it essentially transfers atomic clock time down from space.



In conclusion, the generation of a GNSS 1 PPS is a synergy of **hardware clock generation and software/time solution discipline**. Whether through periodic resets or continuous oscillator control, the GNSS receiver ensures that each pulse-per-second tick is as close as possible to the true second, enabling a myriad of systems worldwide to stay synchronized with high precision. As GNSS technology and oscillator electronics continue to improve, we can expect even tighter integration (for instance, multi-band multi-system receivers with integrated mini atomic clocks) that push the accuracy and stability of 1 PPS signals to new extremes, further enhancing the foundation of global time synchronization.



**Sources:** The analysis above is supported by technical literature on GNSS timing. Key references include GNSS timing receiver studies (e.g. sawtooth noise analysis showing ±50 ns quantization error in older receivers [4]), manufacturer specifications of modern timing modules (nanosecond-level PPS accuracy [16]), and scholarly works on clock disciplining algorithms [12][ttcenter.ir]. These sources collectively describe how 1 PPS signals are formed, controlled, and improved across different GNSS receiver designs.

question: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?
