# Tree Covering in Ordinal vs. Binary Trees


## Introduction to Tree Covering Techniques in Succinct Structures



Tree covering is a technique for representing tree data structures in *succinct* form – using space close to the information-theoretic minimum while supporting fast navigation operations. The general idea is to *decompose* or *encode* a tree’s topology in a compressed way (often using bit sequences or small “micro-tree” blocks) so that queries like finding parents, children, or subtree sizes can be answered in constant time [1]. Succinct tree representations are crucial for handling very large trees (e.g. millions of nodes) efficiently. For example, large XML document trees with hundreds of millions of nodes can be encoded in just a few bits per node with fast query support [2], whereas naive pointer-based representations would require an order of magnitude more space. This has enabled applications in text indexing (suffix trees for computational biology and information retrieval), XML databases, and graph representations [[3]([[36](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=child%28x%2C%20i%29%20in%20O%28i%29%20time,time%20support%20for%20leaf%20rank))][4].



**What is tree covering?** In succinct data structures, *tree covering* often refers to breaking a tree into small components that can be precomputed or indexed for efficient queries [1]. Early succinct tree methods directly encoded the entire tree as a bit sequence (e.g. via parentheses or degree sequences), whereas the tree covering approach (pioneered by Geary et al. and others) hierarchically covers the tree with *mini-trees* and *micro-trees* to support a rich set of operations in constant time [1]. The covering technique creates small subtrees (micro-trees) of bounded size and stores a lookup table for each unique micro-tree shape. This hierarchical structure (micro-trees forming mini-trees, and mini-trees forming the whole tree) allows queries to zoom in on the relevant small piece and answer queries in O(1) time by table lookup [1]. The overarching goal is the same for any tree: represent the shape using ~2·*n* bits for an *n*-node tree (within lower-order terms of the optimum) and support operations like *parent*, *child*, *degree*, *subtree size*, *LCA* (lowest common ancestor), etc., in constant time.



In the following, we clarify the differences between *ordinal trees* and *binary trees*, and how tree covering and related succinct encoding techniques apply to each. Ordinal (ordered) trees are general rooted trees with any number of children per node (with a defined left-to-right order among siblings), whereas binary trees are a specialized case with at most two children (typically distinguished as left and right). While both types of trees admit succinct 2·*n*–bit representations, the encoding techniques and the tree-covering algorithm have some important differences in their application.


## Ordinal vs. Binary Trees: Definitions and Structural Differences



**Ordinal Trees:** An ordinal tree is a rooted tree in which the children of each node are *ordered* (first child, second child, etc.) [5]. There is no fixed limit on the number of children – a node could have 0, 5, or 100 children – but the sequence of children is significant. Ordinal trees are sometimes called *ordered trees* or *rooted ordered trees*. They are a very general model for hierarchical data (e.g. XML DOM trees, parse trees) where sibling order matters. Figure below illustrates a small ordinal tree and one way to encode it (balanced parentheses). Each node is represented by a pair of parentheses in the sequence, and the structure “( … )” nests according to the tree hierarchy [6].



*An ordinal tree (left) and its balanced-parentheses encoding (right). Each node corresponds to an opening “(” and a matching closing “)”.* [6]



**Binary Trees:** A binary tree is a rooted tree in which each node has *at most two children*, conventionally termed *left* and *right* child [7]. This is a restricted case of an ordinal tree – effectively an *ordered tree with at most 2 children per node*. However, a binary tree’s structure distinguishes between the left and right child positions. A node can have a left child, a right child, both, or neither. Unlike a general ordinal tree, if a binary node has only one child, it matters whether that child is in the left or right position.



Structurally, binary trees are often treated as *2-ary cardinal trees*: each node has two *slots* for children (left, right), which may be filled or empty. This means there are implicit “null” children for missing left/right. As a result, representing a binary tree’s exact shape requires acknowledging those empty child positions, which does not arise in a general ordinal tree (where a “missing” child just isn’t present at all). We will see this affects how we encode binary trees succinctly. Despite these differences, binary tree shapes and ordinal tree shapes have similar combinatorial complexity: both have a Catalan-number count of possible structures (approximately $4^n / (n^{3/2}\sqrt{\pi})$ for *n* nodes), so both need about $2n$ bits to encode in the limit [8].



**Navigational Operations:** In an ordinal tree, typical operations include: *parent(node)*, *child(node, i)* (the $i$th child), *degree(node)* (number of children), *next/prev sibling*, *subtree size*, etc. In a binary tree, the analogous operations are often a bit simpler: *parent(node)*, *leftChild(node)*, *rightChild(node)*, and sometimes *subtree size* or *depth*. Notably, “next sibling” in a binary tree would just mean the right sibling (if a node is the left child of its parent, the “next sibling” is the right child of that parent). The fixed maximum degree (2) in binary trees simplifies some queries – for example, finding the left or right child is a binary decision rather than searching among *i* children. On the other hand, ordinal trees require more general solutions to handle an arbitrary *i*-th child or enumerating all siblings.



The table below summarizes key differences:






| **Aspect** | **Ordinal Tree** (Ordered Tree) | **Binary Tree** (At most 2 children) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Children per node** | Arbitrary number *k* (0 ≤ *k* ≤ *n*) | At most 2 (left and right) |
| **Sibling order** | Defined order (1st, 2nd, … *k*th child) | Left vs. right position (at most two) |
| **Missing child** | Not applicable (no slot if no child) | Either left or right pointer can be null (must be encoded) |
| **Succinct encodings (examples)** | Balanced parentheses (BP) [6], LOUDS [eecs.tufts.edu], DFUDS [10], etc. | Adapted BP (with null markers) [eecs.tufts.edu], LOUDS (degree ≤2) [eecs.tufts.edu], bitstring for tree shape (1= node, 0 = null) [eecs.tufts.edu] |
| **Typical operations** | parent, child(*i*), degree, next/prev sibling, subtree size, LCA, etc. | parent, left child, right child, sibling (if any), subtree size, LCA, etc. |
| **Applications** | XML/HTML DOM trees, parse trees, file system hierarchies (ordered data) [2]; also general graph indices (trees as substructures) | Binary search trees, expression trees, Cartesian trees (RMQ structures), suffix tree topology (when binary encoding) [[3]([[36](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=child%28x%2C%20i%29%20in%20O%28i%29%20time,time%20support%20for%20leaf%20rank))], binary tries (e.g. prefix trees for dictionaries) |








## Succinct Tree Covering for Binary Trees



Binary trees, being a restricted form, often allow simpler or more specialized succinct representations. A classic approach to encode a binary tree is to perform a *preorder traversal*, writing a “1” bit for each node and a “0” for each null child (empty pointer). This yields a length `2n+1` bit sequence for a binary tree with *n* actual nodes (because such a tree has *n+1* null pointers) [eecs.tufts.edu]. For example, consider a binary tree with a root and only a right child. A preorder traversal would visit root (output `1`), then attempt left child (output `0` since null), then visit right child (`1`), then left and right of that child (both null: `0 0`). The bit sequence would be `1 0 1 0 0`. This sequence (sometimes called the *implicit null-pointer encoding*) is essentially a balanced parentheses encoding with an extra 0 at the end; if we drop the final 0, the remaining 2*n* bits form a balanced parentheses string that corresponds to the tree structure [eecs.tufts.edu]. Indeed, it’s known that there is a one-to-one mapping between such 1/0 sequences and binary tree shapes, and this representation is information-theoretically optimal (it can distinguish all $C_n$ Catalan-shaped binary trees) [eecs.tufts.edu].



**Balanced Parentheses (BP) for Binary Trees:** The balanced-parentheses technique can be adapted to binary trees, but we must handle the ordered pair of children. One approach is to integrate the null-child markers into the parentheses representation. Munro and Raman showed that one can encode an *n*-node binary tree in $2n + o(n)$ bits by a balanced parentheses string with slight adjustments [14][15]. In essence, each node is represented by an “(” and a matching “)” as in ordinal BP, but the relative positions of those parentheses capture the left/right subtree structure. In fact, in the BP encoding of a binary tree, if you read off only the “(” symbols in order, you list nodes in *preorder*; if you read only the “)” symbols in order, you list nodes in *inorder* [16][17]. This property is unique to the binary case – it arises because the closing parenthesis of a node appears after its left subtree but before its right subtree in the traversal, effectively signaling the node’s inorder position [16][17]. (By contrast, in a general ordinal tree, closing parentheses correspond to postorder.) Using this BP encoding, we can support constant-time navigation of binary trees: given a node’s position in the sequence, we can find its parent or either child in O(1) time by matching parentheses and using rank/select operations [18][19]. For instance, finding the left child corresponds to finding the next “(” after the node’s own “(”, and finding the right child means jumping to the “(” that comes after the node’s “)” which marks end of left subtree [16]. The details are intricate, but the key point is that the BP encoding can be interpreted in a way that preserves left/right distinctions and still uses 2*n* + o(n) bits [20][15].



**LOUDS and DFUDS in Binary Context:** The level-order unary degree sequence (LOUDS) and depth-first unary degree sequence (DFUDS) are general techniques, but we can consider their effect on binary trees. *LOUDS* encodes a tree level by level: for each node, it writes a sequence of 1’s equal to the node’s number of children, then a 0 to mark the end of that node’s children list [eecs.tufts.edu]. For a binary tree, each node has degree 0, 1, or 2, so the LOUDS bitstring will consist of patterns like `10` (for a node with 1 child) or `110` (for a node with 2 children) followed by `0`. For example, a node with two children produces `11 0`, one with one child produces `1 0`, and a leaf produces just `0`. The entire LOUDS sequence for an *n*-node binary tree has `n` zeros (one per node) and `n-1` ones (one per non-root edge), totaling `2n-1` bits (usually reported as 2*n* + o(n) with lower-order padding) [eecs.tufts.edu][21]. Navigation with LOUDS uses rank/select on this bitvector: the *i*-th “1” corresponds to the i-th child in level order, enabling constant-time *parent*, *first-child*, *next-sibling* queries [21]. In a binary tree, *first child* = *left child* (if exists) and *next sibling* = *right sibling* for a left child. Because each node has at most one next sibling, sibling navigation is simpler than in arbitrary-degree trees. In fact, Clark and Munro showed how to support parent/child/sibling in O(1) on LOUDS by using an extra constant-time rank/select structure [22]. The limitation of basic LOUDS on binary trees is that it doesn’t explicitly tell you if a node with one child is a left or right child in the original – but since for many binary tree algorithms the structural shape (ignoring which slot is empty) is enough, LOUDS works well, for example, in succinct *trie* representations and binary Patricia tries [eecs.tufts.edu].



*DFUDS* (Depth-First Unary Degree Sequence) is another succinct encoding that was introduced by Benoit et al. [10][23]. In DFUDS, a node of degree *d* is represented by *d* consecutive “(” symbols followed by a “)” symbol. All nodes are listed in *preorder*, with an extra initial “(” at the start of the whole sequence [10]. For an ordinal tree, this yields a 2*n* + O(n) length parentheses sequence. For a binary tree, degrees are ≤2, so a node with two children contributes “(( )”, with one child contributes “( )”, and a leaf contributes just “)”. DFUDS can represent binary tree shapes as well (it essentially also produces a balanced parentheses string of length ~2n). It supports constant-time *parent*, *child-rank*, *degree*, etc., by index calculations on the parentheses string [23]. However, like LOUDS, basic DFUDS doesn’t directly encode which specific child is left or right if only one child exists – it just encodes a single child in unary. In practice, for binary trees one can augment DFUDS or BP with an extra bit per node to indicate the presence of a left child (or right child) explicitly if needed. Even without that, many binary tree queries (parent, leftmost child, etc.) are still answerable.



**Tree Covering for Binary Trees:** The tree covering technique can be applied to binary trees as well, often yielding a simpler scenario. The Farzan–Munro covering algorithm (originally developed for ordinal trees) has a special behavior when restricted to binary trees: all the *micro-trees* in the cover are *disjoint* (non-overlapping) in the binary case [[24]([[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00573v1#:~:text=The%20Farzan%E2%80%93Munro%20tree,5))]. Intuitively, in an ordinal tree with high degree nodes, the cover algorithm may choose micro-tree boundaries that cause some nodes to serve as roots of multiple micro-trees (overlapping covers), but with binary branching this complication disappears – each micro-tree is an independent small subtree of the original. In fact, when you compress each micro-tree to a single super-node, the structure of connections between micro-trees is itself a smaller binary tree (sometimes called the *top-tier tree*) [[25]([[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00573v1#:~:text=The%20binary%20tree%20decomposition%20obtained,satisfies%20the%20following%20additional%20properties))]. Another simplifying property in binary trees is that if a node has two children that belong to different micro-trees (i.e. two outgoing edges from a micro-tree), then that node *must* be its own micro-tree (of size 1) [26]. In other words, a binary node with two large subtrees won’t be grouped into a larger component – it stands alone as a micro-tree because including either child would violate the size limit or the “at most one outgoing edge” rule [27][28]. This means the covering decomposition of a binary tree tends to create many small micro-trees (often just single nodes in cases of full branching) and relatively simple connections among them.



Despite these differences, a covered binary tree can be represented very compactly: we store the shapes of all distinct micro-trees (of size up to some *M*) in a table, and encode the top-tier structure using a standard binary succinct representation. Navigational queries first jump to the appropriate micro-tree (using the top-tier tree to reach the micro-tree’s root) and then use a precomputed micro-tree lookup to answer within that micro-tree. Since the micro-trees are disjoint, we don’t need complex backtracking pointers. This approach still uses ~2*n* bits overall and achieves constant time for operations like parent, left child, right child, etc., matching the performance of direct BP/LOUDS encodings [[24]([[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00573v1#:~:text=The%20Farzan%E2%80%93Munro%20tree,5))][[25]([[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00573v1#:~:text=The%20binary%20tree%20decomposition%20obtained,satisfies%20the%20following%20additional%20properties))]. The added benefit is that more complex queries (like subtree size or depth) can also be answered by leveraging micro-tree precomputation, and the approach extends to dynamic or labeled trees more easily. However, as researchers have noted, the pure tree-covering based structures often require many auxiliary pointers or index arrays (o(n)-sized) in practice, making them challenging to implement efficiently [31][32]. Recent work by Hamada *et al.* has aimed to simplify the tree covering representation (using BP as a base) to reduce these overheads and make practical implementations feasible [33][34].


## Succinct Tree Covering for Ordinal Trees



For general ordinal trees, the tree covering technique was a breakthrough that enabled supporting a *full suite* of navigational queries in constant time within $2n + o(n)$ bits [1]. Prior succinct representations (like BP, LOUDS, DFUDS) each supported most basic queries, but some operations were non-constant or required extra bits. For example, the original BP representation by Munro and Raman supported parent and depth in O(1), and *child-rank* and *child-select* in O(1), but an arbitrary *child(node, i)* query was O(i) in their initial scheme [35][[3]([[36](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=child%28x%2C%20i%29%20in%20O%28i%29%20time,time%20support%20for%20leaf%20rank))]. Similarly, LOUDS by Jacobson (1989) supported only parent, first-child, and next-sibling efficiently (initially in O(log n) bit-probe, later O(1) on RAM) [21]. The tree covering approach, introduced by Geary, Raman and Raman (2006) [[37]([[57](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=,Succinct%20ordinal%20trees%20with))] and refined by He *et al.* (2007) [38], overcame these limitations by a two-level decomposition:


* **Mini-trees:** The algorithm partitions the *n*-node ordinal tree into a set of disjoint *mini-trees*, each of size about *Θ(M)* for some parameter *M*.
* **Micro-trees:** Each mini-tree is further broken into *micro-trees* of size about *Θ(M’)* (with *M’* typically much smaller, e.g. O(log n)).



The covering is done in a way that any two mini-trees share at most one boundary node, and each micro-tree is a tiny tree that can be encoded by a few bits. Geary’s algorithm ensures each micro-tree has at most one “link” to the outside (apart from its root), which simplifies connections [39][40]. After covering, each distinct micro-tree shape (of ≤M’ nodes) is stored in a dictionary and assigned an *ID*. Then the entire tree can be encoded by recording the “topology” of mini-trees (how mini-trees connect) and a sequence of micro-tree IDs. This structure supports *all* typical operations (parent, i-th child, sibling, degree, subtree size, depth, LCA, etc.) in constant time [1][41]. Essentially, queries navigate from the top-level structure into one or at most two micro-trees and answer via precomputed lookup. For example, to find the 17th child of node *x*, the structure would identify which micro-tree contains node *x*’s children and use the micro-tree’s encoding (or a stored prefix-sum of degrees) to retrieve that child in O(1) time.



One difference in ordinal tree covering (compared to binary) is that ordinal trees can have *overlapping micro-tree roots*. Geary et al. describe that their cover algorithm may label some nodes as roots of multiple micro-trees (these are *preorder boundary nodes*, essentially demarcating where a subtree gets split between micro-trees) [42]. Farzan and Munro’s improved algorithm introduced the idea of *extended micro-trees* to handle these overlaps, ensuring that each node is contained in a limited number of micro-trees [[43]([[44](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=Geary%20et%20al.%20),1%20%28or)][44]. This added complexity isn’t needed in binary trees – as noted earlier, in a binary tree micro-trees became disjoint. But in a high-degree ordinal tree, a node with many children might be the connecting point for several micro-trees (one for each child sub-tree perhaps), requiring careful bookkeeping. Farzan and Munro’s cover guarantees O(n/M’) micro-trees total and limits the overlaps, at the cost of additional index structures [45][46].



In terms of encoding, ordinal trees are often represented by the **balanced parentheses (BP)** method in practice, so recent research has focused on implementing tree covering *on top of a BP representation* [47][[48]([[49](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol308-esa2024/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64.pdf#:~:text=3,that%20every%20micro%20tree%20corresponds))]. Hamada *et al.* (ESA 2024) propose a simplified tree covering for ordinal trees using BP as the underlying sequence, observing that every micro-tree corresponds to a contiguous parenthesis substring of the BP sequence [47][[48]([[49](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol308-esa2024/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64.pdf#:~:text=3,that%20every%20micro%20tree%20corresponds))]. They exploit this to avoid storing heavy auxiliary pointers: micro-trees can be located by their parenthesis interval, and standard BP operations (like finding matching parentheses or enclosure) can help navigate between the cover components. The result is a more *practical* structure that still achieves constant-time navigation but with far fewer extra bits than the original Geary et al. scheme [34][[50]([[51](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol308-esa2024/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64.pdf#:~:text=the%20data%20structures%20based%20on,knowledge%2C%20there%20is%20no%20practical))]. This is important, because although the theoretical space was $2n + o(n)$ bits, earlier tree-covering implementations had large hidden constants from many pointer blocks [31][[50]([[51](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol308-esa2024/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64/LIPIcs.ESA.2024.64.pdf#:~:text=the%20data%20structures%20based%20on,knowledge%2C%20there%20is%20no%20practical))].



**Summary of Operations and Complexity:** Both ordinal and binary tree representations via tree covering achieve *O(1)* time for basic navigational queries. Both use space close to $2n$ bits (plus lower-order terms). However, a notable difference is in the *degree* and *child* queries: in ordinal trees, finding the $i$th child may involve scanning within a node’s children in some schemes (e.g. BP had *O(i)* originally [52]), whereas binary trees only ever have to check up to 2 children. Tree covering methods remove even that linear scan by precomputing child pointers in micro-trees, so ordinal trees can get $O(1)$ child access as well [23]. Another difference is that ordinal tree operations include *nextSibling/prevSibling*, which are trivial for binary (a left child’s next sibling is just the right child) but non-trivial for arbitrary degree. Succinct ordinal structures handle sibling queries typically by a select on the bit sequence or using an array of child offsets [53][54].



From a use-case perspective, **ordinal tree succinct structures** are heavily used in areas like XML indexing, where an XML document tree (with elements having varying numbers of children) is represented in a compact form and queried (e.g. for XPath navigation) quickly [55]. They are also used in representing suffix trees or tries of large alphabets by treating each node’s outgoing edges as an ordered list [56][[37]([[57](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=,Succinct%20ordinal%20trees%20with))]. **Binary succinct structures**, on the other hand, show up in representing *Cartesian trees* for RMQ problems (the Cartesian tree of an array is a binary tree that can be succinctly encoded to solve RMQ queries optimally) [58][59]. They also appear in applications like *balanced parentheses sequences* (which themselves correspond to binary tree structures) and in succinct representations of *binary decision diagrams (BDDs)* and other graph structures that can be mapped to binary trees [60]. In computational biology, succinct *suffix trees* often rely on binary shape encoding at some level – e.g. a suffix tree can be transformed to a binary structure via parentheses encoding for traversal [[3]([[36](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=child%28x%2C%20i%29%20in%20O%28i%29%20time,time%20support%20for%20leaf%20rank))]. In full-text search and information retrieval, binary Patricia tries for dictionaries can be stored in LOUDS form (effectively a binary tree of bit strings) to enable fast prefix queries in compressed space [eecs.tufts.edu][eecs.tufts.edu].


## Conclusion and References



In summary, tree covering is a unifying technique enabling *succinct* (near-minimum space) and *navigable* representations for both binary and ordinal trees. Binary trees, with their limited degree, allow slightly simpler cover decompositions (disjoint micro-trees) and can often be encoded by a single clever bit sequence like BP or LOUDS with minimal overhead. Ordinal trees require more elaborate handling due to arbitrary degree – using unary degree sequences or balanced parentheses plus auxiliary structures, or the full tree-covering decomposition into micro-trees to handle all queries efficiently. Both approaches achieve the holy grail of tree succinctness: using about $2n$ bits of space and answering core queries in constant time [1][20]. This has opened the door to handling massive tree-structured data (from web graphs [62] to DNA suffix trees [56][4]) entirely in-memory and with speed comparable to pointer-based representations, but using an order-of-magnitude less space.



**References:** Key developments in this field include Jacobson’s 1989 introduction of LOUDS for static trees [eecs.tufts.edu], Munro and Raman’s 2001 balanced-parentheses representation for binary and ordinal trees [6][35], Benoit *et al.*’s 2005 work on DFUDS [10][23], and a series of papers on tree covering by Geary *et al.* (2006) [1] and Farzan & Munro (2009). Applications to XML and suffix trees were explored by Delpratt *et al.* (2006) [63] and by Munro *et al.* (2001) in suffix tree compression [[3]([[36](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220897517_Succinct_Ordinal_Trees_Based_on_Tree_Covering#:~:text=child%28x%2C%20i%29%20in%20O%28i%29%20time,time%20support%20for%20leaf%20rank))]. More recent work (Jansson *et al.*, 2007; Lu & Yeh, 2008) further optimized operations on these representations [64][65], and very recent research by Hamada *et al.* (2024) has revisited tree covering to make it practical in real implementations [34][47]. The combination of these advances provides a rich toolkit for representing both binary and ordinal trees in a memory-efficient yet query-efficient manner.

question: What are the leading approaches to automatic scientific paper review generation and what are their strengths and weaknesses?

sections.title: Report
sections.text:
# Automatic Scientific Paper Review Generation



Peer review is vital for scientific progress but faces severe bottlenecks due to reviewer shortages and increasing submission volumes [1]. This has spurred research into *automatic scientific paper review generation* – using AI to draft peer-review reports for research papers. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in understanding and generating academic text, yet producing high-quality reviews remains challenging because it requires deep comprehension of technical content, evaluation of novelty and soundness, and adherence to field-specific standards [2]. This report surveys the leading approaches (2021–2025) for automated review generation, covering key method categories, datasets, evaluation practices, applications, and a critical assessment of the state of the field with open challenges.


## Categories of Methods



Research on review generation has explored a range of techniques. The major approaches can be grouped into a few key categories:


### Fine-Tuned Large Language Models (LLMs)



One dominant approach is to fine-tune large pre-trained language models on corpora of paper–review pairs. By training on thousands of expert reviews, these models learn to emulate the tone and content of peer reviews. For example, *OpenReviewer* fine-tuned an 8-billion-parameter LLaMA model on **79,000** conference reviews, enabling it to generate structured, critical reviews that follow standard peer review templates [3][4]. Such specialized models can outperform general-purpose LLMs like GPT-4 in realism and criticality – OpenReviewer’s outputs were found to be more critical (less lenient) and closer to human reviewers’ rating distribution, whereas GPT-4 tended toward overly positive assessments [5].



Fine-tuned models can be trained to produce the common sections of reviews (summary, strengths, weaknesses, suggestions) in a coherent manner. For instance, models based on *BART* have been trained on academic review datasets to generate aspect-specific comments (e.g. remarks on originality or methodology) [6]. Yuan et al. (2022) introduced the **ASAP-Review** dataset with ~28k ML paper reviews and fine-tuned a model for aspect-conditioned review generation. However, they found the generated reviews were *less constructive and factual than human-written reviews* [[7]([[9](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375948754_ReviewRobot_Explainable_Paper_Review_Generation_based_on_Knowledge_Synthesis#:~:text=,)written%20reviews.)], highlighting a limitation of naive fine-tuning. In general, models that consume the entire paper at once tend to produce high-level, generic feedback, missing low-level details [8]. Recent works address this by increasing model size, training on more data, or incorporating additional structure. Overall, fine-tuned LLMs leverage their powerful language generation ability and domain knowledge learned from data, but they can suffer from **factuality issues** (e.g. misidentifying paper content) and **hallucinations** if not grounded in the paper’s specifics [[7]([[9](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375948754_ReviewRobot_Explainable_Paper_Review_Generation_based_on_Knowledge_Synthesis#:~:text=,)written%20reviews.)]. Ensuring the model truly understands the technical content and doesn’t just generate fluent-sounding but incorrect feedback is an ongoing challenge.


### Retrieval-Augmented Generation



To improve factual accuracy and content coverage, some approaches augment generation with retrieval of external information. The idea is to provide the model with relevant knowledge (beyond the paper text itself) so that the review can be more informed. The earliest system, **ReviewRobot** (Wang et al., 2020), pioneered a *knowledge-enhanced* approach: it was trained on OpenReview data and linked to multiple external knowledge graphs to inject domain-specific facts into the review [[7]([[9](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375948754_ReviewRobot_Explainable_Paper_Review_Generation_based_on_Knowledge_Synthesis#:~:text=,)written%20reviews.)]. By querying knowledge bases (e.g. citation networks, concept graphs) about the paper’s topics, ReviewRobot could include background or comparisons, aiming for a more *explainable* review that justifies criticisms with external evidence. This kind of controlled knowledge-driven generation is unique – ReviewRobot remained the only tool explicitly using *knowledge graphs* for reviews, and its performance depended heavily on the quality of information extraction feeding those graphs [9]. In practice, while knowledge augmentation can increase the specificity of comments (e.g. noting missing citations or comparisons [10][11]), it adds complexity. Errors in retrieved information or integration can lead to incorrect statements in the review.



A related thread is **retrieval of textual evidence**. Instead of structured knowledge graphs, some methods use IR techniques to fetch relevant text from the literature or the paper itself to ground the review. For example, multi-step *agent* frameworks like **SWIF2T** and **MARG** decompose the review task: one component (“investigator”) retrieves details either from the paper or external sources to enrich context, and another component (“reviewer”) uses that context to generate a focused critique [12]. This retrieval-augmented pipeline ensures that specific claims in the review are backed by evidence from the paper or prior work. Such approaches have shown improved specificity and factuality in feedback, as the model is forced to consider concrete details rather than rely on general knowledge [13]. The downside is higher system complexity and runtime – multiple stages (planning, searching, writing) must work in tandem, and failure in one stage (e.g. retrieving irrelevant content) can derail the output. Nonetheless, retrieval augmentation is a promising direction to make AI-generated reviews more *grounded* and trustworthy.


### Template-Based and Aspect-Based Approaches



Another category centers on using predefined structures or aspect guidance to shape the review. **Template-based approaches** explicitly enforce the standard format of peer reviews. A simple form is to prompt or train the model to output sections like *Summary, Strengths, Weaknesses, Suggestions*. Many conference review forms use such templates, and specialized models have been trained to follow these guidelines [4]. By structuring the task, template-based generation can ensure that key elements of a good review are present (e.g. a summary of the work, comments on originality, clarity, etc.). For example, OpenReviewer’s training data was formatted with conference review templates, so it reliably produces well-structured feedback covering all required sections [4]. Template-based methods can be implemented as pipeline generation: first generate a summary, then generate strengths, etc., which keeps the model focused. The strength of this approach is **coverage** and **clarity** of organization – it reduces the chance of the model forgetting to comment on an important aspect.



A related idea is **aspect-based summarization**: guiding the generation by specific review aspects or criteria. Research in peer review NLP has identified aspects like *Originality, Soundness, Clarity, Impact,* and models have been conditioned on these aspects. Yuan et al. (2022) introduced *aspect-aware review generation*, where the model generates text targeting a given aspect category [14]. For instance, one could prompt the system to “Comment on the paper’s originality,” then separately on methodology, etc., and combine these. This aspect-wise approach ensures the review touches each evaluation dimension. Indeed, some systems explicitly generate scores or sentiments for each aspect as an intermediate step [14], then produce textual comments accordingly. The advantage is **comprehensiveness** – covering each evaluation criterion systematically – and potentially more *controllable* output (since editors or users could request emphasis on certain aspects). However, a drawback is that aspect-by-aspect generation can become **fragmented** or formulaic. If not carefully coordinated, the final review may read like disjointed bullets rather than a cohesive critique. There is also a risk of focusing only on high-level aspect summaries and missing context; prior studies noted that models processing an entire paper often give overly high-level feedback [8]. Newer work like MARG attempts to mitigate generic, shallow comments by breaking the review into finer sections and increasing specificity [15]. In summary, template and aspect-based methods bring *structure and completeness*, but balancing structure with natural, detailed analysis is an ongoing research focus.


### Hybrid and Advanced Techniques



Recent approaches often combine elements of the above categories. For example, **multi-stage generation** frameworks use large LLMs in *planner* and *writer* roles (and sometimes a *critic/controller*) to simulate the human review reasoning process [12]. They might first summarize the paper, then explicitly ask targeted questions (retrieval) and finally generate a review, thus mixing template (stages), retrieval, and LLM generation. Other works explore **human-in-the-loop** setups, where an AI draft is edited by humans or vice versa. There is also interest in using *reinforcement learning* or preference modeling to fine-tune review generators based on human quality judgments (to address the fact that maximization of BLEU/ROUGE may not align with what makes a review useful). Overall, the state-of-the-art is trending toward *hybrid systems* that leverage powerful LLMs but also include explicit reasoning or retrieval steps to ensure factual accuracy and depth.


## Common Datasets and Benchmarks



Progress in this field has been driven by the creation of peer-review datasets and benchmark tasks. Early on, data scarcity was a major hurdle – peer reviews were not widely available. The **PeerRead** corpus (Kang et al., 2018) was a seminal contribution, releasing the first public dataset of scientific peer reviews [16]. PeerRead collected ~10k reviews (with scores and decisions) from venues like ACL, NeurIPS, and ICLR, along with the submitted papers, enabling initial studies on review analysis and prediction. This provided a foundation, but truly large-scale corpora for generation only emerged more recently.



Key datasets and benchmarks since 2021 include:


* **ASAP-Review (Yuan et al., 2022):** A large collection of about 28,000 peer reviews from machine learning conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS), with aspect annotations. It was introduced to facilitate aspect-specific review comment generation [17]. Models trained on ASAP-Review were used to generate full reviews and to predict aspect scores. This remains one of the largest academic review datasets (focusing on CS/ML domain).
* **Yes-Yes-Yes / ACL Rolling Review (2022):** The “Yes-Yes-Yes” dataset (van der Dycke et al., 2022) contains reviews from the ACL Rolling Review in 2021 (an open-review repository for NLP conferences). It captures the review text and final recommendations (yes/no decisions) for NLP papers [18]. This effort was part of a movement toward *open peer review data* in the ACL community.
* **F1000Research Reviews (F1000RD, 2022):** Kuznetsov et al. (2022) released a corpus of reviews from the *F1000Research* platform, covering multiple domains (beyond CS) [18]. F1000Research publishes reviewer reports openly alongside articles, providing a rich resource for varied review styles. This was notable as a multi-disciplinary dataset (breaking out of only CS/AI conference data).
* **NLPeer (2023):** An aggregated dataset by van der Dycke et al. (2023) that *combines* the ACL Rolling Review, COLING, CoNLL, and F1000Research peer review data into one large benchmark [19]. NLPeer aimed to be a comprehensive peer review dataset spanning conference and journal reviews, useful for training robust models and evaluating generalization across venues.
* **ORB (Szumega et al., 2023):** A dataset including OpenReview-based reviews (hence “OR”) along with paper *accept/reject* decisions and numeric scores. ORB was intended for both review generation and submission decision prediction [20]. However, documentation of ORB is limited, and it’s a bit less commonly used compared to the above.
* **ReviewRC & Others:** Researchers have also created specialized evaluation sets. For instance, *Review Revision MCQ (RR-MCQ, 2024)* is a multiple-choice questionnaire dataset for quickly testing an LLM’s reviewing capability [21]. Liu and Shah (2023) prepared a test set of papers with *planted errors* to see if an AI reviewer can catch factual mistakes [22]. Additionally, datasets for related subtasks like **Pragmatic Tagging** of review comments (PragTag 2023) were released to label the function of each sentence (praise, criticism, suggestion, etc.) [23] – useful for training aspect-aware models.



Collectively, these datasets have become standard benchmarks. Automatic review generation methods are evaluated on held-out sets of such corpora, comparing the AI-generated review to the human-written ground truth review for a given paper. Many works report results on ASAP-Review and segments of the OpenReview/ACL datasets [17][24], enabling head-to-head comparison of different model architectures on the same testbed. A persistent challenge, however, is that these datasets are still relatively small by LLM standards (tens of thousands of examples) and often domain-specific (mostly CS/AI papers), which limits the ability of models to generalize to other fields.


## Evaluation Methods



Evaluating the quality of an automatically generated peer review is complex, as it involves both *textual quality* and *substantive assessment*. Researchers use a mix of **automatic metrics** and **human evaluation**:


* **Automatic Metrics:** Standard NLG metrics like BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR are used to measure overlap between the generated review and the reference review written by a human. For example, Yuan et al. (2022) report ROUGE scores to assess how closely their model’s output matched actual reviews [[7]([[9](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375948754_ReviewRobot_Explainable_Paper_Review_Generation_based_on_Knowledge_Synthesis#:~:text=,)written%20reviews.)]. Some works also use BERTScore or embedding-based similarity to capture semantic overlap. These metrics provide a rough quantitative gauge of relevance and coverage. In addition, aspect-specific evaluations are employed: e.g., measuring if the model mentioned the same key points or aspects (originality, etc.) as the human reviewer. *Content fidelity* checks – whether the review contains factual errors about the paper – are increasingly important. Automatic factuality metrics (similar to those in summarization tasks) or even a retrieval-augmented checker can be used to flag potential hallucinations in the review. While automatic metrics are convenient, their limitations are well-known: a review can have low ROUGE to the reference yet still be valid (since reviews are subjective, not one-to-one summaries), and conversely a review might get decent overlap scores but miss critical issues.
* **Human Evaluation:** Given the shortcomings of automatic metrics, nearly all recent studies include human judgments of review quality. Typically, experts or authors are asked to rate the AI-generated reviews on dimensions such as **helpfulness, specificity, accuracy, coherence, and coverage**. For instance, Robertson (2023) and Liang et al. (2023) compared GPT-4-generated reviews to actual human reviews by asking humans to blind-evaluate their helpfulness [25]. Interestingly, they found GPT-4’s feedback was roughly on par with human reviews in terms of helpfulness, but it lacked *specific actionable feedback* and often failed to comment on low-level details [25]. Such human studies highlight where AI reviews fall short (e.g., being too generic). In another evaluation, Zhu et al. (2023) had domain experts judge whether generated reviews identified the correct strengths and weaknesses of the paper; the results showed current models often miss the novelty aspect when criticizing, and make inconsistent recommendations [26]. Human evaluation is also used to directly compare methods: for example, a study of SWIF2T versus baselines included both automatic similarity measures and human ratings for specificity, comprehension, and overall usefulness [27]. SWIF2T’s AI feedback was frequently preferred over even human-written feedback in certain cases, demonstrating the potential of carefully designed systems [13].



It’s worth noting that evaluation of review generation is still evolving. Unlike straightforward summarization, a “good” peer review may not align closely with any single reference text. Thus, there is growing emphasis on *agreement with human reviewers on key points* (e.g., does the AI identify the same major flaws?) and on *downstream usefulness* (e.g., would the authors find the AI review helpful in improving their paper?). Some works propose task-specific evaluations: e.g., measuring how well an AI’s proposed review score or decision matches the actual outcome, or whether an author’s revision in response to an AI review leads to improvements. These complementary evaluations go beyond surface text similarity to assess the *impact* of the review. In summary, current practice combines automated metrics for breadth with human judgement for depth, ensuring that improvements in models translate to genuinely better peer feedback.


## Applications and Use Cases



Automatic review generation has several envisioned applications in the academic publishing process:


* **Peer Review Assistance:** Perhaps the most immediate use is helping human reviewers. An AI system could draft an initial review that a human then edits, saving time on routine summary or writing. For example, a reviewer pressed for time might use a model to generate a first draft of the review after reading the paper, then refine it with their own insights. This is analogous to writing assistance in other domains. Early experiments with GPT-4 in the loop showed that while it can provide a decent starting point, a human is needed to inject actionable specifics [25]. Still, such assistive tools could lower reviewers’ workload and reduce fatigue.
* **Author Feedback and Pre-submission Review:** Another use case is providing *authors* with an automated “review” of their manuscript before official submission. This can highlight likely weak points and suggestions for improvement. Systems like OpenReviewer are explicitly designed for this: given a paper draft, OpenReviewer generates a peer-review style critique to give the author rapid, constructive feedback for revision [28]. This is positioned **not** to replace actual peer review, but to allow authors to catch issues early (like an AI-based writing coach specific to research papers). Such feedback could be integrated into preprint servers or journal submission portals as an optional service. For instance, a preprint platform could offer an “AI review” on upload, summarizing the paper’s contributions and potential concerns, helping authors to iterate.
* **Editorial Triage:** Journal editors or conference program chairs might use automated reviews to assist in decision making. In a scenario with hundreds of submissions, an AI-generated review (or at least a summary with key predicted pros/cons) could help flag papers that need careful human attention. This could work in conjunction with automated technical checks. However, given reliability concerns, this is likely to be a semi-automated use: the AI provides an additional perspective, but editors wouldn’t rely on it solely for accept/reject decisions at this stage.
* **Meta-Review and Review Summarization:** Beyond generating individual reviews, AI can help in writing *meta-reviews* or summaries of multiple reviews. Some recent research focuses on summarizing several peer review reports into a coherent meta-review for area chairs [29]. This is closely related to review generation and uses many of the same techniques (it can be seen as “second-order” review generation). Additionally, tools could aggregate common points from past reviews of similar papers – effectively a retrieval-augmented summary of known feedback on a topic – to assist new reviewers or authors.
* **Educational Use:** For new researchers, seeing an AI-generated review of a sample paper (especially if accompanied by explanations) could be a learning tool. It might illustrate how to structure a review or what kind of critiques are typical. Care would be needed to ensure the AI’s review is high-quality, to not teach bad habits or errors.



It’s important to note that, while these applications are promising, they also raise **ethical and practical questions**. For instance, if authors begin optimizing for AI-generated feedback, this could introduce new dynamics in writing. Additionally, there are concerns about how using AI in peer review might affect fairness and accountability (e.g., an AI might inadvertently reveal information or carry biases). Thus, current consensus is that AI review generators serve *assistive* roles – providing rapid insights and second opinions – rather than acting as independent reviewers. Indeed, OpenReviewer’s creators emphasize it “is not intended to replace human peer review” [30], but to complement it by giving quick feedback to authors.


## Strengths and Weaknesses of Major Approaches



Each of the major technical approaches for review generation comes with its own advantages and limitations:


* **Fine-Tuned LLMs:** *Strengths:* These models leverage powerful pre-trained knowledge and can produce fluent, well-structured text. Fine-tuning on domain-specific review data helps them adopt the tone and criteria of real reviewers [3]. They can discuss a paper holistically and often correctly identify generic strengths and weaknesses due to broad training knowledge. *Weaknesses:* Without additional grounding, fine-tuned models may hallucinate facts or overlook nuances of the specific paper. They often default to safe, high-level critiques and may miss domain-specific issues that weren’t prominent in training data [8]. General LLMs like GPT-3/4 show capability, but have a tendency toward overly positive or uncritical reviews if not specially tuned [5]. Fine-tuned models also require a large, high-quality corpus of reviews for training – which is scarce in many fields – and they struggle with *novelty assessment* and detailed error detection, as observed in evaluation studies [31]. In short, they’re good at mimicking the style of reviews, less so at guaranteeing the substance is accurate and insightful.
* **Retrieval- or Knowledge-Augmented Methods:** *Strengths:* By bringing in external knowledge (papers, citations, data), these methods can produce more *informed and specific* reviews. They are better at factual correctness, e.g. pointing out if important prior work is missing, since they can look it up. Knowledge graphs and literature retrieval help address the knowledge cutoff of the model and provide evidence for claims [[7]([[9](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375948754_ReviewRobot_Explainable_Paper_Review_Generation_based_on_Knowledge_Synthesis#:~:text=,)written%20reviews.)]. This often results in reviews that give concrete suggestions (“the paper should compare to X method” or “missing citation of Y”) which are highly valued by authors. *Weaknesses:* The complexity of these systems is a major drawback. They rely on additional modules (search engines, databases, extraction pipelines), which can fail or return irrelevant info, leading the model astray. The quality of the generated review hinges on the retrieved content – garbage in, garbage out [9]. Integrating the retrieved facts into coherent text is also non-trivial; models might just stick a cited fact awkwardly. Moreover, maintaining an up-to-date knowledge base or access to literature can be challenging (especially outside well-indexed fields). Finally, the evaluation of such systems is tricky: a review might be factual but could focus too much on comparison and miss other aspects, for example. Thus, while retrieval-augmented approaches enhance factual grounding, they must be carefully engineered to truly improve overall review quality.
* **Template/Aspect-Based Approaches:** *Strengths:* Enforcing a template ensures completeness and clarity. These methods excel at covering all the required points in a structured manner [4]. Aspect-based generation can ensure that important dimensions (originality, methodology, etc.) are each addressed, aligning the output with review rubrics used by conferences. Template-based outputs are also easier to read and follow, since they mirror human-written review formats. Additionally, by focusing separately on each aspect, the generation can be made more *controllable* – one can tweak or update one section (e.g., the summary) without affecting others. *Weaknesses:* The risk is that the review becomes mechanical. If a model generates each section independently or with a rigid template, the prose might lack a natural flow and the insights might remain surface-level for each aspect. Aspect-specific comments can sometimes be redundant (“repeats summary in strengths and weaknesses in a slightly different way”). There’s also evidence that purely aspect-driven models tend to focus on obvious, high-level points and may neglect *interactions between aspects* (e.g., how methodology issues impact the validity of results) [8]. In short, while template/aspect methods guarantee structure, they can sacrifice depth and cohesiveness. The best systems try to get the “best of both” by using aspect prompts but still letting the model write a nuanced narrative (perhaps via a planner that weaves aspects together).
* **Multi-Stage / Decomposed Systems:** *Strengths:* Breaking the task into stages (understand -> plan -> critique -> refine) can lead to more *focused and high-quality feedback*. Recent multi-LLM approaches demonstrate that this reduces generic comments – for example, MARG’s multi-component process yielded more specific, higher-quality remarks than one-shot generation [15]. Decomposition allows each model or stage to specialize (one might be good at summarization, another at error finding). It also offers transparency; e.g., the system’s intermediate outputs (answers to questions about the paper) can be inspected to trace why a certain critique was made. *Weaknesses:* However, these pipelines are only as strong as their weakest link. If the planner chooses a poor strategy or the question-answering stage misses a key detail, the final review suffers. They are computationally heavy (running multiple LLM calls per paper) and harder to implement. There’s also the challenge of *evaluation and tuning* – optimizing multiple components jointly for the best review quality is non-trivial. While promising, such complex systems have many moving parts that can go wrong, and they currently require careful prompting or even hand-crafted rules to work reliably [12]. As LLM capabilities improve, some of this complexity might be reduced (a single model might eventually handle multiple sub-tasks internally), but for now multi-stage designs trade simplicity for gains in specificity and correctness.


## Current State and Open Challenges



Automatic review generation has made significant strides in the past few years, but it is **far from a solved problem**. The field currently stands at a point where AI can produce *passable* reviews under certain conditions, yet several open challenges remain before these systems can be fully trusted in real peer review workflows.



**Quality and Trustworthiness:** The foremost challenge is ensuring the *quality* of AI-generated reviews – not just in fluency, but in insight and accuracy. Studies that directly compared LLM-generated reviews to expert reviews reveal some critical gaps. Shin et al. (2025) found that while an LLM might correctly summarize a paper and identify some pros/cons, it **“significantly overlooks novelty assessment”** and struggles with balanced criticism [31]. Models also often fail to provide a decisive recommendation that aligns with their review text (producing poor acceptance decisions) [31]. In other words, current models might catch the *surface* features (e.g., clarity of writing) but miss deeper issues like subtle methodological flaws or the true novelty of the work. This raises concerns about trust: an author receiving an overly generic but polite AI review might be misled about the adequacy of their contribution.



**Data Limitations:** High-quality training data is limited. Even though new datasets (ACL, F1000, etc.) have expanded the pool, there is a dearth of *diverse and large-scale* review corpora. Many fields (e.g., medical, physics, humanities) do not have readily available peer review text for AI to learn from. The existing datasets are also noisy – reviews can be highly variable, and some contain off-topic or very brief comments that are not useful to mimic. **Inadequate data** remains a barrier, noted by Lin et al. (2023) as a primary difficulty for the field [32]. This also ties into generalization: models trained on CS conference reviews may not perform well on, say, biology journal papers, which have different styles and standards.



**Understanding Complex Content:** Reviews require deep understanding and reasoning. While LLMs can parse a well-written paper’s gist, they often falter on complex logical reasoning and math. For instance, verifying whether a theorem’s proof is correct or if an experiment’s design is flaw-free is far beyond current AI. Lin et al. highlight *flawed deep logical reasoning* as a core technical challenge in automated review [32]. An AI might not reliably detect subtle errors in a proof or might accept the authors’ claims at face value when a human expert would question them. Additionally, handling figures, tables, and detailed results (e.g. correctly interpreting a graph) is still difficult for text-based models, though some research is looking at multi-modal capabilities for PDF understanding.



**Integration and Interaction:** Another open problem is how AI review tools interact with humans in the loop. **Human–computer interaction** issues were noted as a barrier [32]. If an AI is used to draft reviews, what is the best interface for a human to guide or correct it? How do we prevent over-reliance on the AI or complacency (e.g., a human reviewer just lightly edits the AI output without critical thought)? There is also the question of *protocol*: If an AI assists in writing a review for an actual conference, should that be disclosed? Some venues currently forbid uncredited AI-generated content in reviews due to ethical considerations. Developing guidelines and best practices for responsible use of AI in peer review is an ongoing conversation.



**Ethical and Practical Concerns:** With the prospect of “AI reviewers”, concerns arise about fairness, biases, and accountability. An AI might inadvertently carry biases present in its training data – for example, being harsher on unconventional research directions simply because training reviews tended to be negative on out-of-mainstream ideas. Moreover, there are *ethical issues* around automating a task that significantly impacts careers. Lin et al. (2023) discuss possible moral questions, noting that any fully automated reviewing pipeline must be approached cautiously [32]. For now, the consensus is that AI should assist rather than replace human judgment. Another practical concern is **gaming the system**: if authors know the criteria the AI optimizes for, they might tailor papers to please an AI reviewer (which could be different from what makes a genuinely good paper). This cat-and-mouse dynamic has been raised in discussions about automated metrics and could extend to AI reviewers as well.



**Evaluation Paradigms:** Finally, evaluating progress reliably is challenging. There is not yet a single agreed-upon benchmark that truly captures “review quality.” Human evaluation is expensive and not standardized across studies – one might rate helpfulness, another specificity, etc. This makes it hard to compare systems. Creating a robust evaluation framework (perhaps including community-wide shared tasks or competitions) is a needed step to drive the field forward.



In conclusion, the field of automatic scientific paper review generation has advanced rapidly, leveraging modern NLP techniques to tackle an age-old problem. We now have systems that can produce review drafts that *resemble* those written by humans, especially for well-studied domains [5]. These systems are already useful in applications like assisting authors and reviewers with initial feedback. However, fully autonomous reviewers are not ready for prime time – there remain significant hurdles in understanding, reasoning, and trust. As research continues, focusing on improving the *depth* of understanding (not just surface-level summarization), expanding to more domains, and carefully integrating AI into the human peer review process will be crucial. The challenges of limited data, parsing technical content, and ensuring ethical use [32] are active areas of investigation. In the foreseeable future, AI and human reviewers will likely **“coexist in a reinforcing manner”**, with AI shouldering some of the load and humans providing oversight [32]. Such collaboration, rather than full automation, appears to be the pragmatic path toward alleviating the pressures on the peer review system while maintaining its integrity and quality.

question: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models?
